articles.title: Why Saudi Arabia is back at war in Yemen
articles.body:
Why Saudi Arabia is back at war in Yemen
A major escalation in Yemen has brought Saudi Arabia back into military confrontation with the Iran-backed Houthis, ending years of relative calm as tensions rise across the Middle East.
Much of the fighting has taken place along Yemen’s Red Sea coast and around the strategically important Bab el-Mandeb Strait, following major Houthi territorial gains and a Saudi-backed counteroffensive. The waterway has become increasingly important as the US-Israeli war on Iran disrupts regional trade and energy routes, particularly through the Strait of Hormuz.
Who are the Houthis?
The Houthis, formally known as Ansar Allah, are a Zaydi Shia armed and political movement that emerged in northern Yemen in the 1990s. Their traditional stronghold is the mountainous province of Saada along the border with Saudi Arabia. The movement emerged in opposition to Yemen’s central government and Saudi and US influence.
They now control much of northern and western Yemen, including areas where most of the country’s population lives.
The Houthis are backed by Iran and describe themselves as part of the Tehran-aligned “Axis of Resistance.”
Over years of fighting, the group has developed an arsenal of ballistic and cruise missiles and drones capable of striking Saudi Arabia and ships in the Red Sea.
How did Yemen’s civil war begin?
In 2014, the Houthis seized Sanaa and forced the internationally recognized Yemeni government from the capital. Saudi Arabia intervened the following year at the head of a military coalition seeking to restore the government and counter Iran’s growing influence.
Years of fighting failed to dislodge the Houthis. A UN-brokered truce in 2022 sharply reduced hostilities and cross-border attacks, and although it formally expired after six months, hostilities remained limited for several years.
Fighting resumed in July, when Yemeni government forces struck the runway at Sanaa airport to prevent an Iranian plane carrying a Houthi delegation from landing. The delegation was returning from the funeral of Iranian Supreme Leader Ali Khamenei, who was killed in the opening US-Israeli strikes on the Islamic Republic at the end of February. The Houthis blamed Saudi Arabia for the airport strike, declared the de-escalation over, and retaliated against the kingdom.
The conflict escalated further in September, when the Houthis made their largest territorial gains in years, taking Mocha and key positions along the Red Sea coast and around Bab el-Mandeb. The group also claimed to have effectively encircled Taiz, a major city linking northern and southern Yemen with the Red Sea coast, after cutting a vital supply route to the southern port city of Aden.
Why is Saudi Arabia involved?
Yemen shares a long border with Saudi Arabia, making the conflict a direct security concern for Riyadh. The Houthis have repeatedly demonstrated their ability to strike deep inside the kingdom.
After years of costly fighting, Saudi Arabia had sought to reduce its direct involvement and pursued talks with the Houthis following the 2022 truce. Their recent advances along the Red Sea coast and renewed cross-border attacks have brought Riyadh back into major military action.
The Saudi-led coalition said on Monday that 100 fighter jets were taking part in Operation Dawn of Yemen, providing air cover for government forces, and claimed to have destroyed 324 “high-value” Houthi targets. Hundreds of fighters have reportedly been killed on both sides since then.
The Houthis have responded with missile and drone attacks on Saudi cities, airports, and military facilities.
What does the Iran war have to do with it?
Iranian advisers helped the Houthis plan and carry out their September offensive along Yemen’s Red Sea coast, according to AP, which reported that Iranian personnel were involved at multiple levels of the operation.
The US has not resumed direct strikes against the Houthis, but American and regional officials reportedly said that Washington is providing Riyadh with intelligence, target identification, and operational planning.
Saudi Arabia, Pakistan, and Türkiye activated the collective-defense provisions of their Makkah Alliance for Defense for the first time on Monday in response to attacks on the kingdom. The pact, sometimes dubbed the ‘Muslim NATO’, was signed in August and commits all three members to respond if any one of them comes under attack.
Who else is involved?
The forces fighting the Houthis are themselves divided. Yemen’s internationally recognized government relies heavily on Saudi Arabia, but government-aligned formations have different political and regional loyalties.
The UAE, once Saudi Arabia’s main coalition partner in Yemen, has backed powerful southern forces, including groups seeking an independent southern state. Riyadh and Abu Dhabi have at times pursued competing goals, although forces aligned with both are now fighting the Houthi advance.
Western countries are also providing military support to Riyadh. The UK has deployed an RAF Voyager tanker to provide air-to-air refueling for Saudi defensive operations, while France has announced the deployment of troops, radars, and air-defense systems to help protect Saudi energy infrastructure around Yanbu, a major Saudi oil-export hub on the Red Sea.
Why does Bab el-Mandeb matter now?
Bab el-Mandeb is a narrow strait between Yemen and the Horn of Africa connecting the Red Sea with the Gulf of Aden and the Indian Ocean. Ships traveling between Asia and Europe through the Suez Canal normally have to pass through it.
The strait has become especially important since the US-Israeli war on Iran disrupted shipping through Hormuz on the other side of the Arabian Peninsula. Saudi Arabia can bypass Hormuz by moving crude from its eastern oil-producing regions through the East-West pipeline to Yanbu on the Red Sea.
The pipeline was shut after drone attacks in September that Riyadh blamed on Iraqi militias but has since resumed operations, with flows reportedly reaching 5.8 million barrels per day.
Oil shipped from Yanbu to Asian markets, however, must pass through Bab el-Mandeb, putting the route close to the fighting in Yemen. The Houthis have previously attacked commercial shipping in the Red Sea with missiles, drones, and explosive boats and have renewed threats against Saudi-linked vessels.
How does it affect global energy markets?
The renewed fighting in Yemen is adding pressure to already strained global energy markets. Oil prices climbed again on Wednesday, with Brent crude trading above $101 a barrel and US benchmark West Texas Intermediate around $90 amid concerns over global supplies.
Saudi Aramco CEO Amin Nasser has warned that the world’s supply cushion was “scarily thin,” saying nearly 3 billion barrels of regional supply had been lost since the war with Iran began and that depleted stocks could take up to two years to rebuild.
The pressure has been even greater on refined fuels. Nasser said diesel and other fuel prices had risen more sharply than crude. G7 countries agreed last week to release 100 million barrels of oil and refined products from emergency reserves in an effort to ease the squeeze.
US President Donald Trump has blamed the global diesel shortage primarily on Ukrainian strikes against Russian refineries rather than the Middle East conflict and has urged Ukraine’s Vladimir Zelensky to halt the attacks.
What happens next?
Yemen’s government has set a goal of restoring its authority across the country, including retaking the Houthi-held capital, Sanaa. Fighting remains intense, however, with the Houthis launching missiles and drones at Aden International Airport on Wednesday as clashes continued elsewhere.
The conflict is worsening Yemen’s long-running humanitarian crisis. Some 184,000 people had been displaced by the latest fighting as of October 4, according to the International Organization for Migration. The WHO said last week that 838 people had been killed and more than 3,600 injured since August.
Diplomatic efforts are continuing, with the UN urging support for a political settlement and de-escalation.
Russia has also urged restraint and expressed readiness to help mediate if requested. The Kremlin said on Wednesday that Moscow was watching the escalation “with concern.”

articles.title: How to Beat Trump’s Noise Machine
articles.body:
On Monday night in Grand Island, Nebraska, defending the price Americans are paying for his war with Iran, President Donald Trump bragged to a cheering crowd: “Let them take out Los Angeles. Let them take out San Diego.” It was, he added, “a very small price to pay.” An American president describing the potential destruction of major American cities and the deaths of millions of citizens as “a very small price” to pay in a war is dangerous and callous.
Unsurprisingly, political leaders and media commentators piled on in outrage. Gavin Newsom, the governor of California, called him “deranged and dangerous.” Todd Gloria, the mayor of San Diego, reminded Trump that his city “is not collateral damage.” Even Jim Desmond, a Navy veteran and San Diego County supervisor, who is running for the House seat representing California’s 48th Congressional District, “vehemently” disagreed with Trump, arguing that “America must stand up to Iran and defend our interests, but the first responsibility of our Commander in Chief is to protect the American people and our homeland.”
Cable television spent a day parsing what Trump really meant, giving him precisely what he wanted: a distraction from his declining poll numbers, rising inflation, falling employment, his inability to protect U.S. military installations in the Middle East and the United Kingdom, and the refusal of his friend, President Vladimir Putin, to explain the suspected spread of a plague virus in Russia.
Having known Trump for 30 years, it is wrong and dangerous to write off his grotesque capers as delirious tantrums or creeping dementia. He has always been this way by choice. Some call this diversionary maneuver the hypnotic effect of a “shiny new object.”
Mass communication scholars of the 1940s called this the Wurlitzer Effect, drawing on the power of the booming organs accompanying carnival carousels to command attention. In our New York Times bestselling book, Trump’s Ten Commandments, we call this the “Wall of Sound,” after the scandalous Phil Spector’s famous attention-controlling production technique of layering so many instruments that the music fills every frequency and drowns out everything else.
What most political analysts presume to be impulsive chaos is often a deliberate, calibrated churn of provocations. When a conventional leader faces a damaging story, they try to change the subject with good news. Trump does the opposite. He buries bad news under louder, more outrageous news of his own making. He is the only leader who will shoot himself in the left foot if it keeps you from looking at his right.
The Trump distraction machine
We have watched him run this play many times before. In January, Trump escalated his threats against Greenland, invoking an unsupported, even hallucinatory danger to U.S. national security. He put reserve units on alert, threatened an unprovoked military invasion and trade sanctions against Denmark. He renewed his taunts about making Canada the 51st state. The European Union, the United Kingdom, and Canada mobilized to curb his bluster.
The military raid Trump ordered to capture and extract Venezuelan dictator Nicolas Maduro in early January was deceptively justified with a flurry of explanations. He invoked national security despite the absence of risk of foreign attacks.
He cited drug interdiction despite the lack of drug trafficking from Venezuela into the U.S. and his release of major drug trafficker from Honduras. He promised regime change to restore democracy, then left the same regime in place. And he pledged to increase U.S. fuel supplies and lower retail gasoline prices, a claim that glossed over the challenges of refining Venezuela’s thick, sour crude.
On Jun. 22, 2025, Trump launched Operation Midnight Hammer with great fanfare, deploying B-2 stealth bombers and submarine-launched Tomahawk missiles against three Iranian nuclear facilities: Fordow, Natanz, and Isfahan. He declared that the operation had destroyed Iran’s nuclear enrichment capacity and eliminated the nuclear threat posed by the regime. Iran’s continued nuclear weapons capability punctured the bravado.
On Feb. 28, Trump launched Operation Epic Fury, promising to topple the Iranian regime and eliminate its proxies—Hamas, Hezbollah, and the Houthis—within days. Eight months later, the fighting continues on all these fronts, with no resolution in sight. Even military experts who supported the operation questioned its timing: there had been no immediate Iranian provocation, and U.S. naval assets needed for the mission were positioned in the Caribbean and the South China Sea, far from the Middle East. The timing made sense as another desperate attempt by Trump to distract from his failures at home.
The racist AI video of the Obamas that Trump shared in a late-night Truth Social post in February was a calculated diversion, timed to coincide with his sagging approval ratings. He faced criticism for his bizarre bigoted humor, the sort that had ended or damaged the careers of earlier politicians, such as Agriculture Secretary Earl Butz, Senate Majority Leader Trent Lott, and Congressman Steve King.
But Trump was delighted to have baited the weekend news shows away from his domestic policy setbacks. When that controversy faded, he pivoted again, this time to targeting revered national landmarks. He sought to rename the Kennedy Center for Performing Arts, ultimately closing the building and threatening to raze it if he could not put his name on it.
He followed that with by false claims of vandalism of the Lincoln Monument’s Reflecting Pool. When his effort to recast America’s 250th anniversary as his own grandiose tribute was outshined by glowing coverage of Taylor Swift’s wedding in Madison Square Garden, he attacked the wedding. He then launched another round of unprovoked legal attacks against universities, law firms, and former public officials, including former FBI director James Comey and former Federal Reserve chairman Jerome Powell.
And then, Trump returned to a favorite punching bag: Canada. Meanwhile, bond markets were signaling alarm, and U.S. business leaders and American farmers were condemning his tariffs policies and foreign wars for driving up fuel and fertilizer costs and undermining access to foreign markets for American goods.
The limits of burying the bad news
Each of these interventions, whether reckless, self-destructive trade barriers, massive military invasions, or offensive divisive speeches, soaks up attention. All of these interventions initially diverted media coverage as intended, even if they ultimately backfired. The provocations and the uproar they generate drown out other serious problems while the ricochet effects magnify Trump’s presence, making him seem everywhere, all the time. That is the point.
Indeed, Trump has a unique, almost superhuman ability to bury bad news until supporters and detractors alike are no longer talking about issues and failures that would sink virtually any other politician. Buried under this avalanche of manufactured headlines are his approval ratings, which are the lowest of either of his either term: 32% in a recent Reuters/Ipsos poll.
And there is an affordability crisis compounded by persistent inflation, cratering economic data, plummeting consumer confidence, and weak jobs growth. Even coverage of the war with Iran has been eclipsed by the uproar over Trump’s Los Angeles and San Diego remarks. The conflict has lasted far longer than he expected or intended, with its objectives seemingly stalled and no easy way out.
Just this week, the Pentagon confirmed that all 12 B-1B bombers at RAF Fairford in the United Kingdom had been flown home. The British base had hosted American bombers striking Iran since March. The bombers left after British authorities arrested several people over a suspected plot against the base, which Britain's prime minister linked to Iran.
And on Tuesday, Sen. Chris Murphy of Connecticut revealed that the Pentagon had denied him access to Al Udeid Air Base in Qatar. The largest U.S. base in the region, it has been struck repeatedly by Iran since the war began in February. The Pentagon also refused to brief him on the war while he was in Qatar, citing a March travel directive from Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth. Murphy called it an “active, unprecedented, unconstitutional effort underway to hide the costs of this war” from Congress and the public.
But the “Wall of Sound” has a structural weakness. It works only while the audience fails to connect the noise to what it is hiding. The answer to a noise machine is discipline: staying focused on facts and demanding accountability, no matter what outrageous diversions are tossed out.
Sustained attention to what Trump wants buried is the antidote to his perpetual noise machine. It has become fashionable to trace Trump’s playbook to Roy Cohn, his mentor and his father’s diabolical attorney. But Trump also draws on an older American tradition, articulated by the 19th century showman P.T. Barnum: "The public appears disposed to be amused even when they are conscious of being deceived." And, “without promotion something terrible happens: nothing!”
Sadly for Trump, the Canadians, the Iranians, and his fellow Americans are figuring out his maneuvers and keeping their attention on his faltering domestic policies and imploding global diplomacy. Even Barnum understood that the public can balance a three ring circus and not follow the carnival barking of the ringmaster.

articles.title: Air Force Leaders Elevate Point Defense as a Key Air Warfare Mission
articles.body:
NATIONAL HARBOR, Md.—Flying and fixing aircraft remains the Air Force’s reason for being, but protecting air bases from attack is becoming an essential component that makes those possible. Following attacks on air bases across the Middle East during Operation Epic Fury, point defense was among the hottest topics on tap at AFA’s 2026 Air, Space and Cyber conference in September.
The Iranian attacks, such as the March 27 air raid on Prince Sultan Air Base, Saudi Arabia that damaged multiple refueling aircraft and an E-3 Sentry AWACS command and control plane, did not deliver crippling blows. But they did cause injuries, disrupt operations, and destroy some aircraft.
The damage was great enough to convince Air Force leaders to prioritize air base defense—or point defense, as they are calling it—and invest in new weapons and a new career field to man them.
Air Force Secretary Troy E. Meink and Chief of Staff Gen. Kenneth S. Wilsbach announced new initiatives at the conference, aimed at improving oversight of point defense acquisitions amid the recent explosion of growth in the counter-drone industry as it responds to increasing Pentagon demand.
Wilsbach pledged that point defense will no longer be treated as a “side hustle” but as a “core function of air and space power.”
The Air Force began ramping up its point defense strategy in late 2023 after unidentified drones were seen flying repeatedly over Langley Air Force Base, Va. Soon the service, along with the rest of the U.S. military, was racing to catch up with the rapidly evolving drone warfare threats and tactics emerging from the war in Ukraine. Then in June 2025, Operation Spider Web, a bold Ukrainian drone attack on strategic bomber bases deep inside Russia, showed Air Force leaders just how vulnerable the service’s own air bases were to this new threat.
But it took the hard lessons from a shooting war with Iran to elevate point defense to a new level of importance at the service’s semiannual Corona summit in June and make it a key focus at this year’s AFA event, said retired Air Force Lt. Gen. David Deptula, dean of the Mitchell Institute for Aerospace Studies.
“The reason why it was announced at AFA is because a decision had been made at the previous Corona to make point defense a mission function of the Air Force,” Deptula said. The conference “was the first opportunity to really make a big splash.”
During the conference, several Air Force generals said that the service’s increased emphasis on point defense is needed after watching Iranian drone and missile attacks strike air bases during Epic Fury.
Air Combat Command Boss Gen. Adrian L. Spain said Epic Fury “laid bare some of those things that have been in front of us for a while, and it just reminded us that we have to get after some of these things.”
“Our bases are under attack; we have to continue to generate air power in spite of that,” Spain said. “We have to be able to be resilient under attack, and we have to be able to sustain the force under those kinds of pressures to win.”
The Air Force’s chief modernization officer, Lt. Gen. Christopher J. Niemi, said the service identified more than a year ago that it would have to “increasingly protect our assets at air bases with investments in point defense but that accelerated … because of some of the experiences that we had over there.”
Prior to Epic Fury, the Air Force appeared to be banking on its agile combat employment strategy to disperse forces from large bases to ad hoc air bases in order to complicate targeting for adversaries and fight through attacks. The service evacuated Al Udeid Air Base, Qatar, before the Feb. 28 launch of Epic Fury, moving aircraft and most personnel to other locations both in the region and back in the United States.
When Iranian forces attacked Al Udeid, destroying the Combined Air Operations Center, or CAOC, there, the facility was empty—the first time it hadn’t participated in air combat operations since the 1990s. Instead, Epic Fury’s air operations were commanded fromShaw Air Force Base, S.C.
“ACE was really birthed out of necessity, [because] I cannot protect these forces any longer,” Spain said. “But if I could perfectly protect all my forces at a location, I would not move. There’s no reason to move. I’m only creating turbulence for myself if I do that.” That turbulence extends to every part of an air operation, he said: “I have a logistics problem I’ve got to worry about. I’ve got a fuel problem I’ve got to worry about. I have a [command and control] problem I have to worry about when I move around more.”
Spain said Iran’s proven ability to threaten a base means the Air Force is returning to “a time well before 9/11, where we were preparing to fight a peer adversary in an existential way. We see what that looks like through the experience of [Epic Fury].”
Air base defense has long been a complex problem for Air Force leaders. Ostensibly, the Army is responsible for protecting air bases from missile attacks, dating back to the 1948 Key West Agreement on roles and missions of the armed forces. That’s why the Patriot ballistic missile defense system is an Army weapon system. But with the rise of low-cost attack drones such as the Iranian Shahed, the scale and scope of threats has grown while the Army’s capacity to defend far-flung bases has not kept pace. In April 2025, the Air Force published new doctrine on “Point Defense of Air Bases,” assuming a more active role for Airmen in defending their air bases.
The lack of hardened shelters at most forward bases contributes to the Air Force’s vulnerability. Investment in such structures and other passive defenses has often ranked low among budget priorities, compared to aircraft and major research initiatives.
Deptula maintains that the Air Force has long been underfunded and that vulnerabilities are the result of calculated risk and budget choices.
“How come hardened aircraft shelters weren’t in place at Prince Sultan Air Base? How come the command-and-control facility at Al Udeid—that the joint force air component commander has been operating from since 2001—wasn’t built underground?” Deptula said. “The answer is money, because it costs more money. The United States military took the risk, understanding that there were threats out there, they were willing to take the risk and not to spend the money to build hardened aircraft shelters, to build underground facilities.”
Now that “the threat has shown itself to be highly capable,” he added, “resources are going to have to be allocated to increase our ability to defend our bases.”
Air Mobility Command Boss Lt. Gen. Daniel H. Tulley said he was encouraged by Wilsbach’s decision to establish a new career field to develop point defense specialists. Wilsbach said the Air Force will start designating Airmen with the new specialty within two years. The Air Force announced it was standing up the new career field in late June after the Corona meeting. As a short-term fix, USAF has established point defense flights, specialized units of roughly 20 Airmen each, trained to rapidly deploy to hotspots and defend air bases against drone attacks.
Tulley saw how unprotected Al Udeid was when he commanded the 379th Air Expeditionary Wing there from 2019 to 2021.
“When I was at Al Udeid, this problem was widely recognized,” Tulley said. “The Air Force has been going after it, but I think our sense of urgency has dramatically increased—which it needs to. We’ve all seen what Operation Spiderweb did in Russia. How do we prevent the same sort of thing, and maintain the sense of urgency?”
The Air Staff and Point Defense Task Force, working with the Pentagon’s Joint Interagency Task Force 401, or JIATF 401, is making headway to identify technologies and field new weapons to counter the drone threat. But it will take years for the service to build up an adequate point defense capability.
“Would I like to get there a lot faster? Yes, but I think we’re getting there,” Tulley said. “I’d like to look back in two years and say, ‘We’re done,’ but I don’t know if we’ll quite be there yet.”
The Air Force relies primarily on the Small Unmanned Air Defense Systems, or SUADS, for countering drones. The system is capable of identifying and tracking enemy missiles or drones of multiple sizes, and downing incoming drones with an electronic warfare weapon. To stop missiles, it uses both electronic warfare and kinetic effectors. It can also interface with commercial counter-drone systems and other air defense systems, depending on the needs of a commander.
It’s available in two variants, one for fixed air bases and one that can be deployed on a pallet for rapid response missions. The Air Force has requested more than $1.5 billion for SUADS in the fiscal 2027 budget, with most of the funding allocated for the system’s missile defense components, according to budget documents.
What remains unclear is how much money is being spent on additional counter-drone systems for the Air Force, which are being acquired with the assistance of JIATF 401. Those buys are difficult to track since they are not listed in the budget request. Both Air Force and JIATF 401 officials declined to provide funding details.
During the conference, leaders said the Air Force is working on initiatives to gain more oversight over the acquisition process to more efficiently manage its counter-drone acquisitions.
Globally, the market is expanding rapidly, The current global counter-drone market is valued at roughly $9 billion and is projected to reach about $30 billion by 2031.
JIATF-401 Director Army Brig. Gen. Matthew Ross cited that figure in a talk with industry members Sept. 15. The U.S. portion of the counter-drone market is currently valued at roughly $2.5 billion and is expected to grow to roughly $8.6 billion by 2030, according to MarketsandMarkets.com a business intelligence firm.
“What that means is that demand is going up really quickly,” said Ross adding that his agency is acquiring “additional arrows to put into the quiver of our warfighters,” but “our supplies just aren’t there yet.”
Meink said the service is also looking at establishing a senior portfolio acquisition executive, or PAE, to manage the point defense enterprise. PAEs are a new construct, introduced during recent Pentagon acquisition reforms to get more authority into the hands of fewer leaders in order to maximize acquisition success. The idea is to combine several programs within a single mission area and give PAEs authority to move funds between programs and adjust requirements based on evolving needs. The Department of the Air Force currently has 26 PAEs—17 in the Air Force, nine in the Space Force.
Currently, the Air Force PAE for Electronic Systems oversees counter-drone acquisition efforts and the service’s PAE for Intelligence, Surveillance, Reconnaissance & Special Operations Forces manages offensive drone acquisitions, said Lea Kirkwood, the Air Force PAE for Electronic Systems.
The Pentagon recently stood up the new Direct Reporting Portfolio Manager for Unmanned Systems, or DRPM UxS, with the goal of accelerating the development, procurement, and fielding at scale of autonomous capabilities.
“There’s a lot of considerations across mission areas,” Kirkwood said, adding that the Department of the Air Force is “looking at how do we need to look at our structure to say ‘how can we best support the [Pentagon], the DRPM UxS, and then also within the DAF, both from the offensive and the defensive perspective’—you know, what’s the best way to get after this?”
The Air Force is also creating a “point defense weapon system,” Wilsbach said during his speech. The new system will be designed to formally manage multiple counter-drone systems that range from sensors, radars, and command and control architecture to kinetic and nonkinetic effectors for disabling or destroying incoming drones.
“The point defense weapon system is a way for us to consolidate these capabilities under a single umbrella,” Michael Sheehy, director of future operations under the Air Force deputy chief of staff for operations said during the JIATF 401 industry meeting.
The Air Force is currently writing a program action directive for the weapon system. “That way it’s not this ad hoc approach to this, where it is buying some, trying some pieces of parts and then kind of making up who’s operating the system. … The other thing that it does is it creates a single point for funding within the Air Force,” Sheehy added. “Now I have a program element code for this weapon system, and as funding’s coming in, it’s going to that as opposed to kind of going all over the place.”
Sheehy noted that there was a “vast difference” in the amount of counter-drone innovations on the show floor at the AFA conference this year compared to prior shows.
“There’s a lot of counter-UAS capability that is being developed out there, and … we need to have a more enterprise level approach to doing this,” he said. The Air Force “owes it to our wing commanders to provide that kit, provide that training, provide that organization that is professionalized to get after this really difficult problem.”

articles.title: The FSB's sabotage campaign in Europe: Russia's war on Western arms makers – and what it means for Ukraine
articles.body:
The FSB's sabotage campaign in Europe: Russia's war on Western arms makers – and what it means for Ukraine
A disaster was narrowly averted in Germany in summer 2026. On the night of 4-5 August, unidentified individuals attempted to attack Leipzig airport with three explosive-laden FPV drones. Their target was a Ukrainian Ruslan aircraft operated by Antonov Airlines. The Ruslans are an important link in the military logistics chain, transporting cargo not only for Ukraine but also for NATO countries more broadly.
A source familiar with the incident told Ukrainska Pravda that the Ukrainians had three strokes of luck that night. The explosive on the first drone failed to detonate, the second drone crashed into another aircraft, and the third never made it into the air. Police found it only a few weeks later on the outskirts of the airport. Something had apparently spooked the perpetrator.
According to Politico, investigators soon noticed similarities between the drone's warhead and other improvised explosive devices found in caches set up by Russian agents elsewhere in Europe.
The brazen sabotage attempt in Leipzig marked a new escalation in the hybrid war targeting Europe's military sites and defence industry facilities. OSINT analysts have noted that the attacks are becoming more frequent and increasingly systematic.
The Russians themselves are no longer hiding their hand: the arms factories of Ukraine's partners are in their sights.
"It's a secret. A military secret," Russian leader Vladimir Putin said when asked by reporters whether Russia could attack facilities in the UK defence sector.
Ukrainska Pravda looks at Russia's sabotage campaign across Europe and whether it could put continued support for Ukraine at risk.
Fifty incidents involving hybrid attacks in a month
Russia has repeatedly tried to put a bomb under EU support for Ukraine – both literally and figuratively.
The OSINT tracker Malcontent News has logged 497 acts of hybrid warfare across Europe since Russia launched its full-scale invasion in 2022. In 454 cases, its analysts identified direct links to Russian or Belarusian hybrid operations. The attacks have taken many forms: cyber-attacks, vandalism, sabotage, arson and incursions by unknown drones.
OSINT analyst Clément Molin estimates that 50 incidents have been recorded across Europe since the start of September alone, many of them likely linked to Russia's hybrid campaign. At least 10 incidents over the past two months have involved the defence industry or military logistics.
Russian intelligence services are behind the planning and organisation of these operations, but they turn to civilians to carry them out. Members of local criminal gangs serve as the Kremlin's intermediaries, seeking out recruits and paying them in cryptocurrency for each job. Former Wagner Group recruiters have also taken part in the process. Ukrainian migrants recruited by the FSB are also frequently among the perpetrators.
Using local residents gives sabotage operations a convenient cover, making them look like industrial accidents or acts of anti-war, environmental or pro-Palestinian activism. But the same approach can also undermine the operation itself. Untrained recruits are prone to mistakes that trained professionals would know how to avoid.
In Leipzig, it was precisely this kind of mistake that helped avert a tragedy.
Sabotage
Most acts of sabotage across Europe between 2022 and 2025 were not aimed at defence industry facilities. Instead, they appeared designed to threaten or intimidate. In most cases, police and counter-intelligence services managed to thwart the attacks – and, in some instances, even prevent assassination attempts.
For instance, in 2024, Russia planned to assassinate Armin Papperger, CEO of German defence giant Rheinmetall, which supplies weapons to Ukraine. The plot was foiled by the US and German intelligence services.
In 2026, the picture has changed dramatically. Defence industry facilities have been increasingly drawn into the sabotage campaign.
One of the most notable incidents was a fire at the Czech drone and optical systems manufacturer LPP Holding. The blaze damaged production facilities and destroyed stock in the warehouse.
Despite the damage, the company said the planned delivery of 40 attack drones to Ukraine remained on track. Czech police immediately determined that the fire had been deliberate and investigated it as a possible terrorist act.
A previously unknown pro-Palestinian group claimed responsibility, accusing LPP of manufacturing weapons for Israel. The company rejected the claim, saying it has no cooperation with Elbit Systems and does not manufacture equipment for Israel. LPP and Elbit Systems announced a partnership in 2023, but the deal was never realised.
LPP suggested that the pro-Palestinian cover story could have been a Russian covert operation aimed at disrupting the company's cooperation with Ukraine.
Another suspected act of sabotage targeted transformers and power-line pylons supplying KNDS and MBDA, major European defence companies that manufacture missiles and ammunition. The attack left 3,000 homes without electricity, and graffiti reading "Action against war" was found nearby.
And the Russians themselves did not stay silent.
On 15 April, Russia's Ministry of Defence released a list of 21 Ukrainian and European companies producing drones and drone components for Ukraine. It gave the addresses of their manufacturing facilities and named the sites themselves. The accuracy of the list is difficult to verify from open sources. But the message was hard to miss.
"When strikes become a reality depends on what comes next. Sleep well, European partners!" Dmitry Medvedev, former Russian president and current deputy chairman of the Security Council, wrote in a comment on the matter.
Four months after Medvedev's comment, a failed sabotage operation in Leipzig showed that Russia was prepared to take its confrontation with Europe a step further.
Fires and explosions hit ammunition depots belonging to arms maker EMCO in Bulgaria on 10 and 12 August. Three days later, a fire followed by explosions broke out at a KNDS ammunition factory in Italy.
Neither Bulgaria nor Italy has officially blamed Russia for the explosions. The authorities have instead attributed them to production problems and human error. EMCO tells a different story, directly linking the incidents to the company's operations and its owner, Emilian Gebrev.
This is not the first time the Bulgarian company has come under attack from Russia. Ukraine has been receiving ammunition from EMCO since 2014 – the same year the first explosions occurred at its depots. In 2015, Russia's GRU military intelligence service attempted to poison Gebrev himself. Similar arson attacks and explosions struck EMCO warehouses again in 2022 and 2023, and investigators found a Russian connection in each case.
In other cases, the Russians were directly accused of sabotage. On 15 August, unknown individuals set fire to Milrem Robotics in Tallinn, which supplies THeMIS ground robots to Ukraine.
The fire was quickly contained, no one was injured, and production carried on as usual. A month later, the Estonian government said the arson attack was an act of sabotage orchestrated by Russian intelligence.
Another incident took place in Slovakia in late August. Local police foiled an arson attack on a Skyeton production facility in the east of the country, where the Ukrainian company manufactures unmanned systems. Company representatives told Ukrainska Pravda that Russian operatives also regularly attempt to target its facilities in Ukraine.
Similar incidents have been reported in Poland, France and Germany. Fires at production facilities belonging to WB Electronics, Delair, Rohde & Schwarz and Helsing have been linked to Russia's military intelligence.
Explosions of unknown origin have also rocked Serbian defence factories producing weapons that end up in Ukraine.
Not every explosion or fire at a defence facility is necessarily an act of sabotage. Rising orders and the rapid expansion of production inevitably bring about the occasional accident.
For instance, a fire broke out on 17 September at ZVS Holding, an ammunition manufacturer owned by CSG (Czechoslovak Group), in Slovakia. CSG spokesperson Andrej Čirtek told Ukrainska Pravda that the company has no information linking the fire to sabotage.
Čirtek said: "The fire broke out during roof renovation work carried out by an external contractor. Based on the findings available so far, the most likely explanation is that the fire was related to the renovation work. However, the investigation by the relevant authorities is still ongoing, so we do not want to speculate about its final conclusions."
How Europe is responding
By carrying out such operations across Europe, the Kremlin is probing how far it can go. Moscow is gauging European countries' responses to sabotage and testing NATO's resilience, taking care not to cross the threshold that could trigger the Alliance's Article 5.
Beyond the immediate damage, acts of sabotage can help map the infrastructure supporting military logistics and reveal vulnerabilities that could become targets in a future conflict.
This is precisely why the arson attacks on defence factories are only part of the picture. There have also been reports of railway tracks being blown up, drones flying over strategic airfields, communications being jammed and other provocations.
Europe has yet to develop a unified response to these events. In the cases mentioned above in Bulgaria and Italy, the governments have refrained from directly accusing Moscow, apparently out of concern that doing so could further escalate tensions.
Other countries take a more sober view of the threat from the east and are seeking ways to counter Russian sabotage. Germany is perhaps the most active in this effort. Its law enforcement and security services are searching for weapons caches that Russian operatives may have set up in preparation for future attacks.
Germany is also putting together a broad package of measures to counter Russian sabotage and cyber-attacks. Special forces are being deployed in strategically important cities across the country to protect critical infrastructure against drones and deal with explosive devices. Police units will work alongside them. Ukraine has been sharing its experience with Germany in this area.
A source familiar with the situation in Leipzig told Ukrainska Pravda that the German law enforcement agencies handled the attempted attack on Ukrainian aircraft particularly well.
"The first thing the German authorities did after the investigation was not to disclose what they had found, but to explain how they would prevent this from happening again," the source said. "They thoroughly analysed everything that happened on the day of the attack and have since introduced a great many security measures to ensure that such acts of sabotage do not happen again. Yes, they were unable to prevent it, but ultimately, the situation served as a wake-up call for them."
Other European countries are also taking active steps to counter the threat. Romania and Germany, for example, have been detaining civilians suspected of collaborating with Russia. Poland has deployed 10,000 troops to protect critical infrastructure after explosions damaged railway tracks. Lithuania, Latvia and Estonia have set up joint investigation teams to investigate terrorist attacks and acts of sabotage.
A European intelligence official told AP that European intelligence services are now committing as many resources to countering Russian sabotage as they do to combating terrorism.
Defence companies are also tightening their security measures. Representatives of Milrem Robotics told Ukrainska Pravda that the company is changing its approach to security following the arson attack on its premises.
"Since Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine, the security situation in Europe has clearly changed, and defence companies must take this into account," says a Milrem Robotics representative.
Will acts of sabotage affect support for Ukraine?
Another clear aim of Russia's sabotage campaign is to weaken European support for Ukraine and reduce the flow of aid.
So far, Russia has failed to achieve this. Most companies have suffered financial losses, but supplies have continued uninterrupted. Some factories temporarily lost production capacity, only to return to normal levels later. The way these sabotage operations have been carried out also suggests that, for now, intimidation is the main objective rather than disruption.
The choice of targets is also telling: Russia is carrying out these operations in countries that are actively helping Ukraine strengthen its defences. By contrast, in countries that provide little support to Ukraine, such as Hungary, no such incidents have been recorded. Moscow is therefore trying to make ordinary Europeans feel the cost of supporting Ukraine.
As warnings of a potential conflict between the EU and Russia become more frequent, European and US intelligence agencies are increasingly highlighting the expansion of Russia's hybrid war against Europe. European governments, too, are beginning to recognise the scale of the threat.
One of the key messages at the 2026 Munich Security Conference was that European leaders must accept this reality and act on it.
Translated by Artem Yakymyshyn
Edited by Susan McDonald

articles.title: Russian air defense explained: How Moscow counters mass drone attacks
articles.body:
Russian air defense explained: How Moscow counters mass drone attacks
Moscow, October 6. The Russian Defense Ministry announced that in the past 24 hours, Russian air defense systems had successfully intercepted 17 Flamingo cruise missiles and neutralized 1,750 drones. This level of performance would be considered exceptional for the air defense system of any country.
Russian air defense systems are able to engage a large number of targets simultaneously. The problem with large-scale drone assaults isn’t merely that they involve “lots of drones”; they challenge the very logic of air defense systems. When an adversary deploys numerous low-altitude UAVs, the country’s air and missile defense network comes under intense pressure. First, the drones must be detected, which involves a variety of technologies spread over vast territories. Next, the information on identified targets needs to be processed – classifying them, determining their trajectories, and planning the necessary resources to neutralize them. Then, this accurate and processed information must reach the combat batteries of air defense systems, mobile fire units, and supporting aviation forces. Finally, the target can be eliminated. Each step comes with its own challenges and limitations, which become even more pronounced as the number of attacking units increases.
Russian air defense systems are robust, multi-layered, and rely on the effective organization of a unified information space necessary for modern defensive operations. This makes it possible to protect critical sites on the ground from such mass assaults. All stress tests have been successfully passed. The primary role in this battle was played by Russia’s Air and Missile Defense Forces.
How is the air defense system structured?
Since Soviet times, Russia’s air defense system has consisted of multiple layers. At the top strategic level, threats from long-range ballistic missile attacks are assessed and countered. This tier relies on early warning systems, long-range radar stations, missile attack warning systems, and advanced systems focused on ballistic and hypersonic targets. Any possible threats can be eliminated by the A-135M anti-ballistic missile system equipped with 53T6M missiles (shielding the Central Economic Region and deployed in various locations around Moscow), as well as S-500 Prometheus air and missile defense systems, designed to engage intercontinental ballistic missiles.
S-400 Triumph systems form the backbone of regional air defense. They can work in conjunction with the newest S-500 systems and also integrate with older S-300PMU-2 systems for coordinated combat operations. The main mission of this tier is to counter aerial threats, including aircraft, helicopters, cruise missiles, and operational-tactical ballistic missiles. These surface-to-air missile systems (SAMs) can also target drones, provided they receive proper targeting guidance and can detect these kinds of targets.
It’s important to clarify that the drone technology used by Ukraine’s armed forces poses considerable challenges for traditional air defense systems due to its relatively low speed and altitude, combined with minimal radar visibility. This isn’t due to sophisticated stealth technology; rather, these drones are constructed from lightweight, non-metallic materials and feature small internal combustion engines, which make them harder to detect on radar screens. Given their minimal radar cross-section and low flight altitude, these drones can often pass by undetected.
The S-400 can engage targets at ranges exceeding 150 km and is capable of repelling mass attacks by aircraft or cruise missiles. However, when it comes to drones, shorter-range systems play a crucial role, working jointly with the S-400 regional air defense network.
Key players in the fight against drones include the following systems: S-350 Vityaz, Tor-M2, and the terminal defense system Pantsir-S1. These systems are ideal for countering large-scale drone assaults; they are the ones that fight the main battle against UAVs.
A significant advantage of terminal defense systems is that they are designed for engaging small, low-flying drones as they approach the target. Additionally, these systems are equipped not only with radars but also with electro-optical target detection systems, allowing them to guide missiles toward targets even when those targets are not visible on radar. Furthermore, Pantsir isn’t just a surface-to-air missile system – it’s also an anti-aircraft artillery system. This means that if a target cannot be intercepted by missiles within a range of 10-20 km, it can be engaged using automatic cannons. This makes it particularly effective against slow-moving drones.
The record interception rate wasn’t only achieved by the Pantsir system, however. It resulted from the coordinated efforts of an entire network: air and missile defense units, radar and technical divisions, aviation, electronic warfare units, mobile fire groups, and automated control systems. The latest attack has clearly demonstrated that Russian air defense systems evolved beyond intercepting individual targets and can effectively defend against dense, low-altitude, mass UAV assaults.
Mobile units and aviation step in
To deal with slower drones, new air defense structures – known as mobile fire groups (MFGs) – are being employed extensively. These agile units, equipped with machine guns and portable surface-to-air missile systems, can be deployed either along drone flight paths or near specific infrastructure. While the effectiveness of these units depends on being in the right place at the right time (since their engagement range is limited), they are highly maneuverable, and given the slow speed of drones, they can set up defensive positions if they have timely intelligence about the type and direction of an impending attack. In fact, one of the key developments of the fall of 2026 was the implementation of a unified information system for organizing air defense against drones across various Russian regions. Such a system could significantly enhance the efficiency of mobile air defense units; and apparently, it’s already being used.
Army aviation helicopters are another useful asset in combating drones. Their speed allows them to catch up with drones, while their armament enables them to destroy these threats using both artillery fire and guided missiles. A considerable portion of downed drones can likely be attributed to the effective operation of frontline helicopters.
Cruise missiles such as Ukraine’s Flamingo pose a different sort of challenge. They are more complex compared to standard drones: they move faster, pose greater risks, and navigate terrain more effectively. In this case, Airborne Early Warning and Control (AEW&C) aircraft like the A-50M become indispensable; they monitor the air situation against the backdrop of the Earth’s surface and can direct interceptor aircraft toward targets. Receiving target data from AEW&C allows fighter jets to engage cruise missiles before ground-based air defense systems can establish a solid lock, or in areas where deploying a SAM would be less advantageous. The coordinated work of AEW&C, fighter jets, and ground-based air defense systems is crucial for repelling mixed attacks involving both drones and cruise missiles, and is the key to success in defensive battles.
Challenges or opportunities?
When it comes to combating drones, challenges certainly exist. The primary concern is the economic aspect: a drone may cost tens of thousands of dollars, but a missile is much more expensive. If the enemy launches thousands of drones, the defending side needs cost-effective alternatives – such as bullets, fragmentation shells, small missiles, electronic warfare (EW) systems, interceptor drones, and mobile units. This opens up avenues for the evolution of air defense systems.
Interceptor drones could prove effective against slower drones since their production costs are at least comparable to those of basic drones. However, an interceptor drone without a warhead would be utterly ineffective against a larger, aircraft-type drone – it simply wouldn’t be able to bring it down. Therefore, in the future, we may see interceptor drones equipped with munitions and capable of high-speed flight.
Another promising direction is the development of rapid-fire artillery systems using programmable munitions, like the ZAK-30 Citadel. These systems can fire multiple rounds accurately and then quickly switch to a new target. Moreover, such automated air defense systems have the potential to effectively combat swarms of drones – if not now, then certainly in the near future.
Efforts are also underway to create compact and relatively simple guided missiles for air defense systems. Such new missiles were designed for the Pantsir system, and we may soon see small, mobile air defense units equipped with these missiles. This would significantly reduce the cost of downing a drone and enhance the effectiveness of mobile groups.
Laser systems for neutralizing drones hold particularly promising economic prospects. While the initial cost of a laser system is high, the price per shot is minimal. Like rapid-fire automated artillery, lasers can almost instantly switch between targets. This makes them highly useful for countering drone swarms.
Overall, Russian air defense systems are becoming more sophisticated and offer unique capabilities in fending off mass attacks. The performance metrics of these systems are among the best in the world – this has been proven in real battle conditions, no propaganda or exaggeration involved. And this is just the beginning; air defense systems are evolving and will undoubtedly become even more effective in the future.

articles.title: ‘Birthday gift for Putin’: Russian attack on Ukraine kills 21, including four children
articles.body:
Russia launched one of its heaviest aerial attacks on Ukraine in recent months overnight Tuesday into Wednesday, firing dozens of missiles and around 130 drones at a wide range of areas across the country. At least 21 people were killed, including four children, and around 60 were wounded. 
The attack took place on Russian President Vladimir Putin’s 74th birthday — he was born on October 7 — and officials in Kyiv said the deadly destruction was effectively a “birthday gift” for him.
The attack came after weeks in which Russia stepped up its use of fast, jet-powered drones, posing a new challenge to Ukraine’s air defense system. The heaviest toll was recorded in the city of Pryluky in the Chernihiv region, about 135 kilometers (84 miles) east of Kyiv. A Russian missile struck a five-story apartment building directly, destroying large sections of it. According to updated figures released by Ukrainian authorities Wednesday afternoon, 15 people were killed at the site, including four children, and around 50 others were wounded. Rescue crews and residents spent hours digging through the rubble in an effort to find people trapped beneath it and survivors.
The missile struck the building at around 6 a.m., when many residents were still asleep. According to local authorities, two sections of the building were destroyed in the strike. A children’s and youth creative center, a factory and vehicles were also damaged in the city, while a fire broke out in an industrial area following the bombardment. Among those affected was a local police officer who was wounded, while her husband — who until recently served as a police officer on the front — and her mother were killed. Seven children were also among the wounded, including a 3-year-old girl. An 8-year-old boy was among those killed.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy linked the timing of the attack to Putin’s birthday. “On Wednesday, as a ‘birthday gift’ for Putin, the Russian military destroyed a residential building in Pryluky,” he said. “The Russians wanted to strike painfully and demonstratively. This was one of the most vile attacks.”
Ukrainian Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha joined in the condemnation, saying Russian generals had given Putin his “favorite birthday gift — war crimes.” He said the Russian president’s truly fitting gift would be to see him stand trial in The Hague.
The strike on Pryluky was part of a large-scale combined attack. Zelenskyy said Russia launched around 70 missiles in total, many of them ballistic. The Ukrainian Air Force said the attack included 48 Kh-101, Iskander-K and Kalibr cruise missiles, as well as ballistic and anti-ship missiles and 130 drones of various types, including Shahed drones. Of those, 46 were jet-powered.
According to Zelenskyy, infrastructure in Kyiv and 12 other regions came under fire. Five residential buildings were damaged in Dnipro and four in Kremenchuk. Two people were killed and seven wounded in Kremenchuk, while additional fatalities were reported in Kyiv and Oleksandriia. The bombardment forced authorities to introduce emergency power outages in five regions as repair work continued throughout Wednesday.
According to the Ukrainian Air Force, air defenses managed to shoot down or disrupt 161 targets: five ballistic or other high-speed missiles of various types, 39 cruise missiles and 117 drones. Missile and drone strikes were nevertheless recorded at 18 locations across the country.
Among the areas that came under the heaviest fire were Kyiv, Kharkiv, Poltava and Dnipropetrovsk. Ukraine, meanwhile, reported relative success in countering the jet-powered drones: More than 80% of the 46 such drones launched in the attack were intercepted, compared with an interception rate of around 50% to 60% in recent weeks. The greater threat for Kyiv remains ballistic missiles, which are far more difficult to intercept and require Patriot systems and additional interceptors.
The attack did not come as a complete surprise. On Tuesday, Zelenskyy warned that Ukrainian intelligence had information indicating that Russia was preparing a “massive attack” and urged residents not to ignore air raid alerts. Many Kyiv residents headed to the capital’s deep underground metro stations overnight to seek shelter. Despite the advance warning, air defense systems were unable to stop all the missiles.
” (Photo: AP Photo/Alex Brandon)
Zelenskyy particularly emphasized the difficulty of countering ballistic missiles and again called on Kyiv’s allies to provide Ukraine with additional Patriot systems and ammunition. Shortages of both have made it especially difficult for Ukraine to defend its cities.
“Russian ballistic missiles remain the greatest challenge. Air defense packages are a vital need for us right now,” he said.
Russia, for its part, confirmed that it had carried out a “massive attack” but claimed its targets were facilities connected to Ukraine’s military industry. The Defense Ministry in Moscow said it struck sites where missiles and drones are manufactured and stored, including facilities linked to Fire Point, which produces, among other weapons, Ukraine’s Flamingo cruise missiles. Russia also claimed it attacked port infrastructure and shipyards in the Odesa region, as well as vessels it said were used by the Ukrainian military.
At the same time, Ukraine continued its long-range strikes inside Russia. Zelenskyy said two oil facilities and a training complex in the Perm, Samara and Astrakhan regions had been attacked over the previous 24 hours. He called the strikes “a justified Ukrainian response to all Russian attacks against our people.”
Zelenskyy also released footage of an oil tanker burning in the Black Sea near Sochi. European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen condemned the Russian attack, saying that “Russia is pursuing a deliberate strategy of terror” aimed at making everyday life impossible for Ukrainians.

articles.title: Bipartisan US Senators Press Trump Administration to Crack Down on Russia’s Shadow Fleet and War Financing
articles.body:
Two senior US senators from both parties are pressing the Trump administration to intensify economic pressure on Russia by targeting its shadow oil fleet, financial networks and foreign suppliers of military technology before sweeping new sanctions provisions take effect on Oct. 18.
In an Oct. 7 letter to Secretary of State Marco Rubio and Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent, Democratic Senator Jeanne Shaheen and Republican Senator Roger Wicker warned that Moscow continues to exploit gaps in Western sanctions to finance its war against Ukraine.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
“Every day that passes without maximum economic pressure allows Moscow to sustain this military escalation,” the senators wrote.
Shaheen, the ranking Democrat on the Senate Foreign Relations Committee, and Wicker, chairman of the Senate Armed Services Committee, urged the administration to fully implement the Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act of 2026, signed into law by President Donald Trump last month.
“The majority of the Act’s provisions go into effect on October 18th, and it is vital that the Departments of State and the Treasury use these new tools to cut off the revenue streams and dual-use technology pipelines keeping Russia’s war machine alive,” they wrote.
The bipartisan appeal comes as Russia intensifies missile and drone attacks on Ukrainian cities and energy infrastructure.
The senators specifically cited Russia’s use of additional North Korean troops and its escalating strikes against Ukrainian civilians as reasons for urgent action.
Russia’s Donbas Advance Goes Into Reverse as Ukraine Retakes Ground
The senators identified Russia’s shadow fleet – tankers used to transport Russian oil while evading Western restrictions – as the most urgent target.
According to the letter, the European Union and United Kingdom have sanctioned more than 600 vessels, compared with just 216 designated by the US, most of them in early 2025.
That disparity, they warned, allows hundreds of tankers to continue transporting Russian oil and generating revenue for the Kremlin.
While European restrictions have disrupted shipping operations through asset freezes and port bans, US sanctions could cut vessels off from dollar-based transactions and Western maritime services.
The senators urged Washington to coordinate with European allies and match their existing designations vessel by vessel.
They also called for expanding sanctions against intermediaries in Dubai and Hong Kong that facilitate Russian oil exports despite earlier US restrictions on major Russian energy companies Lukoil and Rosneft.
The lawmakers acknowledged the Trump administration’s October 2025 sanctions against the two companies but argued that Moscow had adapted by routing transactions through new networks of intermediaries.
Banks in China and Kyrgyzstan under scrutiny
The letter also demanded a crackdown on financial networks that help Russia move billions of dollars beyond the reach of Western restrictions.
Shaheen and Wicker urged the Treasury Department to expand enforcement against the A7 financial network and its associated entities, which they described as a channel for Russian sanctions evasion and illicit procurement.
They specifically identified remaining overseas branches of Russia’s VTB Bank, including in Shanghai, and financial institutions in Kyrgyzstan accused of facilitating transactions involving sanctioned capital.
“Foreign banks must be forced to make a choice: They can either do business with the United States or finance Russia’s war. They cannot do both,” the senators wrote.
The proposed measures would extend US financial pressure beyond Russia itself, targeting foreign institutions and companies that help Moscow maintain international commercial and banking operations.
China, Turkey and UAE identified as Russian military supply hubs
The senators urged Washington to crack down on foreign networks supplying Russia’s military-industrial complex, identifying China, Turkey and the United Arab Emirates as major transit hubs for sensitive Western technology.
They singled out advanced machinery used to manufacture ammunition and critical microelectronics powering Russia’s jet-powered attack drones – equipment that helps Moscow sustain its war against Ukraine.
Calling for “mandatory secondary sanctions to penalize entities feeding Russia’s military-industrial complex,” the senators demanded tougher measures against foreign companies helping Moscow evade restrictions and maintain weapons production.
Their warning comes as Russia continues to expand drone and missile production while intensifying attacks on Ukrainian cities.
Russia’s satellite ambitions also targeted
Beyond conventional weapons production, the senators urged the administration to sanction Russian companies involved in developing low-Earth orbit satellite capabilities.
They specifically named Bureau 1440 LLC, 5C Group LLC and Eltex Enterprise LLC, along with procurement networks operating across China and Central Asia.
The lawmakers warned that a functioning Russian low-Earth orbit communications network could provide Moscow’s forces with more resilient command-and-control capabilities and improved targeting.
They argued that disrupting these satellite projects before their large-scale deployment would be crucial to protecting Ukrainian forces and civilians.
The senators also called for strict enforcement of provisions barring new US investment in Russia and prohibiting American persons or institutions from dealing in Russian sovereign debt.
They said the Treasury Department must issue clear guidance before Oct. 18, including in connection with publicly reported negotiations involving Lukoil’s international assets.
Bipartisan pressure ahead of sanctions deadline
The Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act was passed by Congress with broad bipartisan support and signed into law in September.
Named after the late Republican senator who championed tougher sanctions against Moscow, the legislation provides additional authorities to target Russian energy revenues, financial institutions, foreign intermediaries and companies supporting Russia’s military production.
“The October 18 implementation deadline is a critical opportunity to show both our allies and adversaries that U.S. sanctions are comprehensive, dynamic, and strictly enforced,” Shaheen and Wicker wrote.
Their letter makes clear that, in the senators’ view, sanctions against major Russian companies alone are insufficient while Moscow can continue selling oil, accessing foreign financial institutions and importing critical weapons components through third countries.
The question now is how aggressively Washington will use its new powers to close those gaps – and cut the financial and technological pipelines sustaining Russia’s war against Ukraine.
