articles.title: President Yotova: Bulgaria Seeks Black Sea Moratorium and Stronger Anti-Drone Defenses
articles.body:
President Yotova: Bulgaria Seeks Black Sea Moratorium and Stronger Anti-Drone Defenses
President Iliana Yotova said Bulgaria will propose a moratorium on hostilities in the Black Sea, seek stronger allied surveillance and anti-drone capabilities, and pursue diplomatic efforts with all Black Sea littoral states following a meeting of the Consultative Council for National Security (CCNS) on the drone attacks against two commercial vessels in Bulgaria's exclusive economic zone.
The CCNS meeting, convened by Yotova, focused on current risks and threats to Bulgaria's maritime security and critical infrastructure in the context of the war in Ukraine. Representatives of parliamentary groups, the Speaker of the National Assembly Mihaela Dotsova, Prime Minister Rumen Radev, the ministers of Defense, Interior, Foreign Affairs, Environment and Water, Deputy Minister of Finance Lyudmila Petkova, the Chief of Defense, and the heads of security and intelligence services took part.
The session lasted five hours. Representatives of the special services reported on threats to shipping security arising from the war in Ukraine and assessed the protection of strategic infrastructure against possible drone attacks.
Yotova said the participants had identified a deterioration of the security environment in the Black Sea and an escalation of hostilities between Russia and Ukraine.
"Russia's war against Ukraine has led to a significant deterioration of the security environment in the Black Sea region. The Consultative Council on National Security discussed current risks and threats to the maritime security and critical infrastructure of the Republic of Bulgaria in the context of the war in Ukraine and in light of incidents that have occurred in the Black Sea in recent days. During the meeting, an escalation of hostilities in the conflict between the Russian Federation and Ukraine was noted, threatening maritime security and freedom of navigation in the Black Sea region," Yotova said.
She said the council had also identified a growing number of attacks involving naval and aerial drones against commercial vessels, with consequences including damage to and sinking of ships and loss of life.
"There is a growing trend of attacks using naval and aerial drones against commercial vessels, resulting in damage to and the sinking of ships, as well as the loss of human life. This has led to restrictions on freedom of navigation, a sharp decline in shipping traffic, increased insurance costs, economic losses, and the risk of environmental pollution," the President said.
The council agreed that the growing use of advanced, long-range unmanned systems is increasing threats to Bulgaria's critical infrastructure not only around the Black Sea but throughout the country.
"A consensus was reached that the use of an increasing number of highly advanced, long-range unmanned systems has significantly heightened threats to the Republic of Bulgaria's critical infrastructure - not only in the vicinity of the Black Sea but across the country's entire territory," Yotova said.
The security of strategic facilities in Bulgaria's defense industry was also examined. According to the position presented after the meeting, the country faces serious challenges in protecting its critical infrastructure.
The CCNS linked the current risks to the inability to resolve the military conflict in Ukraine through diplomatic means and agreed to continue implementing measures already adopted by the Council of Ministers. Participants also called for an analysis of the existing regulatory framework and possible amendments needed to implement those measures.
The council adopted a package of proposals for the executive and legislative branches with a three-quarters majority, as required by law. Representatives of three parliamentary groups voted against the proposals.
One of the decisions directly addressed the attacks on commercial vessels in the Black Sea. The CCNS condemned the strikes as a gross violation of international maritime law and called for an immediate investigation to establish who was responsible and for the government to make the findings public once the investigation is complete.
"The Consultative Council on National Security unequivocally condemns the strikes on merchant vessels in the Black Sea as a gross violation of international maritime law and insists on an immediate investigation to identify the perpetrators. Once the investigation is concluded, the executive branch must inform the public of the findings," Yotova stated.
The proposals also call for Bulgaria to take an active part in diplomatic efforts aimed at ending the war, while continuing government measures against identified risks and threats.
"The greatest guarantee of our security is an immediate ceasefire and the utilization of all political and diplomatic channels to achieve peace. Bulgaria must play an active role in this process," the President said.
The CCNS recommended improving maritime situational awareness through unmanned aerial systems for reconnaissance and surveillance. It also called for faster modernization of the Armed Forces, including the acquisition of anti-drone systems with kinetic engagement capabilities, in close cooperation with NATO and the European Union.
Another proposal requires the executive branch to review the existing legal framework and submit amendments to the National Assembly where necessary, with the aim of supporting physical protection of strategic sites and strengthening the state's ability to ensure maritime security.
"The executive branch should analyze and propose to the National Assembly amendments to the existing regulatory framework in order to support physical protection measures for strategic sites and ensure the country's maritime security," Yotova said.
The council also recommended keeping Bulgaria's national maritime search and rescue system at a high level of readiness.
Regarding NATO, the proposals call for Bulgaria to use its membership in the Alliance and the European Union to protect its security, economic and environmental interests and contribute to stability in the Black Sea region.
"Bulgaria should utilize its capacity as a full member of the EU and NATO to articulate a firm stance and ensure the protection of its security, economic, and environmental interests, as well as regional stability," Yotova stated.
The council said NATO's enhanced vigilance activities along the Eastern Flank provide an opportunity for Bulgaria to seek a greater allied contribution to Black Sea security. The measures could include additional air and maritime surveillance assets, stronger coastal defenses and improved capabilities against unmanned systems.
"There is an opportunity for us to request increased allied contributions to Black Sea regional security, to activate options for deploying additional air and maritime surveillance assets, and to strengthen coastal defense systems and anti-drone capabilities within the framework of NATO’s enhanced forward presence," Yotova said.
The President emphasized that the proposed measures are compatible with the Montreux Convention.
The possibility of seeking consultations with NATO allies under Article 4 of the North Atlantic Treaty was also discussed. Yotova said the council considered such a move counterproductive at this stage because incidents of this kind should instead be discussed within the North Atlantic Council and an Article 4 consultation would not produce new measures.
Bulgaria will also propose that the European Union establish a framework to support free and safe navigation in the Black Sea as part of its strategic approach to the region.
"Bulgaria should propose that the EU develop a framework mechanism for free and safe shipping in the Black Sea as part of its strategic approach to the Black Sea region," Yotova said.
She noted that maritime security is already one of the main pillars of the EU's Black Sea strategy and that a dedicated Black Sea security hub is planned, but said more specific proposals are needed and that Bulgaria could play an active role in developing them.
The proposals include using European satellite surveillance capabilities to identify potential threats at an early stage. Bulgaria could also seek activation of the EU Civil Protection Mechanism if incidents create environmental risks, use monitoring tools of the European Union Satellite Centre to detect threats, and explore financial compensation for losses.
The CCNS called for urgent consultations with Romania and Turkey on coordinated action against attacks on commercial vessels and measures to protect navigation in the Black Sea.
A central diplomatic initiative would involve Bulgaria seeking consensus among all Black Sea littoral states on a moratorium on hostilities at sea and turning the region into a zone of shared security.
"Bulgaria should take an active role in negotiations to reach a consensus among the Black Sea littoral states, Russia, Ukraine, Bulgaria, Romania, Georgia, and Turkey, on a moratorium regarding hostilities in the Black Sea and on transforming it into a zone of shared security," Yotova said.
Bulgaria is also expected to raise Black Sea risks, threats and possible security solutions in all relevant European forums, particularly at the European Union summit on October 15 and 16.
At the United Nations, Bulgaria will seek assistance in clarifying the technical and legal aspects of incidents in the Black Sea and pursue a resolution guaranteeing freedom and safety of navigation. The proposal specifically calls for the involvement of mechanisms of the UN's International Maritime Organization.
The meeting was held after two merchant vessels were attacked inside Bulgaria's exclusive economic zone in the Black Sea. The attacks occurred on October 6 approximately 70 nautical miles, or 130-150 kilometers, from the Bulgarian coast, east of Cape St. Atanas and the town of Byala.
One vessel, sailing under the Togolese flag, suffered severe structural damage and sank within three minutes. The other, sailing under the flag of Palau, caught fire.
The fate of the crew of the sunken ship remained unknown. The Bulgarian ro-ro vessel Dioscuria, which was nearby, saw the explosion and went to the scene. An overturned boat, three capsized life rafts and life jackets were found, but no people were located.
The Navy and Air Force deployed assets to the search, including two helicopters and a Su-25 aircraft. All 18 crew members of the second vessel were rescued. Two sailors were injured, including an Indian national who was hospitalized in Varna in serious condition with burns. The Turkish captain suffered injuries to his head, chest and left leg but was discharged after receiving medical treatment.
Following the attacks, President Rumen Radev held an emergency meeting with representatives of the Defense, Interior, Transport and Environment ministries, the Presidency and security services. He described the incident as an "absolutely unacceptable attack" in Bulgaria's exclusive economic zone and a "flagrant violation of international law." He also warned that the continuation of the war was widening its geographical scope and increasing risks to security and civilian shipping.
The origin of the drones had not been established immediately after the attack. The Prime Minister said it was not possible at that stage to determine with certainty which country the aircraft came from. Bulgaria notified the European Commission and the European Council, while the issue was also raised with NATO.
Authorities were simultaneously monitoring another vessel considered a potential risk after it was struck in August and left drifting without a crew and with a failed control system. The Air Force carried out aerial surveillance, while relevant institutions said they were ready to act if the vessel moved toward the Bulgarian coast. Possible marine pollution resulting from the attacks was also being monitored.
Prime Minister Rumen Radev said Bulgaria would send a diplomatic note to the country responsible if the drones were established to be Russian or Ukrainian.
"At the moment, I can say there is no direct threat to Bulgaria's national security." Radev said after attending the CCNS meeting on the attacks against the ships.
He questioned the effectiveness of relying on military action alone and pointed to the continued use of drone strikes by both sides despite spending on defense.
"How many hundreds of billions have been spent on defending Ukraine against drone strikes? Do the strikes continue? They do. How much has Russia spent on defense? Do the Ukrainian strikes continue? They do. There are many tools in the diplomatic arsenal that are not being used; we are relying solely on military action," he said.
Radev said Bulgaria would establish the nature of the drones before identifying their origin and would follow the same procedure used in the case of the drone in Kardam.
"If the drones turn out to be Russian or Ukrainian, we will immediately send a diplomatic note to the respective country. We will do everything to determine the nature of the drones. That is what happened with the drone in Kardam, too. Initially, we did not announce what it was; we only revealed the drone's identity after the necessary checks and analyses. We will proceed the same way in this case," Radev said.
Kostadin Kostadinov, leader of Revival, left the CCNS meeting saying participants had failed to reach consensus on the proposed position. He said he could not support the draft submitted by the Presidency because it dealt with the consequences of the Black Sea situation rather than its causes.
"Clearly, no decision will be reached. There was, of course, a proposal for a position statement from the presidency - one I cannot support because it contains many points that raise more questions than they answer. The entire statement proposed by Ms. Yotova, regarding which we have not, at least for the moment, reached a common decision, discusses the consequences but fails to address the causes of the very situation that prompted the convening of the Consultative Council," Kostadinov said.
He warned that similar incidents could continue as the war develops and said he had serious concerns that the conflict could intensify.
"Ships have been hit in the Black Sea. Unfortunately, this will continue to happen, and I have very serious concerns, shared by others present at the council, that the conflict will intensify and that there will be other such incidents, let’s call them. We cannot convene a Consultative Council on National Security for every single case of this kind," he said.
Kostadinov also argued that the pre-election environment had influenced the decision to convene the meeting, although he said he attended because of his responsibilities as a statesman.
He objected in particular to the proposal that Bulgaria should participate actively in the peace process, arguing that it was inconsistent with the country's actions toward Russia.
"The proposed document stated that Bulgaria should actively participate in the peace process. I asked a question: how can that be, given that just three weeks ago, Bulgaria, represented by Ms. Yotova herself, supported a declaration condemning the actions of the Russian Federation? How can that be, given that Bulgaria is currently participating in discussions on the next package of EU sanctions against Russia?" Kostadinov said.
He also cited Bulgaria's arms exports and argued that the country should instead seek to act as a mediator between Moscow and Kyiv.
"When Bulgaria acts not as a mediator but as an instigator, when it pursues a policy that is clearly failing right now, given that we are currently exporting weapons worth hundreds of millions of euros (exports haven't stopped at all; they are happening this very moment), how can Bulgaria speak of achieving peace while fueling the war? It is monstrous hypocrisy. And for that very reason, I could not support this proposal," the Revival leader said.
Kostadinov said the meeting had also considered a proposal for Bulgaria to formally address Russia over military activity inside Bulgaria's exclusive economic zone.
He cited the proposed wording as calling on Bulgaria "to demand that Russia cease and refrain from conducting military or other offensive actions within Bulgaria's Exclusive Economic Zone in the Black Sea."
He said information provided during the closed meeting indicated that there was still no definitive evidence establishing where the drones that struck the two vessels had originated.
Kostadinov also disputed Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky's statement that the origin of the drones had been established jointly with Bulgarian security services. He said Bulgarian services had requested information but had not yet received an answer.
"I asked a specific question. Our services have requested information. They do not yet have an answer. They will receive one, but they do not have it yet," Kostadinov said.
He accused Zelensky of lying and suggested that the statement could be connected to Bulgaria's pre-election situation, describing this as his political assessment.
Kostadinov said Bulgaria did not have an independent policy on the war and security in the Black Sea. He added that sensitive information had been presented during the closed session that he could not disclose publicly.
"Other things were said as well, things I cannot share, but they are quite alarming regarding our readiness for surveillance, defense, and so forth. Frankly, all of this reflects extremely poorly on the policies pursued by Bulgarian governments in recent years. And by 'years,' I mean more than a decade. In practice, this policy of vassalage rather than sovereignty has failed. We are seeing the consequences of that right now. I am deeply concerned about our country's future," the Revival leader said.
The CCNS is chaired by the head of state and includes the Speaker of the National Assembly, the Prime Minister, the ministers of Defense, Interior, Foreign Affairs and Finance, the heads of key security agencies and structures, the Chief of Defense, and one representative from each parliamentary group.
After hours of deliberations, Deputy Finance Minister Lyudmila Petkova and State Agency for Intelligence (DAR) head Antoine Gechev were the first participants to leave, at around 5:00 PM.
Bulgaria Is Dangerously Unprepared for Drone Defense
On October 6, drones struck two commercial vessels inside Bulgaria's exclusive economic zone in the Black Sea, roughly 70 nautical miles off the coast near Cape St. Atanas and the town of Byala
Bulgaria Approves New Gunpowder Plant Near Smyadovo
Rumen Radev’s government has approved Emiliyan Gebrev’s planned gunpowder plant after the Council of Ministers decided Wednesday to add the company behind the project to the list of strategic sites considered important to national security

Two commercial vessels were attacked by aerial and maritime drones overnight on October 6 inside Bulgaria’s Exclusive Economic Zone, about 70 nautical miles east of Byala, with one ship sinking, the crew of the other evacuated and two people injured
Expert on Fox News: Russian Geran-4 Drone Likely Used in Black Sea Ship Attack
A suspected coordinated attack by aerial and maritime drones on two commercial vessels inside Bulgaria’s exclusive economic zone was likely carried out using a Russian Geran-4 drone
Bulgaria to Add Five Air Defense Missile Systems Following Black Sea Drone Attack
Prime Minister Rumen Radev said the government will approve an investment expenditure plan for five additional air defense missile systems, while warning that developing capabilities against unmanned systems in the air and maritime domains requires time,

articles.title: Russo-Ukrainian war, day 1687: Russian missile barrage kills 22 in Pryluky on Putin’s birthday
articles.body:
Exclusives
Military
Ukraine says it struck plant making parts for Russian military aircraft engines—a Snizhne factory Russia has used since 2014. Ukraine's 413th Raid Regiment has released footage showing the strike on a facility that produces components for gas-turbine engines used in attack aircraft and combat helicopters.
Intelligence and technology
Ukraine squeezes more defense out of Soviet-era stock, pairing Kub launcher and American RIM-7 interceptors to catch Russia’s jet-powered drones. The hybrid has already downed about 20 air targets.
Kalashnikov, Russia’s biggest small-arms maker, says it fills its entire 2026 arms contract on time with batch of 7.62mm Dragunov sniper rifle. Ukraine's Defense Intelligence said in February that nearly half of Kalashnikov's plants faced no sanctions from any coalition country.
German radar already guarding Ukraine is picked to spot ballistic missiles. Its maker just signed a new deal with Kyiv. Hensoldt and Kyiv will also study jointly operating a bigger radar, the TRL-4D LR, whose naval version reaches beyond 400 km.
Russia’s jet drones fly near 600 km/h now. Ukraine is building simulators for the 900 km/h ones it expects next. When a Russian jet drone and the drone chasing it move at the same speed, the pilot can barely tell the two apart—and the Russian models keep getting faster.
Ukraine finds US-made navigation sensor inside Russia’s new jet-powered drone. The PNI5GA sensor reduces gyroscope drift and improves the drone's autonomous navigation accuracy, according to Ukrainian intelligence.
International
First time since 2018: NATO’s top military body went to Kyiv to study the war it may one day face. Military representatives of all 32 members heard the latest battlefield assessment from Ukraine's command.
Latvia stops armed migrant push from Belarus, then loses border cameras to masked raiders hours later. The escorts threatened Latvian soldiers before the raiders slipped back to Belarus ahead of the border guards.
Humanitarian and social impact
Oleksandr, Kyrylo and Serhii, all aged one, and eight-year-old Maksym were killed in Ukraine’s city by Russian strike on Putin’s birthday. A Russian missile flattened an apartment block in Pryluky.
14 dead in Pryluky, two each in Kyiv, Kremenchuk, and Oleksandriia: Russia’s night of 70 missiles. Five children were among the 26 people injured when a missile collapsed part of a five-story building.
Russia’s war on Ukrainian books: a second strike burns tens of thousands of a Kyiv publisher’s rebuilt titles. Knyholav lost new titles and reprints of books Russia had already burned in July.
Ukraine adds Kyiv trains, prepares pontoon crossings after Russian bridge attacks. Emergency pontoon crossings could take up to three months to build, Ukraine's Minister for Restoration, Infrastructure and Transport says.
Political and legal developments
Russia starts pouring more into war after Putin judged Alaska talks with US would bring no “acceptable” deal to end fighting — Bloomberg. Russia's 2026 budget deficit has nearly doubled to more than $81 billion, as war spending blows past the original plan.
Russia’s war against Ukraine sends the bill to its own companies: bond defaults head for a 17-year high. The squeeze is spreading from small firms to Moscow's own budget, which is running a record deficit to keep the war going.
New developments
Ukrainian drugmakers sold $114 million worth of medicines to Uzbekistan in six months. Now they may lose the right to sell there. That export cash keeps medicine prices low at home. Without it, drugs could get pricier for Ukrainian patients, a former regulator official says.
Taliban and North Korea rubbed shoulders at Russia’s war games—one fuels Moscow’s war, the other needs its help. Two isolated governments in Russia's orbit turned up at the same drills—though only Kabul has said they met.
25-year-old Natalia, born in Russia, served in the Israeli army, returned to Ukraine during the full-scale invasion, and join the Armed Forces of Ukraine. Ukrainian society is not yet ready for the mandatory mobilization of women into the military, she believes.
Read our earlier daily review here.
Read Also
- Russo-Ukrainian war, day 1686: Sanctioned tankers carried fuel from South Korea to Russia
- Russo-Ukrainian war, day 1685: Ukraine fires its first FP-7 ballistic missile
- Russo-Ukrainian war, day 1682: Russian drones repeatedly hit Kyiv’s Southern Bridge, forcing transport restrictions across the capital

articles.title: Pakistan joins Saudi airstrikes on Yemen’s Houthis: report
articles.body:
- A senior Pakistani military official told The New York Times that Pakistani fighter jets have carried out strikes against Yemen’s Houthis.
- A second official called it air support against Houthi drone and missile threats and ruled out a Pakistani ground offensive inside Yemen.
Pakistan Air Force fighter jets are being used in strikes against Yemen’s Houthi rebels, a senior Pakistani military official told The New York Times, the first indication from inside Pakistan’s military that its air force has joined Saudi Arabia’s renewed war against the Iran-backed group.
A second Pakistani official told the newspaper that Pakistan’s role is expected to focus on degrading Houthi drone and missile threats through air support, and not on a ground offensive in Yemen. Neither official said how many aircraft are involved, which targets have been hit, when the strikes began or whether the jets are striking inside Yemeni territory, and Pakistan’s military declined to comment.
Col. David O. Smith, a former U.S. Army attaché in Pakistan and former Defense Intelligence Agency analyst, told the Times that analysts broadly estimate about 8,000 Pakistani troops have deployed to Saudi Arabia, including Pakistan Air Force and Army air defense units. He said they would likely help protect oil infrastructure and were unlikely to fight the Houthis directly, given Islamabad’s effort to preserve its relationship with neighboring Iran.
The report follows Monday’s decision by Saudi Arabia, Pakistan and Turkey to activate the Mecca Joint Defense Agreement, a mutual defense pact the three countries signed on Aug. 7. At an emergency meeting in Riyadh, they agreed to put collective deterrence measures into effect and rapidly deploy Pakistani and Turkish forces to the kingdom, the first time the pact had been invoked. Hours later, Pakistani Defense Minister Khawaja Asif said Pakistani forces were already playing a part, although when reporters asked him on Sept. 30 whether Pakistani forces had joined strikes in Yemen, he did not answer directly.
Pakistan’s military spokesman, Lt. Gen. Ahmed Sharif Chaudhry, confirmed this week that Pakistani troops are stationed in Saudi Arabia but declined to say whether they would operate across the border in Yemen, telling CNN that any involvement would be defensive in nature.
Over the past several days, Saudi Arabia said Houthi missile and drone strikes on King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh and Abha International Airport in the south killed three people, two women at Abha and a Sudanese man at King Khalid, and injured 36. The Saudi-led coalition said it retaliated by hitting dozens of Houthi military sites in Yemen, including missile storage sites and command centers, and on Thursday residents of Riyadh reported hearing several explosions whose cause was not immediately clear.
The Houthis declared a blockade of the Red Sea in July and attacked shipping there, then seized Yemen’s Red Sea coast in a rapid offensive last month, routing Saudi-backed government forces. The Saudi-led coalition says 100 fighter jets are now supporting a counteroffensive by Yemen’s internationally recognized government to retake that territory, and a United Nations agency said nearly 200,000 people have been displaced in Yemen since early September.
Islamabad has long kept its distance from the Yemen war: in 2015, when Saudi Arabia launched its original campaign against the Houthis and asked Pakistan for jets, ships and troops, Pakistan’s parliament voted to stay neutral. Iran’s Foreign Ministry said on Sunday it hoped reports of a Pakistani deployment for the war in Yemen were untrue.
Saudi Arabia and Pakistan signed a separate bilateral mutual defense agreement in September 2025, declaring an attack on either country an attack on both, and the Mecca pact extended that commitment to Turkey, whose parliament has not yet ratified it.

articles.title: ‘War Is His Nature’: Zelensky Says Putin’s Birthday ‘Gift’ Killed 25 Ukrainians
articles.body:
Russian missile and drone attacks across Ukraine on Wednesday, Oct. 7 – Russian President Vladimir Putin’s 74th birthday – killed at least 32 people, including five children, as rescuers recovered more bodies from destroyed residential buildings in Kyiv and Pryluky early Thursday.
The updated death toll followed the discovery of two bodies inside a drone-hit apartment building in Kyiv’s Desnianskyi district and additional fatalities beneath the rubble of a five-story residential building in Pryluky, Chernihiv Oblast.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
Ukraine’s State Emergency Service (DSNS) reported Thursday morning that the death toll in Pryluky had risen to 22, while the discovery of two additional victims in Kyiv brought the reported toll from the capital’s latest attacks to four.
Interior Minister Ivan Vyhivskyi had reported 28 deaths nationwide Wednesday evening, before the latest discoveries.
President Volodymyr Zelensky condemned the attacks, which coincided with Putin’s birthday.
“Such a ‘gift’ Putin gave himself for his birthday. The killing of children, the killing of people,” the Ukrainian leader said in his evening address.
“It is in his interest to wage war. War is his nature, his ideology,” he added.
Five children among 22 killed in Pryluky
The deadliest attack struck Pryluky in Chernihiv Oblast, where a Russian Kh-101 cruise missile hit a five-story residential building, causing sections of the structure to collapse as families were inside.
Kazakhstan Says Talks Underway to Bring Russia’s Kazakh Fighters Home
By Thursday morning, the death toll had risen to 22, including five children. Three of those killed were just one year old.
Around 55 people were injured, according to regional authorities.
Rescuers worked through the night, searching collapsed floors and shattered apartments for survivors.
Emergency workers used ladders to reach the upper floors of the damaged building, bringing 15 people to safety as rescue operations continued.
Photographs from the scene showed excavators and emergency crews clearing piles of concrete and twisted metal where apartments had stood.
“There’s a lot of destruction, especially in the town centre,” Pryluky Deputy Mayor Danylo Savenko told Reuters, describing how he and his wife had rushed into a shelter after hearing incoming missiles.
Interior Minister Vyhivskyi also described the rescue of a five-year-old girl and her mother, who were thrown from their apartment by the force of the explosion.
DSNS squad commander Pavlo Levchenko helped pull them from the wreckage and carried the child to safety.
The attack also damaged a gas pipeline, temporarily leaving more than 18,000 residents without gas.
Kyiv Post previously reported on the children killed in Pryluky, including three one-year-old boys.
Two more bodies discovered in Kyiv
The death toll from Russian attacks on Kyiv also increased early Thursday, Oct. 8, after rescuers discovered two bodies inside a damaged apartment in the capital’s Desnianskyi district.
According to the State Emergency Service, a Russian drone struck a 12-story residential building near the 10th floor, sparking a fire and partially destroying structural elements.
Four people were injured, including two children, while firefighters rescued 22 residents, eight of them children.
The discovery followed two deaths reported in Obolonskyi district during Wednesday evening’s attacks, where falling drone debris set parked vehicles ablaze in the courtyard of a residential building.
Earlier Wednesday, Kyiv had also come under ballistic missile attack, with explosions reported across the capital shortly after 3 a.m.
Russian drones struck a five-story residential building in Solomianskyi district later that day, setting the first three floors on fire and injuring eight residents.
Debris also damaged buildings in other districts as emergency crews responded to fires and destruction.
Kyiv Post has reported on the Russian attacks across Kyiv, including the latest discovery of two bodies in Desnianskyi district.
Russian strikes hit Kremenchuk and Oleksandriia
The Russian bombardment extended across multiple Ukrainian regions, damaging residential buildings, industrial facilities and energy infrastructure.
In Kremenchuk, Poltava Oblast, Russian missiles and drones killed two people and injured dozens more, according to local authorities.
Oleksandriia in Kirovohrad Oblast was also among the cities where fatalities were reported.
Ukrainian authorities said Russia launched 70 missiles, including ballistic weapons, and dozens of attack drones during the large-scale assault.
Air defenses intercepted a majority of the drones, but Zelensky warned that Russia’s ballistic missiles remained particularly difficult to stop.
He said Ukraine was urgently seeking additional Patriot air defense systems to protect civilian lives.
In his evening address, Zelensky accused Moscow of continuing to escalate its war despite diplomatic efforts to secure peace.
“This is exactly what Moscow chooses despite all our efforts with our partners to bring peace closer,” he said.
He urged international leaders not to remain silent over Russian attacks on civilians and called for stronger economic and military pressure on the Kremlin.
Zelensky also criticized discussions about easing sanctions against Russian oligarchs, warning that Moscow still had access to financial resources needed to sustain the war.
“Putin still does not feel that this is creating real problems for him,” he said.
He argued that Russia’s continued ability to export oil and conduct international financial transactions showed that sanctions pressure remained insufficient.
“And this is not only Ukraine’s problem, not only our problem, and not only the problem of our people and our children. It is a problem for everyone in Europe and the Western world,” Zelensky said.
As rescue crews continued searching the wreckage of destroyed Ukrainian homes on Thursday, the death toll from Russia’s Oct. 7 attacks climbed to at least 32 – leaving families mourning children and loved ones killed on Putin’s 74th birthday.

articles.title: Houthi Attacks on Saudi Airports Kill 3 Amid Escalating War in Yemen
articles.body:
The Iran-aligned Houthi rebels said they launched another strike on Riyadh’s main airport, after earlier attacks on Saudi Arabia killed three and injured 36.
The Houthis said they targeted King Khalid International Airport on Thursday, soon after an attack on the airport killed one person and wounded eight. Saudi Arabia has not confirmed Thursday’s attack. Another two people were killed and 28 wounded in an attack on Abha International Airport, the country’s civil aviation authorities said on Wednesday. The earlier attacks happened on Tuesday and Wednesday, although the authorities did not specify the date of each. The Houthis claimed responsibility for those strikes.
On Thursday, Houthi spokesperson Yahya Saree warned airlines “for the last time” not to continue their flights in Saudi airspace, calling it a “theater” for Houthi military operations.
A Saudi-led coalition said late on Wednesday that the attacks “will not go unpunished.” It said it had destroyed 82 Houthi military sites across Saada, Hodeidah, Jawf, and Marib in Yemen.
The rebel group has carried out a series of attacks on infrastructure in Saudi Arabia since Yemen’s government forces launched a major offensive aimed at recapturing key territory around the Bab el-Mandeb Strait that had been seized by the Houthis. Yemeni forces, supported by Saudi airstrikes, said they had reached Mokha on Monday and driven the Houthis back from the strait, although the Houthis dispute those claims.
The fighting has revived the yearslong civil war in Yemen that created one of the world’s worst humanitarian crises. More than 200,000 people have been displaced since the latest exchange of fire began in June, the International Organization for Migration said on Wednesday. The Saudi-led coalition accuses Iran of arming and funding the Houthis, which both Iran and the rebel group deny.
It has also opened up a new front in the U.S. and Israel’s war against Iran, which began on Feb. 28 with a wave of U.S.-Israeli strikes. The Houthis reportedly received direction from Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps to capture Mokha last month to threaten global shipping and energy flows through another shipping route. The battle over Bab el-Mandeb has become more important amid new attacks on vessels through the Strait of Hormuz in recent weeks, as Iran seeks to re-assert its leverage over Hormuz.
Attacks on airports
Attacks on airports are a recurrent tactic by the Houthis.
The attack on the Riyadh airport killed a Sudanese national, and injured five Saudi citizens, two Egyptian residents, and a Pakistani resident, Saudi authorities said. The attack on Abha airport killed a Moroccan woman and an Algerian woman, and injured Saudi citizens, a Bangladeshi resident, and a Filipino resident.
Earlier on Wednesday, Yemeni authorities said ballistic missile and drone strikes targeted Aden international airport in Yemen. One missile landed near the runway shortly before a flight from Cairo was scheduled to land, Yemen’s Transport Ministry said. The Houthis acknowledged a missile strike nearby but said their target was a military camp.
The Saudi civilian aviation authorities also said two airports in the kingdom’s south were attacked on Monday evening, injuring three people. The airports, King Abdullah bin Abdulaziz International Airport in Jazan and Najran International Airport, suffered material damage, the authorities announced on Tuesday.
Last month, Saudi Arabia accused the Houthis of attempting an attack on Mecca, calling it a “red line.” The Houthis denied the allegations, as did Iran.
War widens
Saudi Arabia has sought help from a number of its allies to fight the Houthis. Turkey has sent defensive and technical support, Reuters reported on Wednesday, citing officials. Saudi Arabia signed the Mecca Joint Defence Agreement with Turkey and Pakistan in August, and the three parties agreed to implement its collective defence commitments earlier this week.
Syria, another Saudi ally, is also weighing providing military aid, Reuters reported, which could include defensive aid or deploying forces on the ground to support the Yemeni offensive against the Houthis. The Syrian foreign ministry did not confirm any potential plan to Reuters and said, “Should Saudi Arabia request any military cooperation or exchange of expertise, this would take place exclusively through official channels and within the framework of the bilateral agreements governing relations between our two brotherly countries.”
Saudi Arabia also reportedly requested assistance from the U.S., although President Donald Trump has thus far declined requests for direct U.S. strikes against the Houthis. The U.S. has instead provided the kingdom with intelligence support.
Tanker attacks in Hormuz
Although Middle East oil exports have ticked up in recent weeks, renewed attacks on vessels near the Strait of Hormuz have raised the stakes at Bab El-Mandeb, which became a critical alternative route for Saudi oil exports earlier in the Iran War.
Last week, attacks on tankers in the Strait of Hormuz hit their highest weekly level since the Iran War began. There were at least 12 attacks on oil, LNG, and LPG tankers near the Strait of Hormuz between Sept. 28 and Oct. 5, Reuters reported, citing data from three maritime security sources.
Attacks have continued this week.
India’s foreign ministry reported on Tuesday that 12 crew members were injured after an unknown projectile struck a Panama-flagged oil tanker sailing through Hormuz off the coast of Oman.
An unidentified tanker was also struck by multiple projectiles off the northern coast of Qatar on Wednesday, marking a rare attack deep inside the Persian Gulf. The attack resulted in an unknown number of casualties, the U.K. Maritime Trade Operations (UKMTO) said. Authorities launched an investigation into the incident. No one has claimed responsibility for the attack.
Iran said on Wednesday that it would close “illegal” routes that have been used to bypass Tehran’s blockade in the Strait of Hormuz, including a southern route close to Oman’s coast.
“The Strait of Hormuz is closed, and the armed forces of the Islamic Republic of Iran have full control over it,” Mohammadreza Naqdi, an adviser to the Revolutionary Guards’ Commander, told the IRGC-linked Fars news agency.
Naqdi said the “few routes” circumventing Tehran’s blockade were created by blowing up rocky passages in the Strait. He said the routes were used by “small boats smuggling oil and transferring it to tankers.”
Despite Naqdi’s claims, Middle Eastern crude exports exceeded pre-war levels on 14 days in September, according to maritime analytics firm Kpler, which included shipments via Hormuz, the Red Sea, and other routes. U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio said Wednesday that Iran had “lost complete control of the Strait” as the U.S. Navy continues escorting some vessels through the Strait.
“There’s almost as much oil flowing out now as there was before this conflict began,” he told reporters while on a visit in Athens.
Nevertheless, analysts previously told TIME that increased attacks in the Strait, coupled with the threat to Bab el-Mandeb, could quickly raise shipping costs and disrupt flows. Brent crude again topped $100 a barrel on Wednesday after retreating from nearly $110 a barrel last month.
The White House has also reportedly asked the Pentagon to develop options for strikes on Iran before November’s midterm elections, although no decision has been made. Trump has sought to ease concerns about the war’s economic toll, claiming Iran is holding out in hopes of hurting Republicans in the midterms and predicting that the war will end soon afterward. Strikes before the vote would end a weekslong lull in U.S. attacks on Iran, and could prompt further retaliation from Iran against energy assets and shipping in the Gulf.

articles.title: Iranian strikes forced US troops to ‘abandon’ Kuwait base – CBS (VIDEO)
articles.body:
Iranian strikes forced US troops to ‘abandon’ Kuwait base – CBS (VIDEO)
Iranian strikes forced US troops to effectively abandon a major military base in Kuwait during the opening stages of the US-Israeli war on Iran, according to newly released footage and accounts from American servicemen obtained by CBS News.
Videos shared by American soldiers in breach of the Pentagon’s strict media policy show several drones nosediving into Camp Buehring, a major US Army staging facility roughly 40 km from the Iraqi border, as well as damage to buildings and military equipment. CBS said it authenticated the recordings using embedded metadata and imagery of the aftermath.
The installation came under repeated attack by Iranian ballistic missiles and drones after hostilities began on February 28. A US service member also told CBS that Iranian F-5 fighter jets flew missions against the base “so close to us I could see their helmets.”
Most of the roughly 7,000 troops stationed at Camp Buehring had already been dispersed before the war under what the Pentagon called its “get off the X” strategy, aimed at moving personnel away from fixed positions vulnerable to Iranian retaliation.
Some 100 soldiers, however, remained behind to defend the installation, where they were repeatedly forced into bunkers and ran critically low on ammunition, including Patriot interceptors.
“They hit us bad,” one serviceman told the outlet. “It was horrible... We had to abandon the base.”
The remaining troops eventually fled the base and established improvised forward operating outposts in the Kuwaiti desert, where they remained for weeks. No US personnel were killed, although several were injured, including two who were struck by lightning during desert sandstorms.
“CBKU got demolished,” the serviceman said. “They need to do an investigation. How come no one came to reinforce us?”
The Pentagon declined to comment directly on the CBS report, instead referring the outlet to remarks made by Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth in March, when he acknowledged that more than 90% of American personnel had been moved away from US regional bases.
The revelations come days after an Associated Press investigation raised separate questions about US preparations elsewhere in Kuwait. An Iranian drone struck an American operations center at Port Shuaiba on March 1, killing six soldiers and wounding dozens in what remains the deadliest known single attack on American troops during the conflict. Some of the wounded said troops initially treated each other with basic first-aid supplies and had to use Google to locate the nearest hospital in Kuwait City. The Pentagon has maintained that its medical response was appropriate.
The devastation at Camp Buehring was part of a much broader campaign against the US military footprint across the Middle East, with Iranian missiles and drones striking bases and installations in multiple countries and damaging aircraft, radar systems, hangars, barracks, and other infrastructure.
By September, CENTCOM said the war had already cost Washington $43.6 billion, a figure that did not include extensive damage to US bases across eight countries. The true personnel toll has also remained disputed: the Pentagon publicly listed 18 military deaths as of mid-September, while military sources cited by the Washington Post put the figure at 22 or 23.
As the damage mounted, the Pentagon tightened control over images emerging from the region. After an Iranian missile and drone strike on Muwaffaq Salti Air Base in Jordan on July 17 killed three US service members, CENTCOM commander Admiral Brad Cooper warned troops against filming strike sites, claiming that publicly posted footage was helping Tehran assess the accuracy and effects of its attacks. US allies hosting American bases have likewise imposed strict bans and penalties on filming military sites and strike aftermaths, making independent footage of Iranian attacks increasingly rare.

articles.title: Ukraine war latest: Russian attack on Pryluky kills at least 20, including 5 children
articles.body:
Ukraine war latest: Russian attack on Pryluky kills at least 20, including 5 children
Key developments on Oct. 7:
- Russia slams Ukraine with missiles, drones on Putin's 74th birthday, at least 26 dead including 5 children
- Huge blaze breaks out at Russian oil facility in Samara Oblast
- EU provides Ukraine 1.2 billion euros for drones and missiles
- Russia carried out sabotage against Danish defense firms, intelligence says
- Erdogan raises Black Sea safety in call with Putin
At least 26 people have been killed in yet another Russian overnight mass missile and drone attack on Ukrainian cities on Oct. 7, coinciding with Russian President Vladimir Putin's 74th birthday.
In the city of Pryluky, in Chernihiv Oblast, a Russian cruise missile hit a residential building, killing at least 20 people, including five children, and wounding at least 55, including seven children.
Three of the dead children, named Oleksandr, Kyrylo, and Serhiy, were only one year old, President Volodymyr Zelensky said in a post on social media. The other child was an eight-year-old named Maksym, he added.
A fifth child was killed by the Russian strike, as Ukraine's state emergency service (DSNS) said as of 7:13 p.m. local time.
"Today, as a 'birthday gift' to Putin, the Russian army destroyed a residential building in Pryluky, in the Chernihiv region," Zelensky said.
"It was an ordinary five-story apartment block. There may still be people under the rubble. First responders are working nonstop at the site – doing everything possible to find every person," he added.
Chernihiv Oblast Governor Viacheslav Chaus said that on Putin's birthday, he hopes "the Russian dictator ends up in custody in The Hague or in hell."
"That is all he deserves."
Pryluky resident Halyna Osovyk, 55, woke up, and soon after, her flat was shaken by an explosion, she told the Kyiv Independent. Then came more strikes, smoke, and shattered windows. Across the road, two entrances of a neighboring apartment building were destroyed, and rescuers were searching the rubble for people.
The woman herself was still shaking as she spoke. Her hands and legs trembled.
"It was just sheer horror. And the sound of the missiles — you simply cannot put it into words," Osovyk said.
She knew some of those affected. One family was trapped under the debris – the mother, grandmother, and one child were killed, while another child was rescued and taken to the hospital. Another woman and her child were also pulled from the rubble and hospitalized, Osovyk said. As rescuers continued clearing the ruins, people waited for news of relatives who were still missing.
Pryluky had experienced Russian attacks before, she added, but never a morning like this. Asked what she would wish for Putin on his birthday, she replied: "I wish he could have what we are going through now."
read also
Huge blaze breaks out at Russian oil facility in Samara Oblast
Large fires have broken out at a major oil pipeline and storage facility in Russia's Samara Oblast, according to footage shared on social media and NASA satellite monitoring.
Footage posted to social media showed large fires and clouds of black smoke above the facility, which is a major node in Russia's network of oil pipelines.
NASA's Fire Information for Resource Management System (FIRMS), which uses satellite data to detect thermal anomalies and fires, detected multiple hotspots at the facility.
The facility, which is located near the village of Prosvet, in Samara Oblast, includes pumping stations, tank farms, and blending stations. It has been a repeated target during Ukraine's campaign of deep strikes against Russian oil infrastructure.
Earlier that day, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky alluded to a Ukrainian strike on oil facilities in Samara Oblast, without specifying which facility had been hit.
read also
EU provides Ukraine 1.2 billion euros for drones and missiles
The European Commission announced the disbursement of 1.24 billion euros ($1.4 billion) of defense support to Ukraine on Oct. 7, part of the bloc's 90 billion euro support loan ($100 billion) for Kyiv.
"Today's disbursement will help strengthen Ukraine's defense industry. And Ukraine's ability to defend itself. To protect people and infrastructure," said European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen in a press statement.
"The money will be spent on drones, drone interceptors, drone ammunition, and missiles manufactured by Ukrainian entities," reads the press release.
The EU's 90 billion euro loan to Ukraine, approved in April 2026, was intended to provide two-thirds of Kyiv's financial and defense needs until the end of 2027.
In 2026, 28.3 billion euros ($31.7 billion) was earmarked for defense, and Ukraine's plans for how to spend that money have all been submitted and approved by Brussels.
read also
Russia carried out sabotage against Danish defense firms, intelligence says
Russia has stepped up efforts to disrupt Danish companies involved in supplying weapons to Ukraine, Denmark's intelligence service representative told Reuters on Oct. 7.
Josefine Christensen, an analyst at the Danish national security and intelligence service (PET), said Russia was increasingly focusing on targets directly connected to Western military support for Ukraine.
According to Christensen, Russia planned a lot of operations in spring but carried out "very little," while in early summer they started to carry out "a lot more."
She added that Russia's operational boldness is growing as it is now trying to hit targets that have a direct impact on the front line, meaning weapons production.
Russia is relying on individuals recruited online to conduct such operations. Some are first tasked with gathering information or photographing potential targets before being offered more serious assignments.
European drone manufacturers and suppliers have attracted particular attention. Christensen cited a list released by Russia's Defense Ministry in April that included European companies involved in producing drones and related components.
read also
Erdogan raises Black Sea safety in call with Putin
Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan called Russian President Vladimir Putin on Oct. 7, telling him Turkey is ready to contribute to efforts for direct talks between Russia and Ukraine, and stressing the importance of the safety of navigation in the Black Sea, according to Erdogan's office.
The two Presidents discussed bilateral relations, as well as regional and global issues, Turkey's Directorate of Communications said.
Erdogan also congratulated Putin on his birthday and his party's success in the latest Russian parliamentary elections, the office said.
The security situation for Black Sea shipping has worsened over the past weeks.
On Oct. 5, a cargo ship caught fire in the Black Sea off the Romanian coast after a Russian drone strike, killing two, injuring at least 11 more, and prompting a large search-and-rescue operation.
After Romanian media and authorities initially reported a fire on the grain ship Royad Mammadov, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky confirmed that a civilian ship was attacked by two Russian drones, adding that it was a Turkish-owned ship transporting corn.
According to Zelensky, the ship was crewed by citizens of Azerbaijan and India. While the Russian strike killed the vessel's captain, Zelensky said. Romania's interior ministry said that two people were killed in the attack.

articles.title: Syria mulls military aid to Saudi Arabia in fight against Houthis
articles.body:
Syria is weighing military assistance to key ally Saudi Arabia, U.S. and Syrian officials said, as the Iran-aligned Houthis step up missile and drone attacks on the kingdom that killed three people at Saudi airports this week.
The possible entry of Syrian forces into the battle, a spillover of the US-Iran conflict, shows how Yemen's reignited civil war has added new chaos to a region already aflame and risks drawing regional states into grueling mountain fighting.
Saudi Arabia has pushed for support from allied nations, including Türkiye and Pakistan, even if only in a logistical or purely defensive capacity, an effort made more urgent by the Houthi strikes on its infrastructure such as this week's deadly airport attacks.
A succession of loud booms were reported in Riyadh Thursday morning. There was no immediate official comment and no public early warning alerts, although some diplomats said they had received warnings, and some schools in Riyadh warned parents of shelter in place orders, according to Reuters.
Yemen's Houthi rebels, however, claimed Thursday that it had attacked King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh with a ballistic missile. The Saudi government media office did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
One person had been killed in a strike on Riyadh airport and two others in an attack on Abha airport in the southwest Tuesday and Wednesday, Saudi Arabia said late Wednesday.
Meanwhile, the U.S. and Syrian officials said Damascus was carefully considering military support, including the option of defensive aid to protect Saudi Arabia from attacks or deployment in an offensive capacity to help Saudi-backed Yemeni troops take the fight to the Houthis.
Yemen's long-running civil war, which paused with a cease-fire in 2022, has erupted again in recent weeks with the Houthis seizing stretches of the Red Sea coast last month, including along the vital Bab el-Mandeb Strait.
The Houthis have said they were responding to attacks from the Saudi-backed government, which the government denies.
The group's threats to shipping along a waterway that has become ever more critical for Gulf oil exports since Iran's attacks in the Strait of Hormuz and its targeting of Saudi cities and infrastructure, have drawn the kingdom back in.
In response to a request for comment to the Syrian Foreign Ministry, a Syrian diplomat said Syria stood firmly with Saudi Arabia in the face of Houthi attacks but that the government's primary focus was on domestic priorities such as recovery from the country's 14-year civil war.
"Should Saudi Arabia request any military cooperation or exchange of expertise, this would take place exclusively through official channels and within the framework of the bilateral agreements governing relations between our two brotherly countries," the diplomat said in a statement.
This week, Saudi-backed forces launched a counterattack, taking back areas around the strait as they push to reverse the Houthis' gains of last month.
However, in a messy war with several frontlines, the Houthis have also made some gains of their own this week, surrounding the country's third-largest city of Taiz by taking territory along its main mountain road to Aden.
The fighting, which pits the Houthis against a coalition of Saudi-backed forces under the internationally recognized government, has led to a humanitarian crisis in the poorest Arab state, displacing 200,000 people since the conflict resumed.
Saudi Arabia this summer agreed the Mecca pact with Türkiye and Pakistan, committing all three countries to come to each other's defense, though Ankara still needs to ratify the treaty internally.
NATO-member Türkiye said Wednesday it was sending mainly defensive and technical support to the kingdom to help in the fight against the Houthis, and a Turkish official said this was expected to take the form of military equipment, intelligence sharing and weapons systems.
Pakistan, meanwhile, has flown cargo planes of military equipment to Aden in southern Yemen to help in the battle against the Houthis, sources in Pakistan have said and has deployed troops inside Saudi Arabia to help defend the kingdom's borders.

articles.title: Europe is in revolt – its leaders are preparing for war
articles.body:
Europe is in revolt – its leaders are preparing for war
Europe’s leaders have grand plans – spend more on weapons, prepare for war, and tighten citizens’ belts. The people have more immediate concerns however, like finding somewhere to live, keeping their jobs, and getting an education. Across France, Germany, Spain, and other EU states, the widening rift has started to spill into the streets.
Recent weeks have seen housing marches across Spain, student riots and public-sector strikes in France, and demonstrations against military recruitment and industrial job cuts in Germany. Immigration has added to the anger over housing and overstretched services, while the prospect of conscription has young Germans asking whose wars they are expected to fight.
The demands differ, but a recurring complaint unites them – aside from those simply looking for an excuse to wreak havoc: governments aren’t listening. Instead of putting domestic problems first, European leaders are telling their constituents to accept less and sacrifice more, while committing billions to preparations for a suicidal war with Russia. That’s despite Moscow and even Europe’s own intelligence services repeatedly saying there is no imminent threat.
Spain: Priced out and fed up
Spain’s housing crisis has pushed tens of thousands into the streets. After years of soaring rents, the eviction of an 87-year-old woman from her home of 70 years in Madrid last month turned into a rallying point for those sick of being priced out of their homes and the government’s failure to tackle the housing affordability crisis.
The eviction sparked demonstrations across Spain, followed by mass marches and a continuing protest camp in central Madrid. Parliament’s subsequent rejection of emergency tenant protections added even more fuel to the fire, bringing tens of thousands into the streets in around 50 cities last weekend.
Rents in Spain have almost doubled over the past decade as immigration-driven population growth has continued to outstrip housing construction. The population, excluding migration, has meanwhile only continued to decline.
The pressure is even more visible in Ceuta, Spain’s North African enclave, where around 72,000 people crossed from Morocco in late July into a territory with roughly 84,000 inhabitants. Although most returned, thousands remained, overwhelming accommodation and straining public services.
Residents have taken to the streets demanding stronger border controls and faster deportations, accusing Madrid of abandoning them. Protests have escalated into clashes with police, while angry locals have torn down makeshift migrant camps.
Government promises to restore order have done little to quell the frustration of communities left to absorb the consequences.
France: School’s out
France has also been gripped by overlapping protests over wages, spending cuts, public services, and school conditions. Teachers, healthcare workers, firefighters and transport staff have joined numerous strikes in recent weeks, while a growing student movement has added school blockades to the disruption.
The school protests began in mid-September, with students demanding more teachers, smaller classes, repairs to neglected buildings, and lighter schedules. Thousands of teaching posts have been eliminated this year, with further cuts planned for next year.
Around 266,000 people joined demonstrations nationwide on Tuesday. More than 6,500 have been arrested over three weeks, while hundreds of students and police officers have been injured, including a 15-year-old who lost his hand to a police grenade and a 16-year-old who reportedly lost sight in one eye after being hit by a rubber bullet.
As the movement has grown, violent groups have joined the protests, torching buses, attacking emergency workers, and damaging schools. Across France, 24 schools have been burned or ransacked.
Similar demonstrations have spread to neighboring Belgium, where students have opposed education reforms, higher transport costs, and rising tuition fees. In Liege, school blockades have been accompanied by vandalism, fires and arrests.
France: The cuts keep coming
The student demonstrations came on the heels of wider protests that have gripped France for weeks, with public-sector workers protesting a squeeze on wages and services, compounded by soaring fuel prices.
Since 2017, public-sector pay has risen by 5%, while cumulative inflation has reached 24%. The government’s proposed €54 billion ($60.4 billion) budget package, which includes spending cuts and freezes affecting pensions and benefits, has only deepened the anger.
Other demonstrations have also challenged continued funding for Ukraine, with protesters arguing that the money should go toward hospitals, education, and lower fuel taxes.
Separate rallies in more than 20 cities have also opposed a bill that could give police shootings the presumption of legality, which critics say would make officers harder to hold accountable.
Germany: Factories shrink, the military grows
In Germany, workers and students have taken to the streets as Berlin pursues a frenzied military buildup in the midst of a deepening industrial crisis with hundreds of thousands losing their livelihoods and young men facing the prospect of being drafted.
Around 45,000 students joined protests in some 100 cities and towns in late September, carrying banners reading ‘We won’t fight in your wars’ and ‘Education instead of bombs’.
The government meanwhile is pressing ahead with plans to expand the armed forces to more than 260,000 active troops and 200,000 reservists by 2035 to align with Chancellor Friedrich Merz’s fixation on creating “Europe’s strongest conventional army.”
Young men are already required to register for potential service, but politicians have been pushing for a return to conscription if voluntary recruitment fails to fill the ranks.
Aside from the thousands protesting such plans in the streets, resistance is also showing up in applications to avoid military service. More than 12,000 people sought conscientious objector status in the first eight months of this year – over three times the total for all of last year.
Tens of thousands of automotive workers have also protested sweeping job cuts and threats to factories. Volkswagen, for example, plans to shed 100,000 jobs across its brands, while other manufacturers are cutting production or moving it abroad.
Germany’s industrial woes have been further compounded by the loss of cheap Russian energy, which helped make its manufacturers competitive. Higher energy costs, US tariffs, and Chinese competition are now squeezing businesses and threatening jobs across the sector.
For arms manufacturers, however, Berlin’s priorities and its latest €108.2 billion defense budget have been good for business. While Volkswagen shares have fallen more than 75% from their 2021 peak, Rheinmetall’s have soared over 1,100% since early 2022. One Volkswagen factory is even set to shift toward producing military equipment for an Israeli arms company.
More guns and more fear
Even with streets burning and protesters demanding relief, European leaders have not let the turmoil distract them from their military ambitions.
In France, Macron marked Tuesday’s mass demonstrations by publicizing a nuclear missile test, posting a photograph of himself watching the launch with his back to the camera. While his constituents marched for better living conditions, his message was that France “must be feared to remain free.”
In Germany, Merz and NATO chief Mark Rutte smiled and waved through boos and chants of “murderers” and “blood on your hands” after the military bloc received the Westphalian Peace Prize last week. Inside the ceremony, officials praised military strength as the foundation of peace.
Those priorities are also taking shape in Brussels’ budget negotiations. Germany and five other EU states have demanded cuts to the bloc’s next budget, pushing to sacrifice funding for farmers and poorer regions in favor of ever-growing military spending.
The urgency is being justified by the supposed threat of a future Russian attack. However, Moscow has repeatedly denied any such plans, while even Finland’s president has admitted that his intelligence services see no imminent military threat.
Nevertheless, for European leaders, preparations for that hypothetical conflict, which they appear to almost count on, continue to take precedence over the mounting problems already bringing people out onto the streets.

articles.title: Sam Altman says AI will make ‘bad things’ happen. Exhibit A: needless death | Moustafa Bayoumi
articles.body:
Sam Altman, the chief executive of OpenAI, has some words for you about his company and the future of artificial intelligence.
“One of the differences between us and some of the stricter AI safety people is that we believe that the world should accept some bad things happening for the benefits of this technology and people having the agency [to use it],” Altman told Politico’s new technology podcast and newsletter Decoded.
Yikes. This statement – and the approach it represents – is, well, problematic, to say the least. It’s also emblematic of precisely the kind of world-building and world-destroying that is happening with today’s technology in front of all our eyes, with precious little input from the rest of us.
Altman’s mention of the “bad things” that AI might bring makes it sound like AI’s failures mistakenly create innocent, minor problems or even silly little episodes, such as the time when Google’s “AI Overviews” told users to put non-toxic glue on pizza so the cheese will be less likely to slide off. Good advice is helpful. Bad advice? Chalk it up to being a bad thing.
But culinary adventurism is hardly the only realm that AI operates in and the damage AI is inflicting has already and repeatedly proven itself to be dangerous and even potentially deadly to humans.
OpenAI is embroiled in a lawsuit after the tragic suicide of Adam Raine, a 16-year-old student who initially began using OpenAI’s ChatGPT for homework help. The family’s lawsuit alleges that the teenager took his own life with the chatbot’s encouragement. (OpenAI has claimed Raine misused the platform.)
And Raine’s action is hardly the only one. OpenAI is facing multiple lawsuits filed by different families of victims of suicide and self-harm.
Nor is suicide the only “bad thing” to emerge in the AI universe. In February of this year, on the first day of the war in Iran, two Tomahawk missiles struck the Shajareh Tayyebeh elementary school in the city of Minab, killing at least 120 children. (A UN fact-finding mission concluded that the US was likely responsible for the strike.)
In a recent investigation into the attack, Bloomberg News reported that an AI-linked system was used to target the school. In this case, the system is called Maven, and it is made by Palantir.
Unnamed defense officials told Bloomberg that “inside Centcom, which conducted the US attack, some personnel relied too much on the artificial intelligence embedded in Maven Smart System”. The report also adds that “in the past year, the Defense Department has rapidly made Maven a cornerstone of the US military apparatus”.
AI is helping to produce these tragic and needless deaths, but bad things happen, I guess.
Or there’s the little detail that the US may have come within a hair’s breadth of starting a major war against a superpower, all due to an AI error.
In September, CNN reported that an unidentified AI chatbot used by the US military decided that a Chinese ship in Middle Eastern waters was carrying components of a nuclear weapons program. According to CNN, US planes took off on an interception mission and US military personnel were preparing to board the ship.
Only then did the military look more closely at the report they were basing the mission on and realize the chatbot’s mistakes.
Also found in CNN’s frightening story is that the analyst who used the chatbot to come up with the shoddy analysis then used AI again to write the report, which set the whole thing in motion. A twofer of bad things, I suppose.
Why does it seem that these technologies, which, in the words of Trump’s White House, are “empowering Americans to achieve what was previously impossible across science, medicine, and nearly every other domain of human endeavor”, get such serious stuff so wrong and so often?
And isn’t it true that the more we rely on AI, the more dangerous these little mistakes become? And why were we never consulted about any of this in the first place?
Could it be that what’s behind the artificial intelligence revolution may be less about the utopian or dystopian future (take your pick) that’s just around the corner and more about the enormous amount of money that is being poured into these companies in the present?
AI may be the only thing keeping Trump’s economy afloat right now. And it’s paying dividends. According to the New Yorker, OpenAI “is reportedly preparing for an initial public offering at a potential valuation of a trillion dollars” and Sam Altman “may become one of the wealthiest and most powerful people on the planet”.
Those bad things? They only happen to other people.
Meanwhile, we are being warned almost every day that AI systems are getting so smart that they’ll end humanity.
But maybe the real worry here is not that the machines are taking over.
It’s that the humans are giving up, ceding control and responsibility in the name of hyping up a product that has shown itself as being really good at taking jobs away from people, stealing the intellectual property of others, writing some piss-poor undergraduate essays, spying on you and your license plates and bringing us to the brink of world war three because God forbid humans should actually question the output from machines. Or the makers of those machines.
What we need is real, tangible and enforceable government oversight over these technologies, which are quickly becoming a dominating force in all our lives. We must collectively have the right to decide how AI should be used. And despite what you may hear, China already regulates its AI companies quite aggressively.
Instead, Donald Trump, Mark Zuckerberg, CEO of Meta and Jensen Huang, CEO of Nvidia believe that the AI companies should simply regulate themselves, so they have come up with something called the AI Accords.
Signed by leaders of Meta, Nvidia, Google, Anthropic, xAI, and OpenAI, the accords ask tech companies to “implement robust internal controls and monitor the capabilities and alignment of its models”, among other things. “Over time,” the agreement states, “it may make sense to codify these steps into laws or regulations.”
I’m not holding my breath.
Trump, who has ordered the term artificial intelligence be discarded for “super intelligence”, posted the accord on social media on 29 September. The document, titled The White House Accord on Super Intelligence, can still be seen on his account and the White House’s official account. It’s signed by all six tech leaders and Trump, who in the document is labeled “President of the Unites States.”
Super intelligence, indeed.
In the US, you can call or text the 988 Suicide & Crisis Lifeline at 988 or chat at 988lifeline.org. In the UK and Ireland, Samaritans can be contacted on freephone 116 123. In Australia, the crisis support service Lifeline is 13 11 14. Other international helplines can be found at befrienders.org
- Moustafa Bayoumi is the author of the award-winning books How Does It Feel to Be a Problem?: Being Young and Arab in America and This Muslim American Life: Dispatches from the War on Terror. He is professor of English at Brooklyn College, City University of New York, and a Guardian US columnist

articles.title: Fewer targets, more waves: jet-powered Gerans partly free Russia to concentrate missiles, ISW says
articles.body:
Russia is concentrating missiles on a smaller, more specific set of targets, and its jet-powered attack drones are part of the reason, the Institute for the Study of War (ISW) assessed. Its combined attack overnight on 7 October killed 22 people in Pryluky, the State Emergency Service (SES) said as of the morning of 8 October. Russian milbloggers noted the shift the same day.
Russia often uses concentrated drone and missile strikes to overwhelm localized Ukrainian air defenses and destroy urban centers, ISW noted. Pryluky, where the strike killed children, was one of the areas a Russian channel says drew a significant share of the Kh-101s that night. With winter close, ISW expects the same pattern against Ukraine's energy grid, with jet drones partly letting Russia keep its missiles for priority targets without firing many more.
Missile waves on a few areas, Russian channels claim
Russia launched 48 Kh-101, Iskander-K, and Kalibr cruise missiles overnight on 7 October, Ukraine's Air Force reported. It also fired ballistic missiles, Zircon and Oniks anti-ship missiles, and 130 strike and decoy drones, 46 of them jet-powered Shahed-type models.
Russian milbloggers claimed the same day that Moscow had grouped a large part of its missile salvo into repeated waves on a few areas, while other weapons kept stretching Ukraine's air defenses elsewhere. The pro-war Russian Telegram channel Dva Mayora described the change as a switch from striking with splayed fingers to a series of hits with missile "fists." Defenders must then absorb a sharply rising load around one chosen site as one wave follows another, the channel claimed.
Citing Ukrainian monitoring channels, it claimed that roughly 30 or more Kh-101 cruise missiles flew toward Pryluky, Kremenchuk, Svitlovodsk, and Oleksandriia in Chernihiv, Poltava, and Kirovohrad oblasts. It put the Kremenchuk group at up to 15 missiles, Kh-101s and Kalibrs among them, aimed at the area of Kremenchuk and its hydroelectric plant.
Jet drones take some of the load off Russia's missiles
ISW said the jet-powered versions penetrate Ukrainian air defenses deeper and more reliably than propeller models. In ISW's assessment, that partly lets Russia concentrate cruise and ballistic missiles on priority targets without significantly raising missile use. Russia builds about 3,000 Geran-4 and Geran-5 jet drones a month, Ukraine's military intelligence agency (HUR) told Militarnyi in August.
Ukraine spent three years learning to catch Russian drones—so Russia made them fly faster
ISW expects Russia to apply the pattern in a likely brutal winter campaign against energy infrastructure. Russia likely intends to make city life untenable and force Ukraine to capitulate to its demands, ISW assessed. Such tactics have not worked before and are unlikely to work now, analysts added.
They called cheap countermeasures to jet drones and small cruise missiles vital, alongside Western air defense aid such as US-made Patriots, which can stop ballistic missiles. Ukraine has already paired a Soviet-era Kub launcher with American RIM-7 interceptors to catch jet drones.

articles.title: Syria considers help in Yemen war after Saudi airports come under Houthi fire
articles.body:
Syria considers help in Yemen war after Saudi airports come under Houthi fire
RIYADH, Oct 8 - Syria may deploy troops to help Saudi Arabia fight Yemen's Houthis, a US official and a Syrian defence official said, as the Iran-aligned group steps up its missile and drone attacks on the kingdom, killing three people at Saudi airports this week.
The possible entry of Syrian forces into the battle, an overspill of the US-Iran conflict, shows how Yemen's reignited civil war has added new chaos to a region already aflame, and risks drawing regional states into gruelling mountain fighting.
Saudi Arabia has pushed for support from allied nations, including Turkey and Pakistan, even if only in a logistical or purely defensive capacity, an effort made more urgent by the Houthi strikes on its infrastructure such as this week's deadly airport attack.
A succession of loud booms was heard in Riyadh on Thursday morning which Reuters could not identify. There was no immediate official comment and no public early warning alerts, although some diplomats said they had received warnings, and some schools in Riyadh warned parents of shelter in place orders.
Yemen's Iran-aligned Houthi group said on Thursday it had attacked King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh with a ballistic missile. The Saudi government media office did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
OFFICIALS SAY SYRIAN AID COULD BE PURELY DEFENSIVE
One person had been killed in a strike on Riyadh airport and two others in an attack on Abha airport in the southwest on Tuesday and Wednesday, Saudi Arabia said late on Wednesday.
The US and Syrian officials said Syria was carefully considering military support, including the option of defensive aid to protect Saudi Arabia from attacks or deployment in an offensive capacity to help Saudi-backed Yemeni troops take the fight to the Houthis.
