Yemen's long-running civil war, which paused with a ceasefire in 2022, has erupted again in recent weeks with the Houthis seizing stretches of the Red Sea coast last month, including along the vital Bab el-Mandeb Strait. The Houthis have said they were responding to attacks from the Saudi-backed government, which the government denies.
The group's threats to shipping along a waterway that has become ever more critical for Gulf oil exports since Iran's attacks in the Strait of Hormuz, and its targeting of Saudi cities and infrastructure, have drawn the kingdom back in.
In response to a request for comment to the Syrian foreign ministry, a Syrian diplomat said Syria stood firmly with Saudi Arabia in the face of Houthi attacks but that the government's primary focus was on domestic priorities such as recovery from the country's civil war.
"Should Saudi Arabia request any military cooperation or exchange of expertise, this would take place exclusively through official channels and within the framework of the bilateral agreements governing relations between our two brotherly countries," the diplomat said in a statement.
SAUDI ARABIA SEEKING SUPPORT FROM ALLIES
This week, Saudi-backed forces launched a counter attack, taking back areas around the strait as they push to reverse the Houthis' gains of last month.
However, in a messy war with several frontlines, the Houthis have also made some gains of their own this week, surrounding the country's third-largest city of Taiz by taking territory along its main mountain road to Aden.
The fighting, which pits the Houthis against a coalition of Saudi-backed forces under the internationally recognised government, has led to a humanitarian crisis in the poorest Arab state, displacing 200,000 people since the conflict resumed.
Saudi Arabia this summer agreed the Mecca pact with Turkey and Pakistan, committing all three countries to come to each other's defence, though Ankara still needs to ratify the treaty internally.
NATO-member Turkey said on Wednesday it was sending mainly defensive and technical support to the kingdom to help in the fight against the Houthis, and a Turkish official said this was expected to take the form of military equipment, intelligence sharing and weapons systems.
Turkey, a close ally of Syria's government and a supporter of its forces while they were still rebels fighting the government of Bashar al-Assad, previously brought some Syrian fighters to Libya in 2020 to help in that country's civil war.
Pakistan has flown cargo planes of military equipment to Aden in southern Yemen to help in the battle against the Houthis, sources in Pakistan have said, and has deployed its own troops inside Saudi Arabia to help defend its borders.
The Saudi government media office and Yemen's information minister did not respond to requests for comment. REUTERS

articles.title: Houthis ramp up missile attacks on Riyadh as Saudi-backed war in Yemen widens
articles.body:
Yemen's Iran-aligned Houthis have stepped up their deadly campaign of strikes on Saudi Arabia's capital, Riyadh, where booms were heard on Thursday, flights were disrupted, and some office staff were told to work from home.
The Houthis said they had fired a ballistic missile at Riyadh airport and repeated a threat to force Saudi airspace to close after the kingdom gave support to the forces of Yemen's internationally recognized government in a reignited civil war.
The conflict, now an overspill of the US-Iran war, has added new chaos to a region already aflame, and threatens to draw other states into grueling mountain fighting - with Syria now considering deploying troops to assist Saudi Arabia.
The kingdom has pushed for support from allied nations, including Turkey and Pakistan, even if only in a logistical or defensive capacity, as it tries to reverse Houthi gains in southwest Yemen, by the southern entrance to the Red Sea.
Those requests have taken on more urgency since Saudi authorities said on Wednesday that three people had been killed this week in strikes on Riyadh airport and Abha airport in the southwest.
Civil war reignited by conflict with Iran
The flight tracker FlightRadar24 indicated numerous delayed arrivals and departures at Riyadh's King Khalid International Airport on Thursday.
Several multinational firms based in Riyadh's King Abdullah Financial District (KAFD) told staff to work from home after Thursday morning's loud booms, five people familiar with the matter said, including some affected staff.
The Saudi government did not respond to a request for comment, and KAFD was not immediately available for comment.
Some diplomats said they had received warnings, and some schools in Riyadh told parents there were orders to shelter in place, though authorities did not issue a public alert. Reuters could not identify the source of the booms.
Yemen's long-running civil war, which paused with a ceasefire in 2022, has erupted again in recent weeks with the Houthis seizing stretches of the Red Sea coast last month, including along the vital Bab el-Mandeb Strait.
The Houthis, who control many of Yemen's most populous areas, including the capital Sanaa, have said they were responding to attacks from the Saudi-backed government, which the government denies.
Their threats to shipping along a waterway that has become ever more critical for Gulf oil exports since Iran's attacks in the Strait of Hormuz, and their attacks on Saudi cities and infrastructure, have drawn the kingdom back in.
This week, Saudi-backed forces launched a counterattack, taking back areas around the strait.
However, in a war with several frontlines, the Houthis have made gains of their own, surrounding Yemen's third-largest city, Taiz, by taking territory along its main mountain road to Aden.
The fighting, which pits the Houthis against a coalition of Saudi-backed forces under the internationally recognized government, has led to a humanitarian crisis in the poorest Arab state, displacing 200,000 people since the conflict resumed.
Syrian aid might be purely defensive, officials say
One US and one Syrian defense official said Syria was carefully considering options for military support, including defensive aid to protect Saudi Arabia from attacks, or an offensive deployment to help take the fight to the Houthis.
In response to a request for comment to the Syrian foreign ministry, a diplomat said Syria stood firmly with Saudi Arabia but that its focus was on domestic priorities such as recovery from its own civil war.
Saudi Arabia this summer agreed to the Mecca Pact with Turkey and Pakistan, committing all three to come to each other's defense, though Ankara has yet to ratify the treaty.
NATO-member Turkey said on Wednesday it was sending mainly defensive and technical support to the kingdom to help in the fight against the Houthis. A Turkish official said this was expected to take the form of military equipment, intelligence sharing and weapons systems.
Turkey, a close ally of Syria's government and a supporter of its forces while they were still rebels fighting the government of Bashar al-Assad, previously brought some Syrians to fight in Libya's civil war in 2020.
Pakistan has flown military equipment to Aden in southern Yemen to help in the battle against the Houthis, sources in Pakistan have said, and has deployed troops within Saudi Arabia to help defend its borders.
The Saudi and Yemeni authorities did not respond to requests for comment.

articles.title: Russian attack on bus kills at least 30 people near Ukraine frontline
articles.body:
A Russian missile strike on a bus in the eastern city of Kramatorsk has killed at least 30 people, officials have said, in one of the worst attacks by Moscow on Ukrainian civilians this year.
The regional prosecutor’s office in the Donetsk region said on Thursday the vehicle had been hit at 10am by an aerial bomb. “As of now, the death toll from this morning’s attack has risen to 30. Eighteen people were wounded,” it said, adding that all local public transport had been suspended.
Images posted by police showed bodies strewn across a street littered with debris, as well as a charred shell of what appeared to be a bus. A second bus had also caught fire, officials said. The strike targeted an area next to a dental clinic on the city’s Yuvileina Street.
Three people had also been killed by shelling in the village of Bilenke, outside Kramatorsk, they added. Volodymyr Zelenskyy said the Kremlin had deliberately targeted an “ordinary public transport stop”.
Some of those killed could not be identified because of the severity of their injuries, Ukraine’s president added. He said the number of victims could “sadly rise”, as doctors fought to save the lives of those wounded.
He said: “This strike will not go unanswered. Russia is trying to destroy all life in Donbas, and a response from the world is a must. A forceful response – exactly as the Russians deserve for all the deaths they have brought. May all those killed rest in peace.”
The bombing follows a gruesome Russian strike on Wednesday on a five-storey block of flats in Pryluky in the northern Chernihiv region. The building collapsed, entombing those inside. At least 22 people were killed, including five children, aged between one and eight.
Visiting the scene with Ed Miliband, the British foreign secretary, Zelenskyy urged the US to expand Starlink satellite internet coverage so that Ukraine could hit targets inside Russia such as launch sites. So far, Donald Trump and Elon Musk have refused Kyiv’s request.
Miliband said there was “no clearer sign of Putin’s evil, evil intent and strategy in this conflict” than this week’s murderous attacks. He said: “Putin once said that he was going to win on the battlefield. He is trying to win by terrorising civilians.”
Writing earlier on social media, Zelenskyy called on western allies to take “concrete steps” to boost Ukraine’s depleted air defences, amid a round-the-clock Russian onslaught in recent weeks featuring ballistic missiles and jet-powered drones.
“Supplies of anti-ballistic capabilities, ammunition for our combat aircraft, and investments in interceptors – all of this is directly helping save lives every day. Important talks with our partners will take place today and tomorrow,” Zelenskyy said.
Kramatorsk and neighbouring Sloviansk form part of a “fortress belt”. They are the last two big cities in northern Donetsk under full Ukrainian military control. Russia has been trying to capture them for more than a decade, after a brief period in which Russian forces occupied Sloviansk in 2014.
The cities are home to thousands of civilians, as well as Ukrainian soldiers. In recent months, roads have been festooned with nets to protect traffic from marauding enemy drones. These defences offer little protection, however, against aerial bombs.
“These are not ‘the consequences of war’, nor dry statistics. These are people killed by the Russian army,” the Donetsk regional governor, Vadym Filashkin, said on Telegram after Wednesday’s strike. “Russia comes to Ukrainian land with death.”
He added: “The Russians are deliberately targeting civilians. For them, a bus full of passengers is an attractive target precisely because a single strike can kill as many people as possible.
“Russia deliberately flouts every conceivable rule of warfare and the norms of international humanitarian law. It selects targets where it can inflict the greatest suffering on civilians.”
There was criticism of the White House’s policy of engaging with Vladimir Putin, whom Donald Trump has invited to December’s G20 summit in Miami, Florida. The Kremlin has yet to say if Russia’s leader will take part.
The former US ambassador to Moscow Michael McFaul said on social media that Russia was guilty of terrorism. “There is no other word for it. Putin is running a terrorist state. That officials from my country call this terrorist a nice guy is deeply embarrassing for me.”
Putin has demanded Ukraine cede the rest of the eastern Donbas region still under its control. Kyiv refuses to hand over its territory, believing Russia will take any concessions and carry on fighting.

articles.title: Journalists analyse intercepted Russian plan to destroy Ukraine's energy infrastructure
articles.body:
Journalists analyse intercepted Russian plan to destroy Ukraine's energy infrastructure
Journalists from Skhemy, an investigative project by Radio Liberty, have examined a Russian plan to pressure Ukraine, which identifies as priority targets for strikes "nodes" near Ukraine's western border through which electricity is imported, major hydroelectric power plants and even nuclear power plants.
Source: Radio Liberty
Details: The journalists obtained a copy of the Russian plan from sources in Ukrainian forces and studied it in detail.
The plan intercepted by Ukraine concerns Russia's strategy to cut electricity and heat supplies to Ukraine's major cities by up to 90%.
"One of the largest attacks took place on the night of 29-30 September, when hundreds of Russian strike drones and ballistic missiles were launched against the energy infrastructure of the capital and Kyiv Oblast," Radio Liberty recalls.
At least three of the facilities attacked that night – two combined heat and power plants in Kyiv and one thermal power plant in Kyiv Oblast – were identified by Skhemy journalists as being included in the Russian plan.
The plan, apparently prepared by the Russian side and provided by Ukrainian intelligence, was presented to Ukraine's partners in Paris on 17 September by Energy Minister Denys Shmyhal at the energy meeting of the Ukraine Defence Contact Group (also known as the Ramstein format), Radio Liberty notes.
The copy of the plan contains an analysis of Ukraine's energy capacity and calculations of the number of missiles, drones and bombs Russia would need to cut major cities such as Kyiv, Kharkiv and Odesa off from electricity, heat and water.
The list of facilities "to be hit" includes nuclear power plants alongside small boiler houses.
However, the plan assesses them solely in terms of Ukrainians' electricity consumption in gigawatts, without any mention of the potential nuclear threat, the analysts note.
The plan identifies four priority targets: power generation and electricity supply, water supply, sewage and heating.
The first priority is to disable "nodes" near the western border through which electricity is imported from Europe.
These include cross-border power lines, high-voltage substations near the border and interconnectors – systems linking the power grids of Ukraine and EU countries, receiving European electricity and transforming it before transmitting it further into the country.
The plan also refers to major hydroelectric power plants, located mainly on the Dnipro and Dniester rivers, and the shutdown of three nuclear power plants – South Ukraine, Rivne and Khmelnytskyi. The Zaporizhzhia Nuclear Power Plant has been under Russian occupation since March 2022.
The plan lists a total of 60 key targets, including the aforementioned hydroelectric and nuclear power plants and interconnectors, as well as thermal power plants, combined heat and power plants, substations, boiler houses, wastewater treatment facilities, pumping stations and other state and municipal facilities on which electricity, water, sewage and heating depend.
The plan says that such attacks would require basic types of weapons: up to 770 Molniya and Geran UAVs and Dan-T/Banderol drone-launched cruise missiles, as well as 170 FABs (here and throughout the article, a modification of a high-explosive aerial bomb equipped with a universal planning and guidance module) and 75 Kinzhal aeroballistic and Iskander-M ballistic missiles.
The plan contains a detailed calculation for each facility, specifying how many weapons and of what type would be needed to disable it, Skhemy reported.
So, two Iskander missiles are envisaged for the destruction of a nuclear power plant (the plan refers to an "outdoor switchyard" – a high-voltage installation located outdoors that receives and transmits electricity). Accordingly, six missiles are required to destroy the equipment at three nuclear power plants.
As for hydroelectric power plants, up to 25 Molniyas, Gerans or Dan-T/Banderols, or three Kinzhal missiles, are allocated for each.
"In other words, for the destruction of 10 major Ukrainian hydroelectric power plants, depending on the distance to the launch site or line of contact, the document calculates a total of up to 30 Molniyas (for facilities located up to 60 km from the line of contact) and around 240 Gerans and Dan-T/Banderols, which can be replaced by Kinzhal ballistic missiles (probably up to 30)," Radio Liberty says.
For combined heat and power plants (five transformers), the calculation is likewise 25 Gerans and so on, or three Kinzhal missiles per facility. The plan also says that each combined heat and power plant could require around 25 FAB-500 bombs and five Iskander-M missiles.
For a substation (three transformers) or an interconnector, the calculation is 15 Molniyas and so on, or three Kinzhal missiles per facility. For housing and utilities infrastructure, it is 25 FABs or five Iskanders per facility, while a boiler house would require 20 Gerans.
Moreover, next to the section on boiler houses, the authors of the plan explicitly note that "due to their proximity to residential areas, the use of other types of weapons could result in civilian casualties".
The Russian plan specifies the types of weapons to be used "depending on the target and distance".
For example, it lists Molniyas and FAB-500s for distances of up to 40-60 km; Geran-4, Dan-T/Banderol and Iskander-M for 60-500 km; and Kinzhal, Kalibr, Oreshnik and Zircon for more than 500 km.
The capital's facilities occupy a special place in the plan, with Kyiv's energy system analysed and presented in detail.
The authors of the plan note that the capital's energy system is fairly extensive but identify five substations in the "Kyiv ring" serving different parts of the city as its "bottleneck", or more precisely, its weak point.
"Overall, according to the document, hitting 12 key substations in the three cities mentioned above should halt up to 90% of electricity supplies. For this, the authors of the document specify 40-50 Molniya drones and 130-140 Geran-4 or Dan-T/Banderol drone-launched missiles," Radio Liberty says.
Experts interviewed by the journalists say the plan is not a final operational plan but rather a set of calculations.
They also say this is not a new tactic, as Russia has systematically attacked Ukraine's energy infrastructure since the beginning of the full-scale invasion, turning cold and darkness into a weapon.
Subscribe on Patreon to back our journalism long-term.

articles.title: It was built to shield Russian crops from hail. Now it’s being pitched as a drone interceptor
articles.body:
Russia has shown a drone interceptor built on the Alazan, a civilian anti-hail rocket, Militarnyi reported. The sample went on display at a weapons exhibition that Russian dictator Vladimir Putin toured at the Chebarkul training range in the Urals on 2 October.
Ukraine now sends drones at Russia by the hundreds, by Moscow's own count. Russia's Defense Ministry claimed its air defenses intercepted nearly 900 overnight into 6 October. Russia's missile-based air defense was built to repel aircraft raids and a few cruise missiles, not swarms of low-flying drones.
In May, Ukrainian intelligence said Russia was adding four regiments, 24 battalions, and 162 batteries to counter Ukrainian strike drones. The converted Alazan, which Militarnyi calls an anti-drone system, is one more piece of that search. Meanwhile, the commander of Ukraine's Unmanned Systems Forces, Robert Brovdi, said his forces struck 300 Russian air-defense assets between January and 19 September.
From hail reagent to shrapnel
Based on the size of the sample on display, the interceptor builds on the Alazan-2M or Alazan-6 series, Militarnyi assessed. The outlet put the stated cost at up to $12,000 per unit but did not say who named the figure. In civilian service, the rocket flies about 10 km, climbs up to 8 km, and carries about 0.5 kg of reagent. For air defense, the developers plan to replace that reagent with a fragmentation warhead.
Militarnyi's analysis of the published photos describes the front end as a steering assembly: four cruciform deflector fins, probably paired with a seeker or a fuze. At the rear sit folding stabilizers and the open nozzle of a solid-fuel motor, held in a metal cradle.
One sample among 300 exhibits
The Kremlin's account of the visit lists more than 300 weapons on display, including interceptor drones, but does not mention the rocket. Propaganda channel Russia 1 aired the interceptor in its report from the visit, and the Kremlin pool of state news agency RIA posted photos.
Read also
- Ukraine squeezes more defense out of Soviet-era stock, pairing Kub launcher and American RIM-7 interceptors to catch Russia’s jet-powered drones
- Ukrainian units hit record number of Russian air defense systems and radars in September, one of them 552 kilometers away
- Ukraine’s answer to Russia’s jet-powered Shaheds: a small new missile named Nika, heading into testing

articles.title: In war-torn Kyiv, Elkin-led Israeli delegation confronts familiar threats while marking Babyn Yar
articles.body:
To the Israeli delegation visiting the Ukrainian capital this week, the sound of sirens warning of incoming drones or missiles was familiar. But one important difference: Ukraine has no Iron Dome, no multilayered Israeli-style air defense system that can provide the same sense of protection as back home. When the alerts sound, people simply head underground and wait.
That was how Tuesday night unfolded for former minister Kharkiv-born Ze'ev Elkin and members of an Israeli delegation visiting Kyiv this week.
As ballistic missiles and drones targeted the Ukrainian capital, the delegation eventually spent the night together in a makeshift shelter arranged by the Israeli Embassy at their hotel, sleeping on beds placed side-by-side inside the protected room.
Elkin and the delegation had arrived in Ukraine for the 85th anniversary of the Babyn Yar massacre, when Nazi forces and their collaborators murdered tens of thousands of Jews in a ravine outside Kyiv in September 1941.
Ukraine today is fighting a war that has entered another dangerous and uncertain phase. Russian forces continue to attack Ukrainian cities, while Ukrainian forces have demonstrated an increasing ability to strike targets deep inside Russia.
The deterioration in the security situation prompted several international delegations expected to attend the Babyn Yar commemorations to cancel their visits. Among the senior-level delegations that did arrive were those from Israel and Germany.
Elkin was part of Israeli delegation, including Yad Vashem officials, to attend Babyn Yar memorial
The Israeli delegation included Elkin, Yad Vashem Chairman Dani Dayan, Yad Vashem representatives, and senior officials involved in Israel’s relations with Ukraine.
The symbolism was striking: a ceremony dedicated to remembering one of the darkest chapters in European history taking place while the same continent is once again experiencing a major war.
The most significant political meeting came unexpectedly. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky invited Elkin and the delegation to meet with him after learning that the Israeli minister was in Kyiv. The two discussed the war, the regional situation, and the strategic calculations surrounding Israel, Ukraine, and the United States.
Zelensky was particularly interested in Israel’s assessment of developments involving Iran and the broader Middle East.
Ultimately, both Israel and Ukraine understand that, as cooperation between Russia and Iran grows, what happens in Kyiv can eventually reach Jerusalem.
According to multiple reports, Iranian and Russian facilities are operating jointly inside Russia, where the two countries are upgrading their drones – with Iran receiving some of the drones.
Zelensky warned the Israeli delegation that the drones Iran is developing together with Russia today, combined with the operational experience the two countries are gaining, could eventually become a threat Israel will have to confront.
Beyond his meeting with Zelensky, Elkin met with senior Ukrainian government officials, including the speaker of the parliament and the minister responsible for rebuilding the country’s infrastructure following the war – a role that parallels Elkin’s own responsibilities for the reconstruction of Israel’s North and South.
Elkin, Israeli delegation held memorial for October 7 victims
Together with the Jewish community in Ukraine and the Israeli Embassy, Elkin and the delegation also held a memorial ceremony for the victims of the October 7 massacre.
The message from the Ukrainians in their meetings was clear: They want to see improved relations.
The central question hanging over Kyiv is whether the war is moving toward a negotiated settlement or another escalation.
Ukrainian attacks have increasingly reached targets inside Russian territory, changing a dynamic in which the fighting was largely concentrated inside Ukraine. At the same time, Russian forces have struggled to achieve rapid breakthroughs along the front.
That combination creates a dangerous incentive for Moscow to search for a new way to alter the balance.
The most difficult issue in any potential negotiations remains the Donbas.
Russia wants Ukraine to withdraw from the remaining Ukrainian-held territory in Donetsk Oblast, effectively demanding that Kyiv abandon positions that Ukrainian forces have defended since the war that began in 2014.
For Ukraine, the problem is not simply political.
The Donbas contains a defensive system built over more than a decade. Ukrainian forces have spent years constructing fortifications and positions there, and Russia’s slow progress demonstrates how difficult those defenses are to overcome.
Giving them up would mean more than surrendering territory. It would mean moving the defensive line westward and creating a new strategic vulnerability.
That is why the issue has become one of the hardest obstacles to any potential agreement.
Elkin's visit carried unavoidable symbolism.
At Babyn Yar, Elkin delivered his remarks in Ukrainian – a gesture that attracted attention in a country where language and identity have themselves become part of the struggle with Russia.
During their meeting, Zelensky highlighted Elkin’s command of Ukrainian, joking that his grammar and pronunciation were better than those of some Ukrainian ministers.
The Babyn Yar ceremony was intended to remember a catastrophe that took place 85 years ago. Yet in today’s Kyiv, remembrance and reality are impossible to separate.

articles.title: Oleksandr, Kyrylo and Serhii, all aged one, and eight-year-old Maksym were killed in Ukraine’s city by Russian strike on Putin’s birthday
articles.body:
Ukrainian rescuers are still pulling bodies from a collapsed apartment block in Pryluky. A Russian missile strike on the five-story residential building in the city of Chernihiv Oblast that borders both Russia and Belarus killed 19 people, including five children, and injured 55, Ukraine's State Emergency Service reported on 7 October.
Russia hit Kyiv and a dozen other regions overnight. Air defense downed five ballistic missiles, 39 cruise missiles, and 117 drones, while missiles and drones hit 18 locations, the Air Force said. The nationwide strike killed at least 24 people, including four children.
Among the dead in Pryluky were three one-year-old boys, Oleksandr, Kyrylo, and Serhii, and eight-year-old Maksym, President Volodymyr Zelenskyy says. Seven of the injured are children. Some residents are still unreachable, and all emergency services are working at the site. Russia keeps using missiles against Ukrainian cities and civilians by deliberate choice, he states.
"My condolences to all the families and loved ones," Zelenskyy says.
The strike comes on Putin's birthday
The attack came on Russian President Vladimir Putin's birthday on 7 October.
"Continuing to use missiles against Ukraine, against our people, our children, is an absolutely conscious choice of terror. This is what Moscow chooses despite all our efforts with partners to bring peace closer," Zelenskyy says.
He urges partners to increase pressure on Russia and bolster defense support for Ukraine, saying it is important that world leaders understand this and that the world not remain silent.
A pattern of strikes on Chernihiv Oblast
Pryluky, about 150 kilometers east of Kyiv, lies in a region Russia has hit repeatedly. The overnight barrage also damaged civilian and utility infrastructure across the Pryluky community, the city council said.
Ukraine had seen the attack. The day before, Zelenskyy warned that intelligence indicated a massive Russian strike was in preparation. Russia fired about 70 missiles overnight, killing two people each in the capital Kyiv and in the cities of Kremenchuk and Oleksandriia in addition to the Pryluky dead.
Read also
- 14 dead in Pryluky, two each in Kyiv, Kremenchuk, and Oleksandriia: Russia’s night of 70 missiles
- Drone attack forces Yandex to shut down its data center on the grounds of a sanctioned Russian machine-tool plant
- A 3-year-old girl came to visit her aunt in Pryluky, Ukraine. By morning, a Russian missile had killed her grandmother and uncle

articles.title: Russia's winter campaign against energy infrastructure has begun. Will Kyiv be left without electricity, heating and water?
articles.body:
Russia's winter campaign against energy infrastructure has begun. Will Kyiv be left without electricity, heating and water?
On the night of 29-30 September – ten days earlier than last year – Russia's winter campaign against Ukraine's energy infrastructure officially began. Ekonomichna Pravda (EP) sources say Russian ballistic missiles and drones have been primarily targeting energy facilities in Kyiv and the surrounding region. Their targets include thermal power plants, combined heat and power plants, hydroelectric power plants and electricity transmission infrastructure.
Last winter demonstrated the problems that massive strikes on critical infrastructure can cause in people's everyday lives. This year Ukraine is heading into the heating season better prepared. Power generation has been restored, backup power sources secured, security measures strengthened, equipment stocked up, and repair crews replenished.
But as everyone knows, no level of protection can fully shield the power grid from Russian attacks, meaning that Ukraine is highly unlikely to get through the winter without some disruptions to electricity, heating and water supplies.
Kremlin leader Vladimir Putin has no desire, and certainly no plans, to agree to an energy truce any time soon, given that he sees further strikes as a means of exerting pressure on the Ukrainian authorities and influencing Kyiv's position ahead of possible negotiations.
Moscow is likely to focus its attacks on Kyiv, Ukraine's most densely populated city, in an attempt to influence the public mood in the capital – something the Ukrainian authorities cannot afford to ignore.
The Kremlin's overall objective is to bring about a humanitarian catastrophe and render the Ukrainian capital uninhabitable. Read on to find out how Kyiv is preparing for the heating season, what challenges lie ahead, and what its residents should expect.
Resilience Plans
In early March, Ukraine's National Security and Defence Council approved Comprehensive Resilience Plans for regions and major cities. The plans set out step-by-step roadmaps to prepare critical infrastructure for the next heating season.
EP has looked at what the plans involve, how much they are expected to cost to implement, and whether they can all feasibly be put into practice before the cold weather arrives. The plans cover four key areas, some of which may overlap.
- The first area concerns protection for critical infrastructure. It covers air defence measures and the completion of Level 2 protective shelters at facilities belonging to Ukrenergo (Ukraine's state-owned electricity transmission operator), Naftogaz (the largest national oil and gas company), the Gas Transmission System Operator of Ukraine, and regional electricity distribution companies.
- The second area involves building 1.5 GW of distributed generation capacity, primarily in the city of Kyiv and Dnipropetrovsk, Odesa, Poltava and Kyiv oblasts. Distributed generation refers to smaller power generation facilities located closer to consumers, rather than centralised in a small number of large plants.
- The third and fourth areas are about ensuring uninterrupted heating and water supplies.
At the heart of the plans is a simulation of a total blackout, designed to answer a crucial question: how would the city keep its heating and water systems running if that were to happen? "The concept has been dubbed 'Dark, but warm.' In other words, the lights might go out after a bombardment, but there must always be water and heating," Oleksandr Kharchenko, director of the Centre for Energy Research, told EP.
Immediately after the government adopted the Resilience Plans, energy sector sources told EP they were overly ambitious and optimistic and said they doubted that all the measures could be implemented before winter.
Three years would be a more realistic timescale for completion of the work, the sources said. What has been achieved so far, and how is Kyiv preparing to go into the heating season?
What will happen to the electricity supply?
Before Russia began to attack its power grid, Ukraine had a significant electricity surplus. Generation comfortably exceeded domestic demand.
Energy Minister Denys Shmyhal says Ukraine currently has over 15 GW of generating capacity available during the evening, when demand is at its highest. And that's with only six of Ukraine's nine nuclear reactors in operation (the other three are undergoing maintenance). The plan is to increase available generation capacity to 19.6 GW by 1 November and 21.4 GW by the end of the year.
Meanwhile, electricity consumption last week ranged from 6,800 MW at its lowest to 10,200 MW at its peak. The sharp drop in consumption across the country is linked to Russia's constant attacks on major metals companies, which have been forced to halt production.
Electricity consumption will obviously go up in winter, but if all the planned repairs are completed, power generation should be sufficient to keep the system balanced in normal winter temperatures, a source at an energy company told EP.
"However, we have to factor in that the energy sector will come under attack," the source noted. "We had enough generation capacity on paper at the end of last September too, but after several waves of attacks, we ended up with a shortfall of 5,000-6,000 MW."
So the main risk this winter is not a shortage of generation capacity at the outset, but how quickly that capacity could be lost due to further Russian attacks.
For Kyiv, this is particularly important. Russian attacks have already destroyed a significant portion of the capital's power generation capacity. Some of that capacity is slated to be restored, but once brought back online, the facilities will become priority targets again.
The second major area of preparation is therefore to ensure a reliable electricity supply for the capital. The Kyiv energy ring is built around four 330 kV substations, supported by dozens of smaller 110 kV substations.
The Resilience Plan envisages providing Level 2 protection for these sites. According to sources who spoke to EP, some of the work is already complete and the remainder is due to be finished by the end of the year, despite government statements about a freeze on capital expenditure. Level 2 protection is designed to withstand drone attacks, but not ballistic strikes.
Another part of Kyiv's Resilience Plan is establishing backup power sources. A document seen by EP puts the capital's peak winter load at 2 GW. Critical infrastructure accounts for around 280 MW, and a reserve of generators and cogeneration units is to be set up specifically to keep those facilities supplied.
EP sources say around 150 MW of the planned 200 MW of distributed generation capacity has already been commissioned. According to an energy market source, the city could have 180-185 MW available by the end of the year. Privately owned facilities with a combined capacity of 55-60 MW could also come online before winter; around half of them are ready to start operating.
The main function of distributed generation is to keep critical infrastructure running if the main generation sources or the grid are damaged.
In other words, if there is an electricity shortage, priority will be given to water supply systems, boilerhouses, hospitals, communications, transport and other essential services. For ordinary consumers, emergency or hourly power outage schedules will be in place, as they were last year. What will this mean for the public?
A senior manager at a state-owned energy company told EP: "If temperatures fall below -10°C and some generation capacity can't be brought back online in time, we could be looking at around eight to ten hours of power cuts per day. That's assuming there are no further attacks.
Then there's the pessimistic scenario – heavy strikes and widespread destruction. In that case there might be only four hours of electricity a day, leaving Kyiv without power for up to 20 hours," the source added. Even so, EP sources say Russia will not be able to plunge Kyiv into a total blackout.
In other words, the worst-case scenario for the capital is prolonged power cuts for most consumers, but critical infrastructure kept powered up.
The source concludes: "No one can give an accurate forecast right now. The situation depends on many factors. It will depend on where and how the attacks happen, which power plants are still working, and how quickly they can be brought back online."
What are the risks to Kyiv's heating supply?
Heating is a more complex issue. Kyiv's heat supply system has historically been highly centralised: around 70% of the city is heated by three large combined heat and power (CHP) plants.
That is why backup heat sources are one of the key priorities of the Resilience Plan: modernising old boilerhouses, building new ones, installing cogeneration units, and creating connections between different sections of the heating network.
The idea is that if a major CHP plant goes down, individual districts will be able to receive heat from alternative sources. The problem is that Kyiv's huge CHP plants cannot be fully replicated in just a few months.
"Kyiv's CHP plants have a capacity equal to that of several regional capitals. They were built over decades, when the Soviet Union had virtually unlimited resources," a source in the Kyiv city administration told EP.
For that reason, Kyiv will not be able to fully protect its heating supply system from losing heat this year. An EP source close to the government said that between 2,500 and 3,000 apartment blocks may be left without a backup heat supply this winter. Another source believes the number could be even higher. There are 12,000 apartment blocks in Kyiv.
"It's hard to say exactly which apartment blocks might be left without heating, but potentially the areas at risk are parts of the Solomianskyi, Holosiivskyi and Pecherskyi districts, Teremky, Berezniaky, parts of the Dniprovskyi district, part of Troieshchyna, and even the Obolonskyi district," Kharchenko says.
As with the power supply, what happens next will depend on the scale of the attacks.
The optimistic scenario assumes that the main heat sources will be partly operational and any damage would be repaired quickly, in which case Kyiv should get through the winter without widespread heating disruptions. Backup boilerhouses and bypasses should help localise any problems.
But if the Russians launch massive strikes on thermal power stations and large boilerhouses, heating problems are inevitable. "There are three major plants in Kyiv that have already been attacked. You don't need a crystal ball to know that they're going to be attacked again," says an EP source at an energy company. On 30 September, Russian forces launched relentless strikes on one of the capital's CHP plants.
If this happens, the city will switch to emergency mode. Backup boilerhouses, generators, emergency response teams and mobile equipment will be deployed wherever possible. Critical infrastructure will be prioritised above all else.
But some residential buildings will have no backup heat supply. In the worst-case scenario, the city will have to rely on electricity to make up for the shortfall in heating.
"As a last resort, if some areas have no heating, they should be exempt from rolling blackouts, or at least the power cuts there should be shorter than in the rest of the city. And people will rely on electric heaters to keep warm, just as they did last year," the source explains.
"There are no guarantees that Kyiv will have heating," the source in the city administration told EP. "Ballistic strikes mean there can be no guarantees in principle. A lot will depend on how intense the attacks are."
But one thing is different from last winter. According to Kharchenko, Kyiv will be more resilient to attacks even in the most challenging scenario, as backup boilerhouses, generators, hospitals, staff and invincibility centres are now better prepared. [An invincibility centre is a heated premises stocked with food and power banks to assist residents facing hardships due to power cuts – ed.]
Kyiv will not be left without water, but there are some caveats
Water is another critical part of the picture, as Russia could target the capital's water supply in an attempt to trigger a humanitarian disaster.
Kyiv's Resilience Plan focuses on keeping the water utility running even if the power goes out. To achieve this, pumping stations and other key water supply and drainage facilities must be equipped with backup power sources.
According to EP sources, almost half of the planned 40 MW of backup power has now been commissioned. The rest is due to be completed by the end of the year.
The good news is that most of Kyiv's water infrastructure is underground, so it is more resilient to attacks. However, the water supply system cannot be fully protected from the effects of massive strikes.
"Most of the infrastructure is underground," an EP source in the government notes. "Even at water intakes and large water treatment plants, a significant part of the infrastructure is underground. But concentrated ballistic strikes could still cause serious damage."
According to the source, even major damage to the system would not automatically leave the entire city without water. In the worst-case scenario, the problem would be water quality and the supply to some districts.
Another EP source did not rule out the possibility that in certain circumstances, some areas of the city could be without water for a week or longer. Residents are therefore advised to ensure they have stocks of drinking water at home.
* * *
To sum up, Kyiv is heading into this winter objectively better prepared than it was a year ago. The city has more backup generation capacity, better-protected facilities, alternative heat sources, generators, and well-rehearsed plans for dealing with large-scale attacks.
But that doesn't mean the winter will be easy. None of these measures offers a cast-iron guarantee, because the scale of future attacks and the damage they will cause cannot be predicted in advance.
So the main question is not whether there will be problems – there will be. The question is how quickly the city can bring damaged facilities back online and whether its backup capacity and reserves will be enough to prevent local problems from turning into a city-wide crisis.
For Kyiv, as for the country as a whole, the biggest unknown is something that can't be predicted or controlled: the scale and intensity of future Russian attacks.
Mykola Topalov
Translated by Artem Yakymyshyn
Edited by Teresa Pearce

articles.title: Syria weighs military aid for Saudi Arabia amid Yemen war, sources say
articles.body:
Syria weighs military aid for Saudi Arabia amid Yemen war, sources say
RIYADH, Oct 7 - Syria is carefully considering providing military assistance to key ally Saudi Arabia amid an escalating war against the Iran-backed Houthis in Yemen, a US official and a Syrian military official briefed on the matter said.
Options being considered include defensive aid to protect the kingdom from attacks, or deployment of forces in an offensive capacity to help Saudi-backed Yemeni troops fight the Houthis, the sources said.
The US official said Saudi Arabia had requested that Syria deploy forces to fight the Houthis.
In response to a request for comment to the Syrian foreign ministry, a Syrian diplomat said Syria stood firmly with Saudi Arabia in the face of Houthi attacks but that the government's primary focus was on domestic priorities such as recovery from the country's civil war.
"Should Saudi Arabia request any military cooperation or exchange of expertise, this would take place exclusively through official channels and within the framework of the bilateral agreements governing relations between our two brotherly countries," the diplomat said in a statement.
The Saudi government media office and Yemen's information minister did not respond to requests for comment.
Saudi Arabia has been requesting assistance far and wide, from the US to Europe and the Middle East, for both defensive and offensive support in a renewed war against the group that follows weeks of Houthi missile and drone attacks on the kingdom.
The war is being led on the ground by a patchwork of Yemeni government forces with Saudi air support. They have made limited advances since the campaign was launched on Monday.
Syrian President Ahmed al-Sharaa made a public visit to Riyadh on Tuesday and met Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman, also known as MbS. He discussed potential Syrian military assistance for the kingdom, among other matters, the US official said.
Footage broadcast by Syrian state media showed that he was escorted back to his plane by Saudi Defense Minister Khalid bin Salman, a brother of the crown prince who has overseen the Yemen file.
DEPLOYMENT COULD DEEPEN TENSIONS WITH NEIGHBOURS
Syrian fighters from opposition groups that battled former leader Bashar al-Assad in the country's civil war have in past years been recruited as mercenaries for other conflicts, notably Libya's internal conflict and the Russia-Ukraine war.
But for Damascus, any potential deployment carries risks.
The militias that made up the armed opposition are now under the nascent Syrian state, which has adopted a policy of avoiding engagement in conflict, including the Iran war, to focus on recovery from the 14-year Syrian civil war.
The state is still piecing together its army from the various militia groups from the former rebel coalition that toppled Assad, which included many hardline Sunni Islamist and foreign fighters, and trying to contain tensions with minorities including the Alawites, a Shi'ite offshoot to which Assad belonged.
A conflict between that army and the Houthis, who are also adherents of an offshoot of Shi'ite Islam, could have divisive religious undertones that the Syrian leadership and its Western partners want to avoid, the US official said.
It is for this reason that it previously rejected a US request to help fight Hezbollah in Lebanon.
Involvement in a battle against the Iran-backed Houthis could also be viewed as a hostile act by Iran and its allies Hezbollah in Lebanon and militias in Iraq, with which the Syrian rebels-turned-rulers have a history of conflict.
KEEN TO SHOW SUPPORT
At the same time, Sharaa is keen to show the country's support for Saudi Arabia and MbS, who played a decisive role helping the former jihadist gain international legitimacy, including by brokering a May 2025 meeting between Sharaa and US President Donald Trump.
Saudi Arabia has also provided financial assistance to Syria and a Syrian show of support could result in that increasing, the US official said.
"A new Syria sending defensive personnel of a very small number to the most holy places in the Islamic world, alongside technical support to neutralise incoming drones, would be tremendously and positively symbolic," said H.A. Hellyer, senior associate fellow at the Royal United Services Institute in London.
"But anything beyond, particularly in terms of Syrian boots on the ground, I think would be a wholly different proposition, and one I think Damascus would avoid, given the priorities they need to focus on in Syria," he said. REUTERS

articles.title: Three years since October 7: Israelis tell Meduza how the worst terrorist attack in their country’s history changed them and the world around them
articles.body:
Three years since October 7: Israelis tell Meduza how the worst terrorist attack in their country’s history changed them and the world around them
The Hamas attack on October 7, 2023, was one of the most horrific events in recent world history. Ahead of its third anniversary, Meduza spoke with residents of Israel, where the terrorist attack touched everyone. Eight people from cities across the country described what happened to them in those days and how they and the world around them have changed since.
Warning: This article contains profanity.
Exactly three years ago, on October 7, 2023, some 3,000 militants from the Palestinian terrorist movement Hamas attacked Israel and took 251 people hostage. About 1,200 other civilians, including 38 children, were killed; more than 350 of them were at the Nova music festival. Some were tortured, others burned alive. The militants also raped a large number of women — Israeli human rights advocates believe this was a deliberate Hamas strategy.
In response to October 7, Israel launched an operation in the Gaza Strip. Tens of thousands of people have died. Hamas has been defeated but still exists. The operation has drawn international criticism and has been accompanied by a rise in anti-Israel and antisemitic sentiment. During the operation, Israel freed 166 hostages. Another 85 died.
Yeva Broyde-Zaitsev, 37, ceramics shop owner and Hebrew teacher, Tel Aviv
In Russia, I worked in the archives of an art college and played in a band. I left Russia 10 years ago through the repatriation program. Russia had already seized Crimea, things were looking ominous, and I wasn’t expecting anything good.
At first, I didn’t think I’d stay in Israel: I planned to get Israeli citizenship and a darkon — an Israeli passport. Then I saw how much more people value human life here, how they respect individual freedom. My friends in Russia started scattering around the world, and in the end, I had no reason left to go back.
Throughout Israel’s history, there’s always been some fucked-up shit happening, terrorist attacks every year. But that happened in Moscow too. Whenever people asked whether I was scared of being blown up, I’d always say that if you’re going to get blown up, it might as well happen by the sea. So moving to Israel didn’t scare me. I think you face far more dangers every day in Moscow than you do in Israel. Here, I’m not afraid that someone passing by will give me grief about how I look or get aggressive. People are much friendlier here.
Before October 7, I didn’t have a feeling that something bad was going to happen. Or rather, this is the Middle East — you can have that feeling every day.
I was looking forward to my birthday on October 12. My friends and I were planning to fly to London and have a fucking amazing celebration. We ended up having to celebrate in a bomb shelter. Lots of people came, even though getting to my place was dangerous. We kept getting bombed, and we got horribly drunk because there was so much stress and terror, and we needed to let it out.
My husband serves in the military’s medical corps. When the siren went off early on October 7, he didn’t even wake up. That morning, I told him this whole nightmare had begun, and he reassured me that if things were really bad, he’d have been called up.
That happened the next day.
Several of my friends died at the Nova festival, where Hamas massacred people and took hostages. I spent the first few days with a friend. We just sobbed.
Whenever I was home alone, I’d sit there with a knife. I thought that if a terrorist broke in, of course I wouldn’t be able to fight him off. The knife was so I wouldn’t be taken captive: I was prepared to kill myself. That would have been much more peaceful than the endless suffering of being a hostage.
From the start of the attack, I also had this strange feeling… Relief, in a way. When Russia attacked Ukraine, I felt guilty because I’m from Russia, and my country had attacked another country. Here, we weren’t the ones attacking — we were being attacked. Finally, we weren’t the bad guys. But then [after the war in the Gaza Strip began], Israelis faced even more hatred than Russians.
In November, a friend in Berlin invited me and a mutual friend to stay with him. He said: Come over, just take a breather. Here, you won’t have to run to a bomb shelter 10 times a day.
We flew to Berlin, walked around the city a lot, and kept coming across pro-Palestinian flyers everywhere. The most progressive neighborhoods in Berlin were plastered with Free Palestine imagery. On one wall, there were photographs of Israeli hostages, and every one of them had nasty things written and drawn all over it.
How is that possible? To me, it’s just the usual barbaric attitude. “We’re so good and innocent, and those Israelis are killing Palestinian babies and deserve to have Hamas take them all captive.” “We can afford to forget that we do terrible things ourselves.” Meduza itself writes a lot whenever Israelis destroy something in Gaza, but not when Hamas destroys something in Israel and people are killed.
Anyway, my friend and I stayed in Berlin for a week and left because it was emotionally hard.
Since October 7, almost every time I meet people in other countries, I have to watch what I say. Because plenty of people take pleasure in hating Israelis. It’s easy to feel virtuous when you say you support everything good and oppose everything evil.
If someone near me starts talking about Palestine, I jump right into the conversation. I feel responsible because there’s so much people don’t know. They don’t know that Hamas literally governs Gaza, that it really is under Sharia law, or how extensive Hamas’s network of tunnels beneath civilian sites in Gaza is. Or that if Hamas had let ordinary Gazans shelter in those tunnels, there would have been far fewer casualties.
I feel I need to share my experience and tell people about Israel. I try to do that without downplaying Palestinians’ suffering.
We have to remember that we’re all human, and you can’t hate someone simply because they belong to a particular social group.
But I want the world to know that rockets landed near my home, that my friends no longer have a home, that people I loved were killed at a music festival — and in this war in general. And how many of us have suffered? All of us — every single one.
Tatyana Konev, 59, marketing specialist, Karmiel
I’ve been in Israel for 30 years — my husband and I came here in 1995. We were born and raised in Donetsk.
The war after October 7 isn’t our first war in Israel. There was the Second Lebanon War in 2006. It was very frightening because we had two small children, and my husband kept getting called up for military training, though he wasn’t sent to the front.
On October 8, this new war reached the next generation: My son got a call-up notice. It came while he was at work, and I packed his backpack while he was on his way home. Then my husband drove him to his military unit.
A couple of hours later, they came back. It turned out that 20% more people had reported for duty than the unit needed because some had shown up without call-up notices. They let my son go because they didn’t need that many people, and he worked at an important medical equipment manufacturer.
I don’t know what would have happened if my son had stayed with the unit. Its soldiers cleared mines from tunnels in Gaza. So many of them died.
In Israel, war is always close by. There’s an old saying here that our children won’t have to fight. Meaning that any day now, the wars will end. But children and grandchildren have been fighting for generations.
October 7 was Shabbat and the holiday of Simchat Torah — “Rejoicing in the Torah.” Religious families had their phones and televisions, all their means of communication, switched off that day. They didn’t know what had happened. October 2023 also marked 50 years since the start of the Yom Kippur War. I kept saying that Israel’s enemies would want to mark the occasion.
I know a family whose kibbutz was invaded by militants. The family hid in a bomb shelter and stayed there for 28 hours. The militants took over their house. The Israeli army came to liberate the kibbutz, and the militants fired back from inside the family’s house. When the family came out of the bomb shelter, their house was covered in blood.
That day turned many Israelis’ worldview upside down. People in the kibbutzim in the south were mostly very left-wing. I often argued with them about left-wing ideas and told them about my life in the Soviet Union. Left-wing people here couldn’t believe things like that could happen under socialism — to them, it was the ideal.
A lot of people on the left thought that if we helped the people of Gaza, they’d warm to us. October 7 showed how badly that idea failed. A colleague of mine called herself a “proud leftist,” and after October 7, she wrote that she’d lost faith in her ideals.
Some people moved further right, others turned to religion. Israelis generally started looking at life differently. So many times before bed, I’ve thought: “Here I am, going to sleep in my own bed. Tomorrow I’ll get up and have coffee. What’s it like to be a hostage underground? To spend a year or two like that, with almost no food or water, under constant threat of violence?”
One of my colleagues served in the army in a role we call the “knock on the door.” When a soldier’s death is confirmed, someone assigned to that task goes to their family to tell them what happened. For two years after the war began, my colleague was hardly ever in the office. She had so many doors to knock on.
And even after all the hostages were released, my colleague was still making lots of visits to people’s homes. We asked her why. She said not all hostages and soldiers are mentally well when they return to civilian life. People can’t cope with what happened and take their own lives.
For example, last year, a young man whose girlfriend had been killed right in front of him at the Nova music festival took his own life.
Another colleague of mine lost his daughter. I’d drawn cards for her bat mitzvah, and then the girl was gone, killed in combat on October 7 or 8.
Now, every morning, I thank God that my house hasn’t been bombed and my children are alive.
Boris Voitsekhovsky, 53, artist, cook, and former journalist, Haifa
In November 2022, my wife and I moved from Moscow to Haifa through the repatriation program because of the mobilization. We’d never been to Israel before. When I left, I had a remote job as the managing editor of Moslenta, but I quit after moving. Now I write children’s books, cook food to order, and paint — a whole range of things.
There was a blizzard in Moscow that November. We were freezing at the airport, and then we arrived in Haifa: warmth, sunshine, palm trees. Beautiful. It was a strange contrast. For the first year, it felt like some kind of extended vacation. There was a forest near our apartment, and we could get to the sea in 20 minutes by bus. We really relaxed and didn’t feel any danger.
That’s pretty much how the whole year before October 7 went: meeting friends, grilling kebabs, drinking wine by the sea. In time, I realized Haifa reminded me of Sukhumi, the largest city in Abkhazia, where I used to spend vacations as a child. Even the smells are the same — the same flowers grow there.
Of course, we understood that terrorist attacks happen regularly in Israel: Someone shoots at a car somewhere, someone gets stabbed. But we saw them all as isolated incidents. There was no sense that trouble was brewing.
On October 7, I was alone in Haifa. My wife had flown to Moscow to see her parents. I was planning to go to a friend’s birthday party. I woke up and read the news. At first, I thought: All sorts of things happen in Israel. Give it a day or two, and it’ll be over. Then reports started coming in that huge numbers of people had been killed, both at the festival and in the kibbutzim…
It seemed like it wouldn’t affect us because Haifa is in northern Israel, and the main events happened in the south, on the border with Gaza. So I went to the birthday party, and my wife flew back the next day.
Toward nightfall, we started hearing explosions. It wasn’t clear exactly what was happening, but it was clearly nothing good.
We started getting daily warnings about the risk of rocket attacks. A special app sent us instructions on what to do if an alarm went off. First, you’re supposed to go into a mamad — a reinforced room in your apartment. But our building is old, and we don’t have one. The instructions say that if you don’t have a room like that, go to the basement; if there’s no basement, go to the stairwell; if there’s no stairwell, stay in a room without windows. We don’t have a basement. We live on the second floor of a two-story building, and the stairs lead straight from the street into our apartment. We even have windows in the bathroom. Basically, as unsafe as it gets.
So every time, my wife and I ran to the stairwell of the building next door. You get an alert, and you have a couple of minutes to get there. But when ballistic missiles started coming from Iran, it got harder because then you only have about a minute.
In 2024, my wife and I spent nights in a bomb shelter at a school. If an attack happens at night, it’s hard to get to the building next door in time. But being in the school’s bomb shelter was great. You get an alert, and you don’t have to go anywhere — you’re already there. We slept on a camping mat. We brought blankets and pillows from home. The concrete floors were cold, and the air was stuffy. My back hurt afterward — it was a concrete floor, after all.
I couldn’t count how many warnings we got, but Haifa itself wasn’t hit all that often. There were deaths, though: In the first few months, for example, a rocket hit an oil refinery outside the city, killing workers.
Some people in Israel are, let’s say, bloodthirsty. They say all of Gaza should be paved over because they’re all scum there. I don’t understand that. Just as I can’t accept the idea that all Russians are assholes because Russia attacked Ukraine. I know plenty of good people in Russia. My parents live there, after all.
But there are fewer bloodthirsty people now — that’s how it seems to me. Because people are exhausted. When the war began, it seemed like it would end quickly, and now it’s been going on for years. People want to make plans and live in peace.
It was impossible not to follow what was happening with the hostages. Everyone was writing and talking about it, and there were constant street protests. I didn’t take part because, of course, the hostages need to be brought back, but I don’t know how rallies could help with that. Is the army going to do more, or what?
But I cooked for soldiers. Jews came to Israel from all over the world to fight. People helped however they could: putting them up in their homes, feeding them, raising money for equipment and footwear.
I don’t know if you could say I have PTSD, but sudden noises bother me. When a car suddenly starts honking, for example, or a tire bursts. Or that bang-bang when a motorcycle goes by. A motorcycle sounds just like a drone. Exactly the same.
When we first arrived in Israel, people had so many plans: They were opening shops, galleries. Now it’s impossible to know how to make plans at all. What’s going to happen tomorrow? Maybe another war? Should we buy property here, start a business? Or maybe move to another country before the kids get called up?
Larisa Zimina, 52, HR specialist, Netanya
In August 2023, there was a hot-air balloon festival at the very spot where the music festival took place, or somewhere very close by. I went with my children. There were several thousand big Israeli families there, with very young children, tents, and dogs. There’s only one road in. It still terrifies me to think that we wouldn’t have gotten out if the attack had happened that day. If I’d felt there was a threat [of a terrorist attack], I wouldn’t have gone.
On the morning of October 7, I was talking to a friend in America. Her son was in Israel and wasn’t answering her calls. She said he’d gone to some event. I said: It’s seven in the morning. He’s been dancing and drinking and partying all night. He’s probably asleep, and maybe his phone’s dead. We joked that trees don’t have power outlets. The guy’s 23, he’s finished his military service. Why keep calling him?
Then I started reading the news and realized things were looking bad. My mother called from Beersheba and said the sirens were going off there. I also remember religious [Jews] stopping me in the street. They couldn’t read the news [on Shabbat] and were asking what was happening.
The boy whose mother I’d been talking to was killed. That boy used to babysit my child. His brother was my son’s best friend. His mother flew in from Chicago right away — on October 9, we were at the missing-persons center that had been set up near Ben Gurion Airport. People were sobbing, screaming, wailing.
October 7 profoundly changed how safe I feel in Israel. It always used to be a short war, a long break, then another, and another. Suddenly, the war turned out not to be short. The odds of losing our “lottery” got much higher.
[Before,] there were knife attacks and suicide bombings, but they didn’t stop me from working, taking buses, going to parties, or just living my life. I used to work in news in Russia, and I know that the chance of dying of any cause in Russia is much higher than the chance of being killed by a terrorist in Israel.
I live my life as I always have — but if I had a house, I’d build a bomb shelter. Many of my friends have gotten gun permits. Now I’d think twice about renting an apartment in Kfar Saba.
October 7 was an astonishing combination of a fuckup and Israel’s usual laid-back attitude. I used to spend a lot of time working on this conflict, working with left-wing organizations that support two states for two peoples. And I understand how complicated it all is — how nobody’s hands are clean. How many stupid things and mistakes both sides have made, Israel included…
But I’m Israeli, and I’m on the Israelis’ side. And it always matters who started it — with the attack from Gaza, that’s obvious.
Really, everyone should be ready for anything. You can start with the basics: stock up on food, water, portable gas stoves, and blankets at home. Be ready for everything to suddenly shut down and another endless war to begin. I teach my children to steer clear of crowds and watch who’s walking behind them.
And you’ve got to keep yourself sane any way you can: exercise, sex, sleep.
Grigory Nedayev, 31, software developer, Tel Aviv
I moved from Moscow to Israel in March 2022, shortly after [Russia invaded Ukraine]. I knew where I was going, so the possibility that one of Israel’s neighbors might fire a rocket at it, or that a terrorist attack might happen somewhere, didn’t surprise me. So I was prepared — and before October 7, I felt safe.
The Hamas attack happened the day after my wife and I got back from a vacation in France. We flew into Israel on October 6 — lovely weather, warm, peaceful. Around 6:30 a.m. the next day, an outdoor warning siren went off. I woke up and thought: Something’s happening.
But something’s always happening here. I went up to the roof of our building. The sky was clear, no rockets or explosions, just the siren. So I went back to sleep. I really underestimated the danger.
That morning, my wife and I started reading the news and realized it was serious. There wasn’t any panic, though. I’m not an anxious person. I thought: There were Hamas attacks in 2019 and 2021 too. And the Gaza Strip is 80 kilometers [about 50 miles] from us. That’s a ridiculously short distance by Russian standards, of course, but it’s still not right on our doorstep. It seemed like it would last a couple of days, so the next day I didn’t even read the news.
I work on Sundays, and at the morning meeting I saw how tense my colleagues were. We didn’t discuss work, just what was happening. Over the next few days, I followed the news closely. Rockets were coming toward Tel Aviv, and the Israeli army was intercepting them. I’d never seen anything like that before — at most, some smoke in the distance from an intercepted rocket. Now it was frightening: Things were exploding right over your head.
I’m pretty resilient, but even I struggled with all the reports of people being burned and brutally killed. You read it and absorb all that horror. You get depressed.
After the hostage deal fell through and Hamas killed six hostages, I was so shaken that I went to a rally. I wanted to, how do I put it, express my opinion.
Then I came across a post looking for volunteers in a Russian-language Telegram chat. I signed up — I wanted to help however I could. They took us somewhere, something like a military base, and we spent the whole day packing food, canned goods, and all sorts of little things for soldiers.
About a year ago, all the hostages came home. There was almost jubilation in the streets. People weren’t exactly walking around shouting “hooray!” but you could see from their faces that they were happy. I felt a kind of happiness too, real relief. Because that horror had dragged on for so long, deals kept falling through, politicians did nothing but argue — you just wanted it to end.
Over these years, I’ve started questioning whether I want to live in Israel, and I’ve become more pessimistic about the future. Even though none of this has affected me personally. I live in a building with a reinforced room — my bedroom is a bomb shelter, so I don’t have to run anywhere. A couple of months after the war began, our company switched to remote work, so I just sat and worked in that room to the sound of rockets exploding. In theory, if a rocket hit the wall of that room, I’d be stunned by the blast, but it wouldn’t kill me.
I haven’t changed. But I think the country has. This war has pretty much killed the idea of peaceful coexistence with Palestine. My impression is that many people who used to be left-wing or centrist have shifted to the right.
Zina Kapitovskaya, 74, retiree, Haifa
When I learned what was happening on October 7, I was overcome with horror, fear, hatred. And sorrow, like any normal person, over the deaths of completely innocent people, including children.
We knew about the balloons they sent from Gaza. We knew they hated us. But we never thought it could turn into such a horrific massacre.
Years ago, I happened to miss a bus that later exploded. For a while afterward, I couldn’t get on buses. Israel is a country where something can happen at any moment. But a massacre like October 7 was unimaginable.
I didn’t see a therapist after October 7: It turns out I’m pretty resilient, and I can cope on my own. Probably partly because October 7 didn’t affect anyone close to me. My grandchildren were in the army at the time, but they didn’t get caught up in that meat grinder. If they had, I’d probably have been losing my mind just like other parents and grandparents in that situation.
I can’t say my everyday routine has changed since October 7. My sense of safety hasn’t changed either. Nor has my attitude toward the Arabs who live near us: I’m not afraid of them.
The worst thing is that no state commission of inquiry into the October 7 attack has been set up. There’s a law specifying how a state commission of inquiry must be formed and who must sit on it. Commissions like that were set up after several wars. Three years have passed, and no one has been held responsible. Only a few people acknowledged responsibility and resigned on their own. Elections are coming up in Israel, and setting up a state commission of inquiry is at the top of the sensible parties’ platforms.
My attitude toward the government changed enormously [after the events of October 7]. I think they bear a lot of the blame, and they absolutely need to be replaced. [Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin] Netanyahu says one thing, but who knows what he really thinks.
Of course, the problem didn’t start on October 7. This has all been going on for a very long time. I’m not a politician. I don’t know how to fix it, but I’m sure war isn’t necessarily the answer.
Gavriel Feldman, 49, editor of Mir Torah (World of Torah), a publication about Judaism, Jerusalem
October 7 was Simchat Torah. I went to the synagogue for the very first minyan [communal prayer service]. Most people go to the other, longer minyan: They sing for hours, dance with the Torah scrolls, and socialize. I went to the first minyan because it’s very short, so I could get home to the children and take them back [to the synagogue] for the main celebration and dancing without rushing.
Large floor-standing air conditioners had been set up in the room for the dancing. They were humming, and we couldn’t hear the sirens. I realized something was happening when I got home during a lull in the sirens.
Then rockets started hitting. We had to decide whether to take the children [to the synagogue]. Something was clearly happening, but we didn’t know what. We decided to go for a little while. The lower hall in our synagogue doubles as a bomb shelter. When we arrived, it was clear that the dancing was winding down.
Rumors started circulating because people in our community were being called up to fight. Secular neighbors told us a few things. We knew militants had broken through and hostages had been taken. A picture was beginning to emerge, but nobody understood the scale of it, how many people had been killed or abducted.
Turning on a phone or television is a direct violation of Shabbat. You can do it if there’s an immediate threat to life, but there wasn’t one. Rocket attacks are fairly routine in Israel.
This [observing Shabbat] is a difficult issue: It’s a holiday, Simchat Torah. There are stories about our great teachers who, even in moments of immense personal grief, set it aside when a holiday began and fulfilled the commandments. After the holiday, a person like that returns to their deep mourning, but during the holiday they rejoice, and it isn’t an act.
But we’re ordinary people… [For us,] that’s quite difficult. The children and I left the synagogue and went home fairly quickly. After that, we started going to bomb shelters…
The next day, once Shabbat and the holiday were over, people started collecting supplies for soldiers. Because it had become clear that the state wasn’t prepared for anything. The army couldn’t provide reservists with what they needed. On the morning of October 8, I bought the most urgently requested items and took bags of them somewhere.
Not long before that, our son had been born, and he had some [health] complications. He was our sixth child. Even as experienced parents, we had to learn a lot of things all over again. We were really tied down [caring for the baby], while the war was going on in the background.
I coped with it fairly easily. It was harder for my wife. Anxiety, not knowing what would happen next, no sense of certainty or safety.
For many people in Israel, October 7 shattered their understanding of the world. For me, it didn’t. If you start from the belief that the Almighty governs the world, while the world’s progressives are trying to take it in the wrong direction, then you understand that stability and tranquility are something of an illusion, a way of fooling yourself. If everything’s okay for you today, you shouldn’t assume it necessarily always will be.
October 7 woke a great many people up. In that sense, some good came out of this horrific tragedy. For a while, you could see the unity in Israel that everyone loves to talk about.
Then, of course, that unity fell apart — turning to “mold and linden honey,” as the Russian song goes. But at least we knew unity was possible.
Vitaly Starov, 44, programmer, Acre
My wife and I left Russia because repression was growing, and we suspected I might be jailed. We understood that we were moving to a country where terrorist attacks could happen, a country that’s constantly at war.
We arrived in Israel about three months before October 7. Luckily, we managed to get all our paperwork done except for my driver’s license. We got identity cards, bus and commuter train passes, and joined a health insurance fund. After October 7, everything closed, then opened only intermittently. It took me six months to get my license.
On October 7, I woke up with an inflamed ear, apparently because I’d walked barefoot on the tile [in our apartment] the day before. My ear hurt, and the pain spread to a tooth. I thought I should probably see a doctor, but then I started reading the news and felt even worse.
The Hamas attack was shocking: a brutal massacre with large numbers of civilian casualties. The videos of hostages being dragged through crowds in Gaza, beaten and spat on, really hit me hard.
That same day, checkpoints were set up at the northern entrances to Acre, and armored vehicles with men carrying automatic weapons were brought in. The Lebanese border is 10 to 15 kilometers [about six to nine miles] north of the city. The thinking was that Hezbollah might break through the border and make it as far as Acre. But it limited itself to rocket attacks. There were fears that unrest would break out among Israeli Arabs, but that didn’t happen.
Hezbollah launched its first attacks from Lebanon a day or two later, and after that, there were air-raid sirens on many days. Almost all the rockets were shot down. Only a few got through. The bomb shelters in Acre, like those in many cities in northern Israel, were full of junk and partly flooded. I went to help clear them out as a volunteer.
My attitude toward Israel hasn’t changed since October 7, but my attitude toward the current Israeli government has. For the worse: They haven’t solved a single problem, only compounded them. No state commission of inquiry into the events of October 7 has been set up. The goals of the war Israel has become embroiled in are unclear, and there are serious questions about how it’s being fought.
I wouldn’t say I have PTSD, and I probably don’t need to see a therapist. But naturally, there’s nothing good about air-raid sirens either. Now, wherever you go, you automatically look around for the nearest bomb shelter. Still, I don’t feel threatened by Arabs — and there are a lot of them in Acre.
After October 7, it became much clearer why so many Israelis carry guns in public. It doesn’t surprise me to see people carrying automatic military rifles while buying groceries in a supermarket.
