articles.title: Three years after October 7: What changed for Israel, the Middle East and Russia?
articles.body:
Netanyahu’s October 7 response has no endgame. Russia has a stake in what follows
On October 7, 2023, Israel faced a horrific attack when Hamas killed over a thousand of its citizens and took hundreds of hostages. This atrocity can never be justified.
But there is another fact that we cannot ignore: Israel’s overconfidence and conviction of superiority over its adversaries led to the country’s most catastrophic security failure. Three years later, Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s government still has no convincing answer as to how the ensuing war is supposed to secure a safer future for the country.
More firepower, no endgame
The Israeli leadership’s main takeaway from the October 7 tragedy was the need to strike earlier, harder, and deeper. Deterrence gave way to destruction and elimination – first of the adversaries’ military capabilities, then of their leaders. The war expanded beyond Gaza, engulfed Lebanon, and finally escalated to a direct confrontation with Iran. Aggression became the guiding principle of regional policy. Yet, the tragedy also demanded a reassessment of the adversary, a sober evaluation of the country’s intelligence, and governmental accountability. Force can punish an enemy, but it cannot rectify the errors that made the attack possible in the first place.
Here, we clearly see the main contradiction of Netanyahu’s policy. Israel can destroy command centers, eliminate commanders, demolish infrastructure, and occupy territory. However, it is incomparably more difficult to shape neighboring societies in a way that would prevent the threat from re-emerging. The government expanded its military objectives but never defined a realistic political outcome. Who will govern Gaza? What kind of international recognition will that authority rely on? How can the daily lives of Palestinians be restored? What will ensure the safety of Israelis once the army withdraws? As long as there are no answers to these questions, every victory necessitates yet another military operation.
It would certainly be a mistake to deny the losses inflicted upon Israel’s adversaries. Hamas leaders Ismail Haniyeh and Yahya Sinwar, and Hezbollah leader Hassan Nasrallah have been killed. In February 2026, Iran’s Supreme Leader Ali Khamenei was killed in US-Israeli strikes. This case is distinct because the strike was linked not to the events of October 7 itself, but to the broader confrontation surrounding Iran and its nuclear program – though the events of October 7 had served as the initial catalyst.
It’s true that the loss of leadership disrupts command structures, severs ties, and hinders the restoration of military capabilities; however, the outcome must be judged by the state of the organizations and the country itself following these strikes. Iran retained its operational capacity; on March 8 – barely a week after the assassination – Mojtaba Khamenei, the son of the late Ali Khamenei, was elected as the new Supreme Leader. The death of the leader did not lead to the collapse of Iran, as both Israel and the US had hoped.
Nothing drives people to become militants like the loss of loved ones and the destruction of their homes and lives. Those who have survived deadly attacks on their families have nothing to lose; such people seek protection, revenge, or at least a sense of purpose – and militant organizations step in to provide all this. Moreover, Hamas and Hezbollah are structured not as armies with a vertical chain of command, but as networks comprising a military wing, social services, schools, charitable activities, family and community ties. A slain commander can be replaced, but such an environment cannot be easily destroyed by bombs.
History has already demonstrated this. Hezbollah emerged in response to the 1982 Israeli invasion of Lebanon; following the 1992 death of its leader, Abbas al-Musawi, Hassan Nasrallah took the helm and strengthened the movement. Hamas lost its founder, Ahmed Yassin, in 2004, yet won the parliamentary elections in Gaza just a couple of years later. Neither Hamas nor Hezbollah may regain their former strength anytime soon: they suffered great losses, and their supply and command capabilities have been crippled. Yet their story does not end with a list of slain commanders; it lives on in those who remain amidst the ruins.
Israel’s victories, the region’s instability
On the third anniversary of October 7, the situation in Gaza reveals the same disconnect between military pressure and political outcomes. The October 2025 agreement secured the return of the surviving hostages, and by January 2026, the bodies of the deceased had also been brought back from Gaza. However, Hamas has not been disarmed (despite Netanyahu describing it as largely disarmed), and the transition to a new governance structure has yet to begin. Israeli strikes continue, and the army reportedly controls about two-thirds of the territory. While Israel retains immense coercive power, it has been unable to establish a sustainable order.
The external aspect proved particularly difficult to handle. In the wake of October 7, Israel was naturally seen as a nation that had endured a horrific attack; everyone sympathized with it. Later, however, the image shifted: the world saw a devastated Gaza, a displaced population driven from place to place, and a humanitarian catastrophe. Now, facing another rainy winter, hundreds of thousands of people in Gaza are living in overcrowded camps where torrential rain floods their tents, or in buildings at risk of collapse. The longer this catastrophe drags on, the less people are willing to believe the explanation offered by Israel – that its actions are merely self-defense.
People all over the world have openly started expressing hostility toward Israel. Such a level of hatred would have been unimaginable just a few years ago. In the spring of 2026, Pew Research Center surveyed residents of 36 countries: on average, 67% held a very negative view of Israel, while only 25% viewed it favorably. Attitudes have deteriorated even in countries that sympathized most with Israel – such as the UK, Italy, Poland, and Australia. While criticism of the government’s actions does not equate to justifying Hamas, global anti-Semitism has risen due to the conduct of Netanyahu and his far-right ministers – Bezalel Smotrich and Itamar Ben-Gvir, who publicly express hateful, dehumanizing statements.
Netanyahu has gradually lost the sympathy of the international community. Public outrage has moved beyond street protests, influencing diplomatic decisions and relations with partners. The stance of Arab states has also shifted. Before the war, they viewed the normalization of relations with Israel as a means of gaining access to technology, investment, and enhanced security guarantees. Now, public fury over the Palestinian tragedy makes direct rapprochement difficult. Saudi Arabia continues to demand irreversible progress toward Palestinian statehood as a condition for normalizing relations with Israel. The assumption that the Palestinian issue could be sidelined by striking deals with Arab governments proved unfounded. The issue could neither be bypassed nor frozen; it has resurfaced in the region in its most destructive form.
The Middle East has become less predictable. The weakening of Iran’s allies has shifted the balance of power but failed to establish recognized rules of coexistence. Regional states are seeking additional external security guarantees and are ramping up their military capabilities. The direct confrontation between Israel and Iran has expanded the scope of potential targets and the number of parties involved in the conflict. Israel’s tactical advantage exists alongside the heightened vulnerability of the entire regional system.
Russia’s stakes in a fractured Middle East
Russia is primarily concerned with Iran’s stability. Tehran is important both as an independent partner and as a participant in Eurasian transport, trade, and energy networks. Strikes on Iranian infrastructure and disruptions to its foreign trade directly affect Russian interests. The North-South Corridor is gaining importance as an alternative transport route, yet it is simultaneously becoming more dependent on Iran’s ability to keep ports, roads, and border crossings operational. Increased demand for the route does not automatically guarantee an increase in its capacity; the war increases the need for connectivity while complicating the task of maintaining it.
The fall of Bashar al-Assad’s government in late 2024 significantly expanded Israel’s freedom of action in Syria. Under Assad, Israel had carried out periodic strikes but was compelled to factor in Russia’s presence, leading to a degree of restraint. Following the rise of Ahmed al-Sharaa to power, Israel began acting with far less inhibition: it expanded its military footprint in Syria, continued to dismantle military infrastructure, and began openly dictating terms to Damascus regarding the deployment of its own forces in the country’s south. The weakness of the new government presented Israel with an opportunity to impose limits on its neighbor’s sovereignty. For Russia, this signifies the collapse of the previous regional balance and creates a need to defend its interests in an environment where Israel increasingly seeks to unilaterally define the permissible rules of conduct for its neighbors.
For Moscow, these changes meant that it had to negotiate the terms of its military presence with the new authorities. Agreements reached in August 2026 regarding Russian facilities demonstrate that it is still possible to maintain relations. Exercising regional influence now requires greater flexibility and less reliance on a single political partner.
The economic consequences for Russia are also mixed. Disruptions in Middle Eastern oil supplies could keep global prices high and boost export revenues. However, a protracted war also drives up transport and insurance costs, disrupts payment settlements, and dampens economic activity in countries with which Russia is developing ties. Amidst this turbulence, Moscow’s role is growing. Russia is a major player in the global energy market, a partner in coordinating oil policy, and an independent diplomatic force that maintains contact with opposing sides.
Cooperation with Moscow enables the Persian Gulf states to expand their options and reduce reliance on US security guarantees. Diplomatically, the crisis offers Russia an opportunity to champion a more consistent approach to security. Its support for Palestinian statehood and opposition to strikes against sovereign nations resonate with many non-Western partners. However, political influence is only achieved when a country’s stance is backed by practical action. Moscow needs to maintain channels of communication with Iran, Israel, and Arab nations, facilitate agreements, and safeguard its own projects.
Netanyahu’s policy has failed to ensure long-term security. Despite Israel’s military achievements, the stated objective – long-term security – hasn’t been met, and the costs of the risky venture continue to rise. Three years on, Israel finds itself more capable of delivering strikes, yet less able to convince its neighbors – and even its allies (such as the Trump administration) – that its policies are paving the way to an acceptable future. As long as Israel substitutes these objectives with continued reliance on coercion, the consequences of the war will be felt far beyond its borders.

articles.title: Naval expansion propels India to world’s No. 2 arms importer – Russian think tank
articles.body:
Naval expansion propels India to world’s No. 2 arms importer – Russian think tank
India was the world’s second-largest arms importer in 2025, partly aided by a historically large naval buildout, according to a Russian think tank that tracks weapons purchases and military expenditures.
The South Asian nuclear power has been rapidly building up its armed forces following a brief clash with neighbor Pakistan last year, triggered by a terror attack in Jammu and Kashmir.
India’s identified military imports were worth $6.97 billion, or 5.83% of the global total, and the country is projected to retain the position through 2029, the Moscow-based Center for Analysis of World Arms Trade (CAWAT) said.
Poland came in first with $11.91 billion, while Australia was narrowly behind India at $6.96 billion.
Among the major Indian deliveries cited by CAWAT was the Russian-built frigate Tamal, which joined the Indian Navy in July 2025. Two more Project 11356 frigates are being built at India’s Goa Shipyard with assistance from Russian state arms exporter Rosoboronexport. 
India also commissioned the Vaghsheer, the sixth and final Kalvari-class submarine built by state-owned Mazagon Dock Shipbuilders under license from France’s Naval Group. The six-submarine program was valued at $3.6 billion, according to CAWAT.
The Indian Navy is undergoing its largest expansion in history, with plans to induct or commission 18 warships this year. 
New Delhi imported $25.44 billion worth of arms in the 2022-2025 period, placing it third behind Saudi Arabia and Qatar in CAWAT’s four-year rankings. Its annual imports rose from $3.87 billion in 2024 to $6.97 billion last year. 
The think tank projects India’s arms imports at $45.65 billion over 2026-2029, keeping the country in the second position. Poland is expected to remain at the top with $55.32 billion worth of imports, followed by Germany at $36.48 billion. The forecast is based on existing contracts, officially announced procurement plans, and expected tenders as of December 2025. 
Poland’s rise has been particularly sharp. Its arms imports climbed from $2.17 billion in 2022 to $11.91 billion in 2025, driven by major purchases including US-made Abrams tanks and South Korean K2 tanks.
CAWAT projects global arms imports at almost $633 billion over the 2026-2029 period, up 52.5% from in the preceding four years. The center expects Europe to take a larger share of global demand during the period.
The ranking covers identified commercial arms deliveries and does not include weapons supplied free of charge, including Western military aid to Ukraine.
CAWAT’s methodology differs from that of the Stockholm International Peace Research Institute (SIPRI), which measures the volume of major weapons transfers using a trend-indicator value rather than their sale price. SIPRI says its figures should not be directly compared with the financial value of arms transfers.

articles.title: Far-right surge threatens Europe’s drive to rearm
articles.body:
The growing popularity of far-right parties across Europe is sparking worries in NATO that they could weaken public support for rearmament and military aid to Ukraine as risks grow of a confrontation with Russia.
In France, Italy, Belgium, Germany, Poland and Romania, these parties are looking to turn voters’ cost-of-living concerns into opposition to aid for Kyiv, and rejection of higher national defense budgets and a greater role for the EU in defense — although each party has often sharply diverging views on those issues.
France’s National Rally leader Marine Le Pen last month called for limiting aid to Ukraine, saying: “financially, we can’t do it anymore.”
Advertisement
Roberto Vannacci, a former general and MEP who leads the far-right National Future party, which is increasingly challenging Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni, called for a rethink of defense spending. “Let’s evaluate whether this military spending is justified: in my opinion, it isn’t, especially at a time when commodity prices are hitting record highs,” he said last week.
The challenge for Europe’s mainstream parties is how to sustain support for higher defense budgets even if that means competing with welfare and other priorities.
“People are struggling with the rising cost of living across the board … so there’s room for populistic rhetoric about how much should we support Ukraine financially, or how much should we invest in defense,” said Janne Kuusela, permanent secretary at Finland’s defense ministry.
The dilemma is sharpening as several large NATO members, including France, Italy and Poland, face elections in 2027, when far-right parties stand a real chance of coming to power. Many countries are also beginning talks on next year’s budgets.
For NATO, a spending slowdown would complicate efforts to meet the alliance’s target of spending 5% of GDP on defense and security by 2035. Four NATO diplomats, granted anonymity to speak freely, said the risk is a growing concern, though some said its effects may not be clear until next year’s budget cycle.
“We’re already in a situation where we need to catch up” with Russia, said a NATO military official. “So far, we’re on a positive trajectory — if someone closes the faucet, there’s a risk of losing capabilities.”
Advertisement
Turning the tide
European countries and Canada are expected to spend $634 billion on core defense needs this year, an 11% hike relative to 2025. But public support has limits.
In eight European countries, an average of 46.2% of respondents said they would not back higher defense spending if it meant higher taxes, while 35.5% were in favor, according to an August poll assessed by the European Council on Foreign Relations and shared with POLITICO. More people were opposed to increasing taxes to finance military spending in Germany, France, Italy, Spain and Poland. Respondents in the Netherlands, Sweden and the U.K. were more likely to accept higher taxes for military spending.
Protests against higher defense spending have taken place in Rome, Brussels and Madrid this year, with demonstrators criticizing cuts to funding for hospitals, universities and social services.
A damaged residential building is seen in Kyiv after a Russian missile strike on July 6, 2026. | Genya Savilov/AFP via Getty Images
Support for Ukraine is declining as well, according to NATO’s internal polling from this spring, falling from 59% in 2025 to 55% this year, with lethal aid the least popular form of support.
Far-right pushback on defense varies across Europe and falls broadly into three categories: opposition to military aid for Ukraine; rejection of EU-level defense projects; and criticism of defense spending more broadly. Yet all threaten to halt the continent’s effort to rearm rapidly and jointly — and limit Russia’s aggression against Ukraine.
The right’s political foes warn that opposition plays into the Kremlin’s hands. “The pressure from the right doesn’t actually come from the right, but largely from Moscow,” German Defense Minister Boris Pistorius said. Parties such as National Rally and the AfD have longstanding ties with Russia, though they have sought to shake off their links in recent years.
Defense spending pressure
The political risk varies by country. Le Pen is a front-runner to become French president, while the AfD has made gains at the regional level but is unlikely to take national office soon.
Far-right gains are putting centrist parties under pressure to defend higher spending or consider cuts to retain public support.
“There is a risk that the formally pro-European mainstream across Europe might be too timid to spend … as would be necessary on defence,” said Paweł Zerka, senior policy fellow at the ECFR.
While Le Pen’s National Rally has indicated that she would respect France’s current trajectory of increasing military spending, Italy’s Meloni last week proposed spending €8 billion less on defense than the government’s initial proposal amid pressure from her far-right coalition partner, the League. Meloni last week proposed spending €8 billion less on defense than the government’s initial proposal amid pressure from her far-right coalition partner, the League.
“You can’t spend on weapons what you can’t spend on pensions, excise tax relief, or utility bills,” Claudio Borghi, a League senator, said last week.
Advertisement
In Poland, President Karol Nawrocki, backed by the right-wing Law and Justice party, tried but failed to block access to nearly €44 billion in EU SAFE defense loans, saying the scheme risked making Poland dependent on Brussels and saddling future generations with debt.
Pressure to rethink defense spending could make it harder for NATO members to fund the capabilities officials say are needed to deter Russia, as capitals begin talks this month on determining the alliance’s war plans, which are due by 2029.
A slowdown by larger members such as France and Italy would have broader effects because they account for a greater share of defense investment and aid to Kyiv, one of the NATO diplomats said.
“If bigger countries stop making progress, then NATO will stop making progress,” the diplomat said. “You weaken NATO, you weaken Europe’s ability to defend itself, and you make Ukraine … more vulnerable.”
It could also affect the sum earmarked for defense in the EU’s next long-term budget if talks stretch on into next year, said Guntram Wolff, a senior fellow and defense economics analyst at the Bruegel think tank.
“Nationalists are all only interested in their country, they don’t want to work together with other European countries,” said German lawmaker Marie-Agnes Strack-Zimmermann, who chairs the European Parliament’s defense committee.

articles.title: France Develops IRIFI Strike Drone With Range Of 2,000 km — Morocco to Be First Customer
articles.body:
French defense company Harmattan AI has unveiled the new long-range IRIFI strike drone, with Morocco set to be its first customer.
Harmattan AI has provided details on the new drone’s specifications.
The IRIFI UAV is designed to deliver high-precision strikes at ranges of up to 2,000 kilometers. The drones will be launched from mobile container-based launchers, allowing for rapid deployment and use in large numbers.
The drone is equipped with an autonomous navigation system that does not rely on GNSS satellite signals, as well as an optical guidance system for the final phase of flight. According to the developer, this ensures resistance to electronic warfare and strike accuracy down to one meter.
Before launch, the operator identifies the target and route, after which the drone autonomously carries out the mission without constant communication with the ground control station.
Harmattan AI positions the IRIFI as a relatively inexpensive means of delivering massive, high-precision strikes. The company has not yet disclosed the warhead’s weight, the drone’s speed, dimensions, or cost.
According to the developers’ plan, a single operator will be able to manage the deployment of dozens of such drones. Artificial intelligence will be used to plan strikes by analyzing satellite imagery. However, the decision to engage targets will remain with a human operator.
The French publication Le Desk reports that on October 7, during the Marrakech Air Show, representatives of the Moroccan Defense Ministry and Harmattan AI signed a letter of intent regarding the procurement, joint development, and production of the IRIFI within the kingdom.
As part of the collaboration, production facilities for the new UAVs are to be established in Morocco. In particular, critical technological components are planned to be developed and manufactured directly in the country with the involvement of local specialists.
At the same time, the signed document is currently a letter of intent, not a final supply contract. The number of drones planned for procurement, the cost of the program, and the timeline for the start of serial production have not been disclosed.
The new program builds on the strategic partnership established in June 2026 between Harmattan AI and the Royal Moroccan Armed Forces. The initial agreements called for the establishment of local production of autonomous defense systems, a research and development center for artificial intelligence, and collaboration with educational institutions.
Earlier, Militarnyi reported that in October 2025, Ukraine’s Skyeton and France’s Harmattan AI announced a partnership to integrate artificial intelligence technologies into Raybird drones.
In February 2026, it was also reported that Harmattan AI planned to integrate its compact Sahara synthetic aperture radars into Ukrainian drones. These radars enable reconnaissance even in cloudy and foggy conditions.

articles.title: Ukraine squeezes more defense out of Soviet-era stock, pairing Kub launcher and American RIM-7 interceptors to catch Russia’s jet-powered drones
articles.body:
Kyiv is bolting two Soviet-era missile systems together to knock down Russia's fastest Geran-4 and Geran-5 drones. Ukraine's 156th Maksym Kryvonis Anti-Aircraft Missile Regiment has downed about 20 air targets using a Kub launcher firing under the radar and fire control of a Buk unit.
Russia has switched to jet-powered Gerans, faster drones that Ukraine's cheap interceptors struggle to catch, so more of them reach their targets. The damage from Russian strikes is set to reach up to $10 billion this year, according to Ukraine's Economy Ministry.
Meanwhile, Western resupply has thinned too. Deliveries of air defense missiles from partners fell threefold in the first half of 2026 against 2025, even though those partners hold the missiles, President Volodymyr Zelenskyy says.
So crews stretch what they have. In the Kub-Buk hybrid, a Kub launcher cannot aim on its own, lacking a radar to light up a target for its missile, according to Militarnyi. A Buk has that radar, so the two fire together, the Kub sending its 3M9 missile where the Buk points. The pairing is possible because both come from the same Soviet design line.
Western missiles in Soviet launchers
The same regiment reaches for a second workaround as Buk missiles run short. Its crews have rewired launchers to fire American RIM-7 interceptors, a Soviet-Western mongrel that troops nicknamed Frankenstein and the US calls FrankenSAM.
The patchwork earns its keep. One crew commander said some of these machines have more than 34 air kills each, and a single launcher has sent up RIM-7s 131 times, Ukrainian troops said.
A layered answer
The hybrids are one thread in a wider web. Ukraine is stitching together a layered defense against the jet-powered Gerans, leaning on electronic jamming, fighter jets, and a new class of homegrown interceptor drones. Each tool has limits, and the newest interceptors still bring down only the occasional jet drone.
The bet now is on numbers. Ukraine aims to build up to 400 interceptor drones a month by the end of October to chase the faster Gerans, Zelenskyy said on 2 October. Until that scale arrives, improvised launchers like the 156th Regiment keep filling the gap.

articles.title: Ukraine’s Drones Hunt Down Russian Osa Air Defense System—and Strike It Twice, Video
articles.body:
- Category
- War in Ukraine
Ukraine’s Drones Hunt Down Russian Osa Air Defense System—and Strike It Twice, Video
Ukrainian drone operators struck a Russian Osa short-range air defense system twice on the Donbas front, according to footage released by the Signum Battalion of the 59th Assault Brigade of Unmanned Systems on October 8.
The video shows Ukrainian drones engaging the Russian surface-to-air missile system during a broader series of strikes against military equipment and logistics.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
Signum operators highlighted the irony themselves, playing on the system’s name—Osa means “Wasp.”
“We ‘stung’ the Osa twice,” the battalion said.
The same footage shows Signum operators targeting Russian logistics across the Donbas, including pickup trucks, UAZ vans, cargo trucks, semitrailers, and other vehicles used to move troops, ammunition, and equipment.
The battalion said its crews routinely work against the routes Russian forces depend on to keep frontline units supplied, with the Osa becoming one of the more valuable targets caught during the latest operation.
The 9K33 Osa is a Soviet-designed mobile short-range air defense system developed beginning in 1960 and introduced into service in 1971. At the time, it was notable for combining its target-acquisition radar, tracking radar, and missiles on a single amphibious vehicle, allowing the system to operate without separate radar vehicles.
Built on the six-wheeled BAZ-5937 chassis, the Osa was designed to accompany ground forces and protect them from low-flying aircraft and other aerial threats. Its radar can detect targets at distances of roughly 30 kilometers, while later variants can engage targets at ranges of around 10 kilometers.
The system underwent several upgrades during its service life, including the Osa-AKM introduced in 1980, which brought improved tracking and enclosed missile canisters.
Earlier, Ukrainian forces destroyed a Russian Pantsir-S2 air defense system using FP-2 strike drones, with footage showing the system burning before its ammunition detonated and tore the vehicle apart.

articles.title: President Zelensky, UK Foreign Secretary honor victims of Russian missile strike in Pryluky
articles.body:
President Zelensky, UK Foreign Secretary honor victims of Russian missile strike in Pryluky
This was reported by an Ukrinform correspondent.
“Today is a very tragic day. We had a tragedy here yesterday. We came here to help, to speak with people, and also to visit the hospital, see what people need and what the conditions are, and honor all those who were killed. During this trip, a horrific strike occurred in Kramatorsk, with a large number of people killed,” Zelensky said during a briefing in Pryluky.
He noted that UK Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband was accompanying him on his trip to Pryluky.
“I certainly want to thank my British counterpart, who came to the capital today, but we invited him to travel with us to Pryluky and see firsthand what is really happening, what these daily strikes look like, and how our people are enduring this struggle,” the President said.
Standing near the destroyed five-story building, Zelensky thanked all the teams that had worked at the site.
“About 500 people worked here, from different teams, from police officers to State Emergency Service personnel. We thank them. They saved 31 lives, 31 people, 15 of whom had been completely buried under the rubble. Unfortunately, the losses are very high: 22 people were killed, including five children, and 54 were injured, including seven children,” the head of state said.
He called on partners, including the UK, to step up assistance to Ukraine, particularly by providing air defense systems.
Zelensky separately stressed the need to intensify the negotiation process.
“Besides air defense, which is in short supply because our country is large and strikes can hit anywhere, we certainly want to draw attention to the negotiating track. In our view, the United States should raise the pressure through sanctions and other measures, as well as through financial assistance and separate assistance to Ukraine with air defense. And through such steps (…) force Putin to sit down at the negotiating table,” the Ukrainian President said.
As reported, 22 people were killed in a Russian missile strike on Pryluky, Chernihiv region, on October 7, including five children.
Photo: Suspilne Chernihiv

articles.title: Polish SIM cards found inside Russian drones in Poland, raising new questions over 2025 incursion
articles.body:
Polish SIM cards were found inside some of the Russian drones that entered Polish airspace during a mass incursion in September 2025, Polish outlet RMF24 reported, citing findings from a Polish prosecution investigation.
SIM cards can allow drones to connect to local cellular networks for functions such as communications, data transmission, telemetry, or navigation-related services. However, investigators have not said what the Polish SIM cards found in the Russian drones were used for. The details remain classified.
The SIM cards were discovered in some of the Russian Gerbera drones recovered after the incursion, RMF24 reported.
Investigators have not disclosed whether the SIM cards were stolen or obtained illegally.
The investigation into the September 9–10, 2025 incursion was ultimately closed after prosecutors failed to identify those responsible for violating Polish airspace.
More than 30 drones entered Poland
The incursion took place overnight on September 9–10, 2025, during a large Russian missile and drone attack on Ukraine. More than 30 Russian Gerbera drones entered Polish airspace from the east and came down at 27 locations across the country, according to RMF24.
Polish forces intercepted and shot down multiple drones, with the Territorial Defense Forces deployed to search for wreckage and other objects that came down on Polish territory. Poland also maintained contact with NATO command throughout the operation.
The incident prompted Poland to close four airports – Warsaw Chopin, Warsaw-Modlin, Rzeszów-Jasionka and Lublin – because of the military activity.
Polish officials described the airspace violations as unprecedented and a serious threat to national security. The incident marked the first time since Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine that Polish forces had used weapons against Russian aerial objects that entered the country's airspace.
The mass incursion subsequently became the subject of a criminal investigation into the violation of Polish airspace and the threat to public safety.
Investigation closed without identifying perpetrators
After months of investigation, Polish prosecutors closed the case because they were unable to identify the perpetrators, according to Lublin District Prosecutor’s Office spokesman Marcin Kozak, as cited by RMF24.
Most of the case files, including the justification for the decision, are classified.
Last September, Poland downed four of 19 Russian drones. This September, drone reached NATO’s missile shield in Redzikowo, and troops guarding it called 112
Prosecutors cleared Poland's military response
Investigators also examined whether the Polish military had responded properly to the drone incursion.
According to RMF24, prosecutors concluded that the military acted in accordance with procedures. Polish troops had the right to use force and shoot down hostile objects, and prosecutors found no irregularities in their response.
The investigation was therefore closed both over the failure to identify the perpetrators and over the assessment of the Polish military's actions.

articles.title: Denmark accuses Russia of sabotage against defence companies
articles.body:
Denmark accuses Russia of sabotage against defence companies
According to Danish intelligence, Russia has launched sabotage operations against Danish companies that supply goods to Ukraine, having concluded that broader destabilisation attempts failed to curb military support.
Source: Reuters
Details: This shift indicates a significant escalation in the hybrid warfare waged by Moscow, said Josefine Christensen, lead analyst at the Danish Security and Intelligence Service (PET), during a homeland security conference in Copenhagen.
Quote from Christensen: "What we saw in the spring was a lot of planning, but very little carried out; what we saw in early summer is that they started to carry out a lot more."
She noted that Russia had concluded that its previous broad-spectrum attacks "did not have the effect of deterring the Western NATO from supporting Ukraine".
Christensen added that Moscow maintains political control over the operations, while operational boldness is growing. Russia is now "trying to hit targets that have a direct impact on the front line. That means weapons production".
Without providing further details, Christensen cited a Russian Ministry of Defence list naming European manufacturers of drones and their components, which Moscow said in April had been designated as potential military targets.
Background: A shipment of Russian sunflower oil bound for India was cancelled and other cargoes were delayed after attacks on Black Sea ports disrupted exports from India's top supplier, an industry official and trade sources reported.

articles.title: Russia Steps Up Sabotage Attacks on Danish Defense Firms, Intelligence Says
articles.body:
Russia has begun sabotage operations against Danish companies supplying military equipment to Ukraine after concluding that broader efforts to disrupt Western support for Kyiv had failed, Josefine Christensen, a lead analyst at Denmark’s Security and Intelligence Service (PET), said Wednesday.
Christensen made the remarks at a homeland security conference in Copenhagen, describing the shift as a significant escalation in Moscow’s hybrid warfare campaign.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
“What we saw in the spring was a lot of planning, but very little carried out; what we saw in early summer is that they started to carry out a lot more,” Christensen said, according to Reuters.
Russia concluded that its previous broad targeting “did not have the effect of deterring the Western (military alliance) NATO from supporting Ukraine,” she said.
Moscow is now “trying to hit targets that have a direct impact on the front line. That means weapons production,” Christensen added.
Russia has repeatedly denied involvement in sabotage or hybrid warfare operations. The Russian Embassy in Copenhagen rejected the allegations Wednesday, accusing Danish authorities of making unfounded claims against Russia.
Christensen also cited an April list published by Russia’s Defense Ministry naming European drone and drone-component manufacturers that Moscow identified as potential military targets.
ISW Russian Offensive Campaign Assessment, November 7, 2026
‘Anyone just looking for quick money’
Russia is increasingly relying on untrained proxies recruited through Telegram and other social media platforms, including homeless people and people addicted to drugs, according to PET.
Recruitment typically begins with low-level tasks such as reconnaissance or photographing potential targets before escalating to sabotage operations.
“It could be anyone just looking for quick money,” Christensen said. “If the first person isn’t successful, they’ll throw another one at the problem until they succeed.”
Denmark’s defense intelligence service said last month that Russia was likely to intensify hybrid attacks against Western countries in the coming months, following Germany’s accusation that Moscow was responsible for an attempted drone attack at Leipzig/Halle Airport in August.
In September 2025, ahead of Denmark hosting an EU summit, drones disrupted air traffic at six Danish airports, including Copenhagen, the Nordic region’s busiest. Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen called the incident a hybrid attack against Denmark.

articles.title: German court orders detention of former intelligence chief after spying arrest
articles.body:
A formal arrest warrant has been issued against Germany’s former top spy, with a judge ordering him to be held in pre-trial detention, a day after he was arrested on suspicion of treason and spying on behalf of an overseas intelligence agency.
August Hanning, 80, is accused of buying secret documents from a former colleague and using them to advise a foreign intelligence service, according to the office of the federal prosecutor.
Hanning’s arrest on Tuesday, along with that of his former office head, referred to as Manfred D. It has sent shock waves through Germany’s political and intelligence community, with analysts calling it potentially the country’s biggest espionage scandal since the end of the cold war.
It has raised questions in Berlin over how Germany’s foreign intelligence service can uphold its reputation internationally, particularly at a time of heightened security concerns. Also under scrutiny is the sustainability of rules governing the conduct of retired senior officials and their ability to earn extra income based on their insider knowledge and professional networks.
Hanning was head of Germany’s foreign intelligence service (BND) between 1998 and 2005.
A lawyer for Hanning denied he had been involved in any wrongdoing on Wednesday, telling the conservative daily newspaper Die Welt: “While it is true that he was in possession of confidential documents, the allegation that he passed on information contained therein to the detriment of Germany, let alone for payment, is incorrect.”
Manfred D, who was also placed under formal arrest on Wednesday by the judge in Karlsruhe, has yet to respond to questions via his lawyer.
Hanning is alleged to have agreed in 2010 to pay for information from Manfred D, who allegedly then smuggled it out of the BND. Manfred D, 64, had worked under Hanning and went on to serve subsequent BND bosses after Hanning, before retiring in March this year.
Hanning is believed to have received about 2,000 documents from Manfred D until June 2022, some of which were classified, according to prosecutors. He is alleged to have used the information in his papers for his private consulting work.
Prosecutors were alerted to Hanning’s alleged criminal activities by investigators gathering evidence in a separate child kidnapping case involving a steakhouse restaurant dynasty, which the former spy chief is accused of participating in using his former contacts with Israeli intelligence. Christina Block, an heiress to the business, allegedly paid Hanning and a retired police officer more than €100,000 (£85,000) for their roles in the alleged abduction of her two children from her ex-husband.
A report in Der Spiegel on Wednesday said investigators were looking into a possible connection to the foreign intelligence service of Azerbaijan as one of the agencies Hanning may have been passing information to.
Azerbaijan’s media and broadcasting council denied any connection to Hanning or the investigation. “The malicious intent of the forces behind this disinformation operation is to damage Azerbaijan-Germany relations,” the council said in a statement.
The scandal has awakened memories of the Günter Guillaume affair, when an East German Stasi spy and his wife posing as refugees infiltrated the government of the then chancellor Willy Brandt, leading to Brandt’s resignation in 1974.
Marc Henrichmann, the head of the parliamentary committee overseeing the intelligence services, which has repeatedly raised questions about the post-career consulting activities of intelligence agency employees but has been told legal obstacles stood in the way of challenging them, said he was “fairly flabbergasted” by the affair, but stressed it was as yet unclear the breadth and extent of the alleged wrongdoing.
“As yet we don’t know exactly what happened,” he told the public broadcaster Deutschlandfunk, while acknowledging the need to “restore broken trust” in the BND.
On Wednesday, politicians and intelligence analysts called for stricter regulation around allowing former security employees to make use of their influence and knowledge after retiring.
The scandal comes at a time when Germany is attempting to make its intelligence agencies, including the BND and its domestic sibling, the BfV, more robust, efficient and independent from those of its allies, in particular boosting their powers of surveillance to more effectively tackle sabotage and hacking attacks, amid rising threats from external powers such as Russia and Iran.
The scandal is yet another blow to the BND’s reputation. Not only is it notoriously dependent on information from foreign agencies to foil terror attacks on German soil, but it has faced other cases of its staff allegedly spying for other countries.
It has also been reeling from the case of a department head, Carsten L, who was accused in December 2022 of spying for Russia. His trial is now being heard by Berlin’s higher regional court.
Sensitivities over the country’s past, when dictatorships misused their powers of surveillance to spy on their own people, have made reform of the agencies hard to pursue.
Hanning, the son of a brickyard owner, rose through the ranks of the intelligence service to become its head. After the attacks of 11 September 2001, he oversaw the investigation into some of the terrorists who had studied in Hamburg. He initiated wide-reaching reforms of the BND including bringing it closer to politics, becoming a close adviser to the then interior minister Wolfgang Schäuble. He spoke out against a “culture of leaks” and was deeply critical of the NSA whistleblower Edward Snowden, calling him an “internal offender”.
Once his civil service career was over, Hanning continued to hold a role as a respected behind-the-scenes negotiator, and frequently intervened in government security policy debates. At the same time he built up his consultant business, founding an agency with his wife, Ruth, called Hanning Consult, and worked for various other global consulting agencies. He even produced a “spy cookbook” with his wife, called “Top(f) Secret” (Topf being the German word for saucepan).

articles.title: Iran and Oman agree on 'safe routes' in Hormuz
articles.body:
Breadcrumb
Iran announces agreement with Oman over 'safe routes' in Strait of Hormuz
Iran has set out its conditions for ending the war on all fronts and establishing security in the region and the Strait of Hormuz clearly and decisively, Iranian Foreign Ministry spokesman Esmail Baghaei said late Wednesday night, adding that a response to US proposals would be delivered through mediation channels.
Baghaei further said in remarks reported by Iran's ISNA news agency that Iran and Oman had reached an agreement regarding the geographical coordinates for safe navigation routes in the Strait of Hormuz and mechanisms to announce them to relevant international authorities.
US President Donald Trump, meanwhile, on Wednesday evening US time that his envoy Steve Witkoff was currently working to reach an agreement with Iran and was making progress.
"Making a deal is not the option I want, but they are actually ready to give us anything so that we stop, and they certainly will never get nuclear peace," Trump said at an election rally in Texas in support of the state's Republican candidate for the US Senate.
In September, Iran prepared a ceasefire proposal that included reopening the Strait of Hormuz within seven days in exchange for lifting the US naval blockade, ending sanctions on oil exports and resuming nuclear negotiations.
But, Trump rejected the proposal and repeating threatened to return to all-out war.
Baghaei's latest remarks come amid US reports about preparations by the US military to launch widespread strikes on Iran, according to reports in the US media.
US officials had told Axios that the Pentagon had instructed US Central Command several days ago to complete preparations to resume the war on Iran.
The Atlantic newspaper also reported, citing two sources in the US administration, that US President Donald Trump was considering a plan to strike Iran before the midterm elections scheduled for 3 November.
Article translated from Arabic by Afrah Almatwari. To read the original, click here.

articles.title: Ukrainian drones strike oil refinery in Russia’s Bashkortostan
articles.body:
Ukrainian drones strike oil refinery in Russia’s Bashkortostan
Ukrainian drones struck Gazprom Neftekhim Salavat, one of Russia’s largest oil refining complexes, in Salavat, Bashkortostan, overnight on October 8, the Ukrainian monitoring Telegram channels Exilenova+ and Supernova+ reported.
Astra, an independent Telegram channel, reviewed photos and videos from eyewitnesses and concluded that the fire likely broke out on the grounds of Gazprom Neftekhim Salavat. Ukrainian drones have targeted the refinery more than once during the full-scale war between Russia and Ukraine.
Bashkortostan authorities declared an air raid alert overnight because of the threat of a Ukrainian drone attack. They have not reported on the aftermath of the attack.
In addition, “drone debris” fell on the grounds of a facility in Krasnodar, according to a local emergency response headquarters. Fragments of the drone damaged a building and sparked a fire. No one was injured, and the facility’s nature was not specified.
Russia’s Defense Ministry said its air defenses shot down 399 Ukrainian drones over Russian regions, occupied Crimea, and the Black Sea since the evening of October 7.
Drone strikes have forced Russian oil refineries to suspend or halt operations, contributing to a fuel crisis in Russia over the summer.
In early October, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky promised that Ukraine would step up its attacks on Russian oil refineries. Russia’s Defense Ministry threatened to respond by expanding its strikes on targets in Ukraine.

articles.title: Slovakia sends military attaché back to Russia for first time in 4 years
articles.body:
Slovakia sends military attaché back to Russia for first time in 4 years
Slovakia and Russia are resuming the exchange of military attachés for the first time since the start of Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine – a decision that has drawn criticism from the Slovak opposition.
Source: European Pravda with reference to Slovak news outlet Aktuality
Details: During his visit to Moscow in May, Slovak Prime Minister Robert Fico promised Russian leader Vladimir Putin during their talks that military and diplomatic relations between the two countries would be restored. As part of these arrangements, the countries are resuming the exchange of military attachés after a four-year hiatus.
Fico's government has sent two military officers to Moscow and Bratislava is awaiting the arrival of a Russian attaché.
The last Russian military attaché to serve in Slovakia left the country four years ago. Sergei Solomasov, who held the post, was expelled by the government of Eduard Heger along with other Russian diplomats after Russia invaded Ukraine. Solomasov was also implicated in an espionage case: he bribed Bohuš Garbár, a contributor to the Hlavné správy website, to disseminate disinformation on his instructions.
According to the latest information, Russia's new military attaché in Bratislava could be 46-year-old Maksim Verezhan. The naval officer previously served at the Russian embassy in Rome and has spent the past few years in Moscow.
Slovakia has appointed its military representatives in Moscow. Brigadier General Slavomír Staviarsky will serve as military attaché and Colonel Ivo Gahír will be his deputy.
Tomáš Valášek, an MP from the Progressive Slovakia party, criticised the government's decision to resume military and diplomatic engagement with Russia. He argued that exchanging military attachés would primarily benefit Russia, as the Slovak representative is unlikely to gain access to important information in Moscow.
Valášek also said the Russian military attaché could have an opportunity to take part in disinformation and influence operations in Slovakia, fuel social tensions and sway public opinion towards Russia.
The opposition politician also suggested that the move to restore military relations may have come from Moscow, with the Slovak government simply accepting the proposal.
Background:
- Slovakia's Foreign Ministry, meanwhile, justified the return of military attachés by saying that the government is seeking to establish pragmatic relations with Russia.
- Slovak Defence Minister Robert Kaliňák recently said that Bratislava does not regard Russia as a threat.
- Slovak Prime Minister Robert Fico has said he does not want Slovakia to become involved in a military conflict "because of some Article 5".
- It was also reported that Slovakia's opposition is demanding explanations from the government and Fico over reports in the German media linking an attempted attack on a Ukrainian drone manufacturer in Prešov to Russian military intelligence.

articles.title: Air defense downs 126 of 142 Russian UAVs – Air Force
articles.body:
Overnight into October 8, Russian occupation forces attacked Ukraine with 142 strike UAVs, including Shahed drones, Gerbera drones, and Parodiya-type decoy drones, the Air Force of the Armed Forces of Ukraine reports.
"According to preliminary data, as of 09:30, air defense shot down/suppressed 126 enemy Shahed, Gerbera, and other types of UAVs," the General Staff's Telegram channel statement reads.
In addition, Russian air attack impacts were recorded at 7 locations, while fallen debris was registered at 4 locations.
The air attack was repelled by aviation, anti-aircraft missile troops, electronic warfare (EW) units, uncrewed aerial systems units, and mobile fire groups of the Ukrainian Defense Forces.
The attack is ongoing, with several Russian UAVs remaining in the airspace.

articles.title: National Security Council condemns strikes on ships in the Black Sea
articles.body:
News
National Security Council condemns strikes on ships in the Black Sea
President Iotova: Russia’s War in Ukraine has significantly deteriorated the security environment in the region
Wednesday 7 October 2026 19:36
Wednesday, 7 October 2026, 19:36
PHOTO BTA
Font size
The Consultative Council on National Security (CCNS), convened by Bulgarian President Iliana Iotova, strongly condemns the attacks on merchant ships in the Black Sea, calling them a gross violation of international maritime law, and calls for an immediate investigation to establish those responsible for the attacks, Bulgaria’s head of state Iliana Iotova said following a five-hour meeting of CCNS. The meeting discussed security risks in the Black Sea and potential threats to the country’s critical infrastructure arising from the ongoing war in Ukraine.
The head of state convened the first Consultative Council on National Security of her term following an incident in Bulgaria’s exclusive economic zone in the Black Sea, where two merchant ships flying foreign flags were hit by military drones on October 6.
President Iotova said that Russia’s war in Ukraine has significantly worsened the security environment in the Black Sea region:
President Iliana Iotova
PHOTO BGNES
“Given the incidents, it was acknowledged that there are serious challenges to protecting critical infrastructure. These threats are a direct consequence of the lack of prospects for a peaceful resolution to the military conflict''.
Iliana Iotova said CCNS members had also agreed to continue implementing the measures adopted by the Council of Ministers to counter risks and threats. ''The Consultative Council on National Security agreed on proposals to the executive and legislative branches, with the proposals being adopted by a three-quarters majority. Three parliamentary groups voted against. We condemn the attacks on merchant ships and call for an investigation to establish those responsible for the attacks”, Iliana Iotova added.
“An immediate ceasefire is the strongest guarantee of our security. Bulgaria must play an active role in this process,” the president also said.
“Bulgaria should urgently hold consultations with Romania and Türkiye on joint action to halt attacks on merchant ships in the Black Sea and ensure the safety of navigation. Bulgaria should take an active role in negotiations and in finding consensus among the countries bordering the Black Sea: Russia, Ukraine, Bulgaria, Romania, Georgia and Türkiye”, Iliana Iotova added.
PHOTO BGNES
It is also necessary to strengthen maritime situational awareness through the use of unmanned aerial systems for reconnaissance and surveillance, as well as to accelerate the modernization of the armed forces with the aim of acquiring counter-drone systems with kinetic capabilities, in close cooperation with NATO and the European Union.
According to the participants in the meeting, Russia’s war against Ukraine has led to a significant deterioration in the security environment in the Black Sea region.
Premier Rumen Radev
PHOTO BGNES
Following the meeting, Prime Minister Rumen Radev said that, at this point, there are no grounds for Bulgaria to categorically say that Russia was responsible for the strikes on vessels in the country’s exclusive economic zone. According to him, determining the origin of the drones used in the attacks should be based on concrete evidence rather than hypotheses.
The Prime Minister said that the government would propose coordination with Türkiye and Romania, while also seeking support from the US partners to investigate the area where the strikes occurred.
Particular attention will be paid to the vessel Able, which is still afloat, in order to determine the origin of the drones, Rumen Radev explained. He also announced that Bulgaria had had contacted the European Maritime Safety Agency (EMSA) to request a free examination of debris from the sunken vessel. “Only then can we say what kind of drone it was and who carried out the attack”, Premier Radev stated firmly.
The Prime Minister stressed that, at present, there is no immediate threat to Bulgaria’s national security. “I cannot say that there is an immediate threat to national security. Of course, there are risks. A war is being waged not far from us. As I said, it is expanding its geographical scope. It has also entered the exclusive economic zone of the Republic of Bulgaria. But at this point, I can say that there is no direct threat to Bulgaria’s national security”, said Rumen Radev.
Ivaylo Mirchev
PHOTO BTA
“What became clear from the Consultative Council on National Security is that there are sufficient indications of clear Russian involvement in the sinking of one of the vessels”, said Ivaylo Mirchev, co-chairman of Democratic Bulgaria. He added: “I don’t remember anyone at the table having doubts that Russia was behind the attack.”
The MP also said that the text adopted by the Consultative Council on National Security was not supported by four parliamentary groups - Democratic Bulgaria (DB), We Continue the Change (PP), Movement for Rights and Freedoms (DPS) and Vazrazhdane.
Stanislav Atanasov
PHOTO BTA
“The issue on which there was no consensus was who the aggressor is, and that is abundantly clear”, said Stanislav Anastassov of the Movement for Rights and Freedoms (DPS) parliamentary group following the meeting of the Consultative Council on National Security (CCNS).
Kostadin Kostadinov
PHOTO BTA
Vazrazhdane is calling for Bulgaria to act as a mediator in the conflict between Russia and Ukraine, rather than participate in policies that, according to the party, fuel the hostilities, said the party’s leader, Kostadin Kostadinov, following the meeting of the Consultative Council on National Security.
Nikolay Denkov
PHOTO BTA
Nikolay Denkov of We Continue the Change (PP) highlighted the vote on the CCNS statement, noting that four of the six parliamentary parties had voted against the document. Regarding the question of who was behind the attacks on the vessels, he stressed that the investigation should be completed before any definitive conclusions are drawn. According to him, the participants in the CCNS were united in their view that the investigation must be completed and that its findings should be provided to the relevant authorities.
The GERB–SDS parliamentary group was represented by GERB leader Boyko Borissov, who made no comment following the meeting of the Consultative Council on National Security.
The meeting was attended by the Speaker of Parliament, the prime minister, the ministers of defence and interior, the heads of the security services, and representatives of the parliamentary groups. The CCNS’s decisions are purely advisory and consultative, serving to foster political consensus and make recommendations on strategic matters related to the country’s security.
Edited by Diana Tsankova
Translated by Kostadin Atanasov
This publication was created by: Kostadin Atanasov

articles.title: Saudi-led coalition says it intercepts three Houthi ballistic missiles
articles.body:
Saudi-led coalition says it intercepts three Houthi ballistic missiles
Saudi Arabia says two of the missiles intercepted were headed towards the capital, Riyadh.
The Saudi-led coalition fighting on behalf of Yemen’s internationally recognised government says it has intercepted ballistic missiles allegedly fired by Yemen’s Houthis towards cities in Saudi Arabia.
In a statement, coalition spokesman Turki al-Maliki said his forces intercepted and destroyed two ballistic missiles heading in the direction of the Saudi capital Riyadh, and one missile in the direction of the city of Khamis Mushait, close to the Yemeni border, on Thursday.
Separately, Saudi Arabia’s civil defence agency said in a statement on X that falling debris from an intercepted missile had caused material damage to a kindergarten and medical clinic complex in Riyadh. It did not indicate if there were any casualties.
Yahya Saree, Yemen’s Houthi military spokesman, said the Iran-aligned group launched a ballistic missile towards King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh on Thursday afternoon, claiming that the missile had successfully hit its intended target, causing damage and disrupting air traffic.
Witnesses told The Associated Press news agency that they heard several explosions in Riyadh on Thursday, including one at the city’s airport that halted flights. Al Jazeera could not independently confirm the reports.
In recent days, the Houthis have warned aviation companies to avoid using Saudi airspace, saying any aircraft operating in the kingdom’s airspace, except over the holy cities of Mecca and Medina, is a target for the Houthis.
Abha International Airport and King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh were targeted in two separate attacks, claimed by the Houthis on Tuesday and Wednesday. At least three civilians were killed and 36 injured, according to a statement from the Saudi General Authority of Civil Aviation (GACA).
On September 18, Saudi-led coalition forces said they intercepted and destroyed a suspected Houthi ballistic missile fired towards the airport in Riyadh from Yemen.
A day later, on September 19, at least one explosion was heard near the airport in Riyadh, and a large plume of black smoke was seen rising from a fuel storage area at King Khalid International Airport.
Fighting intensifies in Yemen
Meanwhile, inside Yemen, explosions have been reported near the airport in the Houthi-controlled Red Sea port city of Hodeidah, according to local sources.
The cause and impact of these explosions are not immediately clear.
Al Jazeera’s Hadeel al-Yamani, reporting from Taiz in Yemen, said intense fighting is raging between armed forces of Yemen’s internationally recognised government and the Houthis in al-Shamayatayn, al-Maafer and the southern and western countryside of Taiz governorate.
“The Houthis are pushing into rural areas that have not seen conflict for years, aiming to open a supply route because their lines towards al-Kadaha and al-Waziiya, which link Aden, Lahij and Taiz, are nearly cut off by advancing government forces”, she said.
Al-Yamani added that pro-government forces are within striking distance of al-Waziiya and the Kahboub Mountains overlooking Bab al-Mandeb strait.
Pro-government forces have reported more than 2,000 operations against the Houthis, and are preparing for a “dangerous escalation”, she said.
More than 200,000 people have been displaced from their homes since fighting in Yemen escalated in recent weeks, according to data released by the International Organization for Migration (IOM).
The IOM described the crisis in a statement on Wednesday as alarming, with displacement figures surging from the 76,000 recorded in mid-September.

articles.title: Ukraine targets Russian industrial hub in Siberia
articles.body:
Ukraine targets Russian industrial hub in Siberia
Ukrainian drones have targeted a major industrial hub in the Siberian city of Omsk, as Kiev carried out another UAV raid inside Russia.
Omsk Region Governor Vitaly Khotsenko confirmed the attack on Thursday, saying Russian air defenses had intercepted most of the incoming UAVs.
“One drone reached the northern industrial hub. Emergency services are working at the scene,” he wrote on Telegram, without providing details regarding any casualties or damage.
The northern industrial hub is home to several major petrochemical facilities, including the Omsk Oil Refinery, Russia’s largest. The area was previously targeted by Ukrainian drones in July, when several UAVs reached the site.
Operated by Gazprom Neft, the refinery has an annual processing capacity of more than 20 million tons of crude oil and is located approximately 2,500km from the Russian-Ukrainian border.
Kiev has ramped up its long-range UAV attacks on energy facilities and civilian targets inside Russia amid continued setbacks on the battlefield in recent months. On Wednesday, a child was killed and four other civilians were wounded in a strike on Belgorod Region, according to local authorities.
Russian Ambassador-at-Large Rodion Miroshnik said that Ukrainian attacks took the lives of 29 civilians, including two children, and wounded another 206 between September 28 and October 4.
Moscow has repeatedly described Ukrainian attacks on civilian targets as acts of terrorism. The Russian Defense Ministry has vowed to intensify strikes on Ukraine’s military and military-industrial facilities and related infrastructure in response to Vladimir Zelensky’s threats to expand attacks on oil refineries.
The ministry has since reported large-scale strikes on Ukrainian facilities involved in producing and storing long-range weapons, including sites linked to the domestically developed FP-5 Flamingo missile.

articles.title: Zelenskyy responds to Rubio: You cannot negotiate with Russia and talk about a diplomatic stalemate at the same time
articles.body:
Zelenskyy responds to Rubio: You cannot negotiate with Russia and talk about a diplomatic stalemate at the same time
President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has rejected US Secretary of State Marco Rubio's statement that the war cannot be ended diplomatically because the situation has reached a "stalemate", and called on the US to help Ukraine gain air superiority and increase pressure on Russia.
Source: Zelenskyy speaking to journalists in Pryluky, where a Russian missile struck an apartment block on 7 October, killing 22 people, including five children
Quote: "We have heard about many different moments during the war. Many hopeless situations, difficult corners and so on. We – people, leaders, politicians – drive ourselves into a corner… Even on the first day of the war, we were not in a corner. Because one person tried to drive an entire nation into a corner, and the nation rose up and defended its state." [Zelenskyy's references to a "corner" are a wordplay on the Ukrainian translation of Rubio's "stalemate" as "глухий кут" ("dead end"), which contains the word "кут" ("corner") – ed.]
Details: Zelenskyy added that getting out of the corner is not difficult and that this requires increasing economic pressure on Russia, giving Ukraine access to Starlink over Russian territory and not negotiating with Russia on future projects.
"You see, you cannot negotiate economic projects for the future with the Russians on the one hand and, on the other, say that we are at a… diplomatic deadlock. We are not at a diplomatic stalemate. Shut down their entire economy. Shut Russia's mouth. Do not feed them with your sales. Just impose sanctions on their weapons. Open Starlink to us, to Ukraine," the president said.
He recalled that the US had already done this when it attacked Iran, when "Israel had complete control of the skies over Iran".
Quote: "So that means that when you need it, it works like that… Just control the skies to protect yourself. The US has this capability. For them, it costs nothing to help Ukraine. And I said frankly: 'Give it to us, help us protect our skies and dominate the skies. And then Putin will sit down at the negotiating table. Why? Because he will lose everything. Three, two months – he will lose everything.' And we are waiting for the Chinese to develop this equivalent and hand it over to the Russians. So where is the truth, where is the honesty? What corner? This is called unwillingness."
Background: Rubio earlier said that ending the Russia-Ukraine war through diplomatic negotiations is currently "proving elusive" because the war has reached a "strategic stalemate". He acknowledged that diplomatic efforts are failing because Russia is demanding full control of the Donbas and Ukraine refuses to accept it.

articles.title: Ukraine strikes Yandex data center in Russia, sparking fire
articles.body:
Update. Yandex confirmed that Ukrainian drones struck its data center in Sasovo. The strike sparked a fire that damaged part of the infrastructure. No one was injured, and the data center has been completely shut down; some Yandex services may be unavailable to users.
A fire broke out at the Sasta machine-tool plant in Sasovo, Ryazan region, which houses one of Yandex’s data centers, the independent Telegram channel Astra reported. Journalists reached that conclusion after analyzing photos and videos from eyewitnesses.
Ukrainian monitoring Telegram channels Exilenova+ and Supernova+ claimed the fire started after a Ukrainian strike. Russia’s Defense Ministry listed the Ryazan region among the areas where air defenses shot down Ukrainian drones overnight on October 8. Local authorities have not reported on the aftermath of the attack.
Yandex said “an incident occurred at the Sasovo data center that affected part of the infrastructure.” The company added: “The situation at the site is now under control, and no one was injured. The team is addressing the aftermath of the incident and restoring the affected services.”
After the attack, several Russian websites became unavailable, the independent Russian broadcaster TV Rain reported. They included the auto-posting platform Postmypost and the Ryazan region edition of Komsomolskaya Pravda, a pro-Kremlin Russian tabloid.
Yandex’s data center in Sasovo opened in 2014 on part of the former premises of the Sasta plant, a maker of pipe-threading machines. The plant supplies products to Russian machine-building enterprises and exports some abroad.
In September, the Russian military carried out several strikes on Ukrainian data centers. Russia’s Defense Ministry claimed these centers “process and transmit intelligence data for the Ukrainian armed forces” and also threatened Ukraine with a “digital detox.”

The story you’re reading was written by one of our living, breathing journalists and translated from Russian using an AI model configured to follow our strict editorial standards. This translation process is the result of extensive testing and refinements to ensure our English-language coverage is timely and accurate. A Meduza editor reviews every draft before publication.

articles.title: New Russian Drone Wave Targets Kyiv and Western Ukraine After Deadly Strikes on Putin’s Birthday
articles.body:
Russian forces sent another wave of jet-powered attack drones toward Kyiv and several Ukrainian regions in the early hours of Thursday, Oct. 8, triggering fresh air raid alerts just hours after deadly Russian strikes killed 28 people across Ukraine, including five children.
Ukraine’s Air Force warned at approximately 12:55 a.m. that Russian jet-powered drones were approaching Kyiv, including the capital’s northeastern Troieshchyna neighborhood.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
Additional Russian drones were tracked toward Brovary, Vasylkiv and Fastiv in Kyiv region, while other threats emerged across northern and western Ukraine.
Kyiv’s Military Administration issued repeated air raid warnings as the drone threat continued overnight. The administration reported an all-clear at approximately 1:24 a.m. Thursday.
Russian drones threaten Lutsk and northern Ukraine
The overnight drone threat extended far beyond the Ukrainian capital.
In western Ukraine, the Air Force warned that a Russian jet-powered drone was approaching Lutsk in Volyn region before reporting that it was directly over the city.
Volyn regional authorities also issued an air raid warning for Lutsk district shortly after midnight as the threat developed.
Further drones were reported heading toward Ovruch in Zhytomyr region and Desna in Chernihiv region, while another was tracked through the Chornobyl exclusion zone toward Zhytomyr region.
Russian drone movements were also reported in the direction of Rivne region.
Bipartisan US Senators Press Trump Administration to Crack Down on Russia’s Shadow Fleet Ahead of Oct. 18 Deadline
Meanwhile, Russian tactical aviation threatened Zaporizhzhia and surrounding areas with guided aerial bombs, prompting additional Air Force warnings.
The alerts indicated continuing Russian aerial activity across multiple regions, although Ukrainian authorities had not confirmed new impacts or casualties linked specifically to Thursday’s early-hours drone wave.
Five children among 28 killed in Wednesday’s attacks
The latest threats came just hours after Russia carried out deadly missile and drone strikes across Ukraine on Wednesday, Oct. 7.
Interior Minister Ivan Vyhivskyi reported that 28 people were killed nationwide, including five children.
The deadliest attack struck Pryluky in Chernihiv region, where a Russian missile hit a residential apartment building, killing 20 people, including five children. Three of the children were just one year old.
The strike destroyed part of the building, leaving rescuers searching through the wreckage for survivors.
In Kyiv, Russian attacks also killed two people and injured residents, including children, as drones struck apartment buildings and sparked fires in residential neighborhoods.
In Desnianskyi district, four people, including two children, were injured when a drone struck a 12-story residential building. Emergency crews rescued 22 residents, eight of them children.
In Solomianskyi district, another drone attack set a five-story apartment building ablaze, injuring eight residents.
The renewed drone threats in the early hours of Thursday followed a devastating day of Russian strikes that destroyed Ukrainian homes and killed entire families.
The attacks unfolded on Oct. 7 – Vladimir Putin’s 74th birthday – leaving 28 Ukrainians dead, including five children.
