articles.title: How Hezbollah's 'Gaza support front' reshaped Lebanon 3 years on
articles.body:
Breadcrumb
Hezbollah and the 'Gaza support front': cost of ongoing Israeli war on Lebanon, three years on
The third anniversary of Hezbollah launching what it describes as "the support front for Gaza" falls on 8 October 2023. Its repercussions continue for Lebanon, amid ongoing Israeli attacks and an expanded occupation over more than 60 villages and towns.
Today, many in Lebanon remain afraid of a third round after the September 2024 and March 2026 Israeli offensives.
On the third anniversary, Hezbollah issued a statement, saying: "The enemy has failed to eliminate Hamas, the resistance factions or the people of Gaza, and has failed to achieve peace, or even a temporary truce and stability. The situation remains open to developments whose repercussions will extend beyond the Gaza Strip to the future of the entire region, the Palestinian cause, and international security and peace."
"Hezbollah in Lebanon, which believes in the justness of the Palestinian cause and does not hesitate to support its resisting and oppressed people, renews its strong condemnation of the blatant Zionist genocide that exposes the false values of the international community and holds the US administration and Western countries that remain silent about condemning Zionist crimes responsible, whether those involving genocide or crimes against humanity," it further said.
"We stand firmly with all these resistance factions so that they remain steadfast and united around their vision and position against the enemy's project, its supporters and those complicit with it. We also warn the region's rulers that remaining silent, accommodating and flattering the enemy and its allies will only lead to the undermining of their authority, weakening them and enabling the enemy to determine the future of their countries and peoples," it added.
Victims of the two support wars
Hezbollah's 'Gaza support front' began on 8 October 2023 and was initially confined to south Lebanon. But the geographical scope, consequences, human losses, and economic cost gradually expanded, particularly after September 2024.
More than 8,900 people have been killed and more than 30,000 injured by Israel since 8 October 2023, while the forced displacement of thousands of families continues, whether because their homes were damaged, their villages were occupied or destroyed, or some were destroyed by more than 90%.
Additionally, financial losses are estimated at more than $27 billion, mostly in the south, as well as damage in the Bekaa and Baalbek-Hermel in eastern Lebanon, Beirut, the southern suburbs of Beirut, and other areas to varying degrees.
The war also brought radical changes.
First for Hezbollah, with the loss of its first- and second-tier leaders, most notably its Secretary-General Hassan Nasrallah on 27 September 2024 and his successor Hashem Safieddine on 3 October 2024.
It was also subjected to one of the largest cybersecurity operations, with the explosions of "pagers" and "walkie-talkies" on 17 and 18 September 2024.
The Islamic group found its military capabilities significant declined, while it also lost key supply lines, most notably the Syrian route, after the fall of the Assad regime on 8 December 2024, and its external support, particularly Iranian support, decreased.
Moreover, Israel is targeting Hezbollah's financing networks, foremost among them the Al-Qard Al-Hassan Association.
Hezbollah's political position was also impacted with a decline in its influence in state centres and institutions with the beginning of the new era under President Joseph Aoun on 9 January 2025, which came with broad US support, sovereignty-focused slogans and historic decisions.
The most important of these decisions was the cabinet's approval of a measure to restrict weapons in Lebanon and its tasking of the Lebanese army with drawing up a plan to implement this, in August 2025, with progress recorded in implementation south of the Litani River.
This came before Hezbollah's security and military activities were banned on 2 March, after it supported Iran by launching six missiles from Lebanon at Israel, following the start of the US-Israeli war on Iran on 28 February, along with other decisions that also affected the Iranian side.
The choice of launching "support fronts", for Gaza and Iran, also affected Hezbollah's alliances, particularly through the "disengagement" between it and the Free Patriotic Movement headed by MP Gebran Bassil, as well as its relationship with the Amal Movement headed by Nabih Berri, amid differences and varying views that emerged in approaching the issue.
Hezbollah and Amal have continued to seek through ongoing meetings to maintain coordination and cooperation, amid some tensions in southern areas associated with both sides.
This followed media reports about attempts by Hezbollah to establish positions and launch platforms in some towns politically associated with the Amal Movement.
Another major shift is that Lebanon and Israel began direct negotiations for the first time on 14 April 2026, resulting in the signing of a framework agreement in Washington on 26 June, and subsequently encouraged political and media discourse calling for normalisation and peace with Israel, marking a major breaking of taboos.
This was particularly evident with Lebanese channels conducting interviews with Israelis and showing blatant bias towards Israeli narratives, eventually leading to direct cooperation between a Lebanese platform and an Israeli one.
Addressing the cost of the ongoing war for Lebanon, Nasser Yassin, director of the Beirut branch of the Arab Centre for Research and Policy Studies, told The New Arab that estimates indicate that the cost since 8 October until today has exceeded $27 billion.
These losses are divided between direct losses related to the destruction and damage to homes, residences, buildings and infrastructure, as well as losses related to the agricultural, commercial and economic sectors, among others.
Yassin noted that most losses are concentrated in the south, alongside damage also recorded in the southern suburbs of Beirut and the Bekaa in eastern Lebanon.
He pointed out that the number of homes destroyed or requiring complete demolition in this war had reached about 132,000, more than those recorded during the July and August 2006 war, when the number of destroyed homes reached around 12,000.
He also said there are currently about 65 occupied villages and towns in the south where destruction and land levelling are taking place continuously.
Yassin was environment minister in the government of former Prime Minister Najib Mikati, during which indirect negotiations with Israel led to a ceasefire agreement on 27 November 2024.
However, Israel violated it thousands of times while insisting on remaining at five southern positions.
The expanded offensive then resumed on 2 March, increasing Israeli control over southern villages and sites.
Yassin noted the 27 November 2024 agreement was based on Resolution 1701, which brought an end to the Israeli offensive against Lebanon in summer 2006.
Under the agreement, Lebanon affirmed its commitment to the deployment of the Lebanese army and the state's exercise of sovereignty through its own forces in the south, particularly south of the Litani River, while Israel was to withdraw from positions it occupied at the time.
"Today, the situation is different. There is a security zone, Israeli occupation and control over about 65 villages, and an area that Israel has completely eradicated and destroyed. Therefore, the discussion is now taking place in a different context," he said.
As for whether the negotiations could produce the anticipated solution, Yassin acknowledged it is unclear whether the negotiations currently underway will lead to an outcome.
However, Lebanon has no option other than negotiations to achieve a withdrawal, whether directly, indirectly or through Arab or international mediators.
Yassin said the negotiating performance should be better and should primarily place Israel's withdrawal at the top of any framework, since Israel is occupying another country's land, namely Lebanon, thereby violating international law.
Therefore, he added, the withdrawal should not be linked to measures and issues as happened in the framework agreement, even though these are important.
Domestic repercussions
Regarding the domestic repercussions, particularly for Hezbollah, political writer Khaldoun Al Sharif told The New Arab that "[the support front] led to major Israeli breaches that affected Hezbollah, beginning with the pager and walkie-talkie operations and the assassination of Nasrallah and ending with the occupation of a large area of the south."
Al Sharif noted that "the assassination of Nasrallah, the symbolic leader of Hezbollah, along with the assassination of leaders in the Radwan Force, the party's elite force, and military officials, fundamentally changed the equation. This included the leadership, capabilities, military capacity and material resources."
At the popular level, Al Sharif does not believe the support for the war changed much.
There had been no national, international or governmental support for the party's constituency, which led to its continued attachment to the party.
He also noted that it is impossible to assess changes at this level or among the opposing Shia constituency because the usual measure is parliamentary elections, which were postponed because of the war.
According to Al Sharif, the war inevitably affected domestic alliances because political forces in Lebanon only agree on specific interests, rather than principles or values.
"The Amal Movement remains committed to its alliance with the party because the fall of the duo, in one way or another, would lead to the Shiite community being left alone. Therefore, the issue of Shiite unity remains fundamental for both of them regardless of the repercussions," he said.
Al Sharif also said the decisions taken by the government in August 2025 and March 2026 have not been implemented to date, adding that what matters is implementation.
However, he noted there is no doubt that these decisions were taken after the balance of power changed, particularly following the assassination of Nasrallah.
Al Sharif argued that there is a division between two camps in Lebanon, with only a small percentage of people in the middle: "the Iranian camp," which has been left alone, and the US camp and its allies.
He said that before the situation in the Gulf and Iran becomes clear, it is difficult to determine where Lebanon will go.
"If Iran is crushed, we will face a new equation. If it is not crushed, the equation will be different. Therefore, today we are in a state of 'status quo', particularly since the latest round of negotiations held in Rome last August. Whether we like it or not, Lebanon has become tied to the existing regional equations and the international equations that will impose new balances of power in this region," he remarked.
Hezbollah alliances in decline
Mahend Al Hajj Ali, a researcher at the Malcolm Kerr-Carnegie Middle East Centre, told The New Arab that the war weakened and destabilised the political alliances Hezbollah had built since 2005.
Presently, there is a threat emerging against the alliance it also established with the Amal Movement.
This is one of the repercussions at the political level, in addition to its relationship with Christian, Sunni and Druze forces that had been allied with it but are no longer as they were and have become distributed among a group of regional powers that are not allied with the party.
Al Hajj Ali said that at the social and demographic level, the repercussions have been enormous for the community that supports Hezbollah, namely Lebanese Shias, who, as a result of the war, have been subjected to ethnic cleansing that displaced them from their homeland across a large part of Jabal Amel in southern Lebanon.
Currently, the other part north of the Litani River is also exposed to ethnic cleansing, and in his view it has begun and could continue if a third war breaks out, which is very possible.
Al Hajj Ali also highlighted the changes that have taken place at the regional level, including the change in the situation in Syria and the collapse of the Syrian regime, which had repercussions for Lebanon and Hezbollah.
He also pointed to the establishment of a new era and a new government in Lebanon, following a line opposed to that of Hezbollah and based on the principle that weapons come first.
Article translated from Arabic by Afrah Almatwari. To read the original, click here.

articles.title: BBC: Eritrea Secretly Deploys Troops to Ethiopia’s Tigray Region
articles.body:
Eritrean troops have crossed the Ethiopian border and advanced deeper into the Tigray region, where fighting is ongoing between government forces and rebel groups.
The British broadcaster BBC reported this on October 7, citing local residents.
According to eyewitnesses, Eritrean troops were moving from the border town of Zalambessa through Adigrat toward Edaga Hamus, located between Adigrat and Tigray’s administrative capital, Mekelle.
One resident of Adigrat said he saw a convoy of approximately 40 trucks carrying soldiers traveling south. Another eyewitness reported seeing 20–30 large trucks with Eritrean license plates heading toward Edaga Hamus.
According to other accounts, the convoys also included vehicles equipped with heavy weapons, including anti-aircraft guns. Some Eritrean troops were traveling on foot. One BBC source estimated that the convoy seen by his relatives consisted of around 60 trucks.
Local residents also report the deployment of Eritrean units in mountainous areas near Edaga Hamus. According to them, drone strikes targeting military positions have taken place near the town.
Meanwhile, the BBC emphasizes that it has been unable to independently verify reports of Eritrean troop movements. Journalists were also unable to verify the authenticity of videos of military convoys circulating on social media.
A new phase of fighting in Tigray began on September 23 following several months of growing tensions between Ethiopia’s federal government and the Tigray People’s Liberation Front (TPLF).
On October 4, government forces and allied formations regained control of Mekelle after TPLF units withdrew. The rebels said they were temporarily relocating their regional administration.
The day before, on October 1, Eritrea severed diplomatic relations with Ethiopia following the closure of the Ethiopian embassy in Asmara and the expulsion of Eritrean diplomats. Addis Ababa accuses its neighbor of supporting the rebels, although Eritrean authorities have previously denied the allegations.
Ethiopian government representative Abraham Belay accused Eritrea of directly participating in the fighting in an interview with Fana Television. According to him, the Eritrean army suffered casualties and captured personnel, and Ethiopia is preparing a response to its intervention.
From 2020 to 2022, Eritrea, by contrast, fought alongside the Ethiopian federal government against the Tigray People’s Liberation Front. The two-year conflict claimed hundreds of thousands of lives and ended with the signing of the Pretoria Peace Agreement in November 2022.
Since then, relations between Ethiopia and Eritrea have deteriorated sharply. One of the main reasons has been the Ethiopian leadership’s demand for access to the Red Sea, particularly through Eritrea’s Port of Assab. Eritrea views such statements as a threat to its sovereignty.
Militarnyi previously reported that on September 21, seven Ethiopian armed groups announced the formation of a unified alliance against the government of Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed. The alliance includes the Tigray People’s Liberation Front, the Oromo Liberation Army, and the Fano militia operating in the Amhara region. The alliance said its goal was to overthrow the current government and establish a transitional administration.
Militarnyi also reported that in August 2026, Tigray People’s Liberation Front rebels used NWF10 FPV drones, manufactured by the Turkish company North Weapon, against the Ethiopian army.

articles.title: Sharaa visits Riyadh amid speculation about Syrian role in Yemen
articles.body:
Breadcrumb
Sharaa visit to Riyadh fuels speculation about possible Syrian role in Yemen war
Syrian President Ahmed Al-Sharaa met Saudi Crown Prince and de facto leader Mohammed Bin Salman on Tuesday in Riyadh amid speculation about a possible Syrian role in Yemen.
A statement from the Syrian presidency said that Al-Sharaa and bin Salman discussed relations between the two countries and ways to develop them, as well as the latest developments in the region.
Al-Sharaa was accompanied on the visit by Syrian Foreign Minister Asaad al-Shaibani.
The statement made no mention of Yemen or the Houthi rebels, which Saudi Arabia has been fighting since September.
However, the visit took place amid intense fighting in Yemen between Saudi-backed government forces and the Iran-backed Houthis, with attempts by government forces to take control of the Red Sea coast and the strategic Bab al-Mandeb waterway.
Saudi Arabia is also attempting to activate its Mecca defence agreement with Pakistan and Turkey amid reports that the latter two countries could offer military support to Riyadh in the war, but without directly fighting the Houthis.
Syria has close relations with both Saudi Arabia and Turkey, with the latter in particular seen as having influence on Sharaa’s government, due to its support for rebel forces prior to former dictator Bashar al-Assad’s fall in December 2024.
Saudi Arabia has previously called on a number of countries for help in the campaign against the Houthis, including the United States and Egypt as well as its Mecca Agreement allies. The US, however, has declined to become involved directly.
Earlier in the current flare-up of fighting in Yemen, a social media campaign, promoted by some figures close to the Syrian government, drew parallels between the Yemen war and the 2024 rebel victory over Assad.
The campaign supported alleged Yemeni government victories over the Houthis and featured AI-altered images of Syrian activists in traditional Yemeni dress.
There have been some unverified reports that Syrian fighters may be present in Yemen, assisting government forces.
Hiba Nasr, the US correspondent for Asharq Bloomberg, said in a post on X on Wednesday that “Syria may join the war in Yemen. No final decision has been made, but the idea is under discussion, according to multiple sources.”
During the Syrian civil war, Syrian fighters reportedly assisted forces of the Turkish-backed Government National Accord against Khalifa Haftar’s forces in Libya.
There are reports that Saudi Arabia may be interested in deploying Syrian fighters to Yemen because of their previous experience operating Turkish-made drones and weapons.
In addition, Saudi Arabia may view them as more reliable amid reports of internal divisions among Yemeni government forces.
"There are no Syrian troops in Yemen, and the Syrian government has not sent any. However, Sharaa’s visit to Saudi Arabia may have been to study possible arrangements regarding Yemen, including the sending of troops," the New Arab’s correspondent in Syria said.

articles.title: Shadow Tanker Hit by Ukrainian Drones Threatens Spill Off Russia's Black Sea Coast
articles.body:
Authorities in the Russian Black Sea resort region of Sochi said that a massive oil tanker set afire and left adrift by Ukrainian drones is no threat to local bathers and waters, and that beaches closed to protect bathers and wetlands are now open to the public, local media reported on Thursday.
Sochi Mayor Andrey Proshunin said in a Wednesday statement that his office was closely monitoring offshore sea quality, telling voters the situation was under control and that citizen safety was his highest priority.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
“At present the open fire on the tanker has been liquidated and rescue vessels are observing. Pollution of water with the oil cargo [carried in the tanker] has not been recorded. The tanker is drifting with the current along the shoreline,” Proshunin said.
“Local environmental watch agencies are checking pollutant levels in water, air and the ground across the greater Sochi region, and as a safe measure all beaches will be closed to swimming until those checks are complete,” he continued.
Proshunin told voters to remain calm.
“I ask all to remain calm, to observe current rules and restrictions, and to trust only reliable sources of information. The situation is under constant monitoring by the city operational staff,” he added.
Russia’s national environmental watch agency Rospotrebnadzor, in a Wednesday announcement published by the Kremlin-sponsored news agency TASS, took the same position but didn’t mention the drones.
Poland Ends Russian Drone Probe After Failing to Identify Perpetrator
“There is no pollution to the Black Sea as a result of the fire aboard the tanker near Sochi. Agencies are monitoring the shore belt and waters of the Black Sea,” the agency said.
Dmitry Plishkin, head of the Sirius region containing Sochi and adjacent towns and villages, said in a Thursday statement that all local waters and beaches had received a clean bill of health for environmental safety and are now open.
Plishkin’s statement made no reference to the damaged 107,000-ton tanker which, according to Sochi-based news platforms, was in international waters drifting slowly northeast in light seas.
The Liberia-flagged Aframax Rio, a 246-meter (807-feet) long and 107,113-ton deadweight vessel built in 2004, is sanctioned by Ukraine as a shadow tanker Russia uses to evade Western oil export sanctions. The Aframax was southbound when it was hit and set fiercely afire in an early Tuesday evening drone attack.
The blaze under clear skies some 15 nautical miles (30 km) off the shore of Sochi – the heart of the “Russia Riviera” Black Sea resort region – was observed by thousands of local residents and tourists.
Video of the burning ship showed flames engulfing the entire top deck, with the fiercest fires concentrated around the middle of the tanker. The US Fire Information for Resource Management System (FIRMS), run by NASA, showed fires burning near the tanker for more than 24 hours before being extinguished.
                                                                                                                                                                         The Liberia-flagged Afromax Rio burns following a Ukrainian drone strike offshore from the Russian resort port of Sochi on Oct. 6, 2026. The vessel, sanctioned by Ukraine as a shadow tanker, was reportedly fully loaded and left drifting. (Photo via sochiradar / Telegram)                             
Imagery of the fire and its expansion recorded live from shore on Wednesday showed the blaze most concentrated in the central portion of the ship’s upper deck, an area often targeted by Ukrainian airborne drones attacking tankers in the past. Ukrainian sea drone attacks in past strikes on tankers have focused on engine rooms and propellers near the stern.
The Russian local news platform Sochi Radar reported that the Aframax Rio was fully loaded and that so much oil had spilled into the water and caught fire that firefighters were prevented from moving to extinguish the blaze quickly.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky, in his Wednesday evening broadcast, said the Ukrainian military had attacked and badly damaged a tanker in the Black Sea, but he did not name the vessel, nor did he specify the type of drones used in the attack.
Local Russian news platforms identified the Ukrainian military as having operated the drones that attacked the tanker.
The US-based shipping information platform Marine Executive, in a Thursday article, said that the fire started in the center of the ship in the cargo tank area and then spread aft down the starboard side. Later that evening, the report said burning oil that had escaped from the tanker’s holds was visible on the water, beneath a towering column of smoke.
According to the world civilian vessel tracking group MarineTraffic, the last time the Aframax Rio turned on its transponder was Oct. 5 off the coast of Georgia, and since then its location has not been visible to satellite tracking. Its registered owner is Rio Enterprises SA, a Marshall Islands company.
The Greek news platform Protothema, in its Wednesday article, reported the tanker “is linked to Andreas Hadjiyiannis’ Hellenic Tankers.” As of Thursday, no major ship tracking platform showed the ship’s location.
Marine tracking platforms showed past port destinations for the vessel included Sapsun, Turkey and Sika, India.
According to Kyiv, both countries help Russia evade sanctions by receiving shadow tankers loaded with Russian crude, which is then refined into legitimate product not subject to sanctions.
The Black Sea shipping tracker Blackseanews.net showed the vessel’s operator as Hellenic Tankers Co LTD, an Athens-headquartered business, and its last officially recorded voyage as from Russia’s Novorossiysk port to Saudi Arabia’s Rabigh port in May 2026.
On Sept. 22, Robert “Magyar” Brovdi, commander of Ukraine’s Unmanned Systems Forces (USF), claimed his strike forces had attacked and disabled 300 Russian “shadow-fleet” tankers since July 6, with 134 strikes in the Sea of Azov and 166 in the Black Sea.
The most environmentally damaging Russian shadow fleet tanker sunk in those waters was the Vologaneft-212, which went down in a December 2024 storm near the resort port of Anapa with more than 4,000 tons of heavy fuel oil aboard.
Leaking product souked hundreds of kilometers of resort beaches and sensitive wetlands on the Russian Black Sea coast and in Russia-occupied Crimea. The most intense period of the Black Sea storm season is from late October through March.
A press release from the ship’s declared operator, a Singapore-based company called Executive Ships Management, said all 23 crew members were safe ashore after the drone strike. The company said it was investigating the ship’s current status, including any potential threat it might pose to navigation, waters or the shoreline in the area.

articles.title: Kyiv police neutralize 2 unexploded ballistic missiles after enemy attack
articles.body:
Explosive ordnance disposal technicians of the Kyiv police have neutralized two unexploded ballistic missiles used by Russia in the attack on the capital on October 7, the Kyiv police report.
"The warheads of two Iskander-M missiles, weighing about half a ton each, fell near residential buildings in the Shevchenkivsky and Darnytsky districts," the capital's police department said in a statement on its Telegram channel on Thursday.
According to the report, police officers neutralized the hazardous components of the warheads and prepared them for safe transport.
"Subsequently, using specialized equipment and in cooperation with State Emergency Service sappers, the missile fragments were transported to a temporary detonation site for subsequent destruction," the capital's police specified.
Law enforcement reminds citizens that upon discovering missile fragments, drones, or other suspicious objects, one must not approach or touch them. "Move to a safe distance and report the finding by calling 101 or 102," the police explained.

articles.title: Russia kills 30 in strike on two passenger buses in Kramatorsk
articles.body:
Russian forces struck the eastern Ukrainian city of Kramatorsk on the morning of 8 October, hitting two route buses carrying residents and killing dozens of civilians. The Donetsk Oblast prosecutor's office opened a war-crimes investigation.
Russia has turned everyday movement in frontline Donetsk Oblast into a lethal risk, striking city buses, ambulances, and cars in places its army has not been able to capture.
A route bus run turned deadly
The attack came at around 10:00, catching two route buses in the impact zone. The prosecutor's office said the attackers likely used a UMPB D-30SN. HUR, Ukraine's military intelligence, describes it as a guided glide bomb that can fly up to 100 km when released from an altitude of 12–15 km and carries a warhead equal to a FAB-250 aerial bomb.
The toll rose through the day, from 12 dead in the first reports to 30 killed and 20 wounded by 14:55, Donetsk Oblast head Vadym Filashkin said. Across Donetsk Oblast, Russian attacks killed 33 people that day, including the 30 in Kramatorsk and three in nearby Bilenke, the State Emergency Service said. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said the strike would not go unanswered.
Buses pulled off the roads
Filashkin ordered the Kramatorsk and Sloviansk city military administrations to suspend public transport, citing the sharp deterioration in security. Buses had become an attractive target for Russian forces, he said, and the authorities could not risk the lives of passengers and drivers. He also urged everyone still in Donetsk Oblast to leave for safer parts of Ukraine. Kramatorsk is a frequent target of Russian attacks. Russia had not commented on the strike as of publication.
The city has been under daily fire. On 5 October, Russian FPV drones hit ambulances and an apartment block in Kramatorsk, killing a woman and wounding four, the prosecutor's office reported. Over the previous day, Russian forces shelled Donetsk Oblast settlements 31 times and 256 people left the front line, Filashkin said.

articles.title: Zelenskyy and UK foreign secretary visit site of Russian missile strike in Pryluky
articles.body:
Zelenskyy and UK foreign secretary visit site of Russian missile strike in Pryluky
President Volodymyr Zelenskyy and Ed Miliband, the Secretary of State for Foreign, Commonwealth and Development Affairs of the United Kingdom, have visited Pryluky in Chernihiv Oblast, where a Russian missile struck an apartment block on 7 October.
Source: European Pravda, citing Ukrinform
Details: Zelenskyy thanked the UK secretary, who arrived in Kyiv on an official visit, adding that Miliband was invited to visit Pryluky to "see for himself what is really happening, what daily strikes look like and how our people endure this struggle".
He called on partners, including the United Kingdom, to step up assistance to Ukraine, particularly with air defence systems.
Zelenskyy also emphasised the need to strengthen the negotiation process.
Quote: "In addition to the air defence factor, which is in short supply because our country is large and incoming strikes happen everywhere, we would certainly like to draw attention to the negotiation track, because, in our view, the United States of America should raise the pressure through sanctions and other steps – both financial assistance and specific air defence support for Ukraine. And through such steps... force Putin to sit down at the negotiating table."
According to the latest data, 22 people were killed, including five children, as a result of the Russian missile strike on Pryluky on 7 October.
Background:
- Estonian Foreign Minister Margus Tsahkna condemned another massive Russian attack on Ukraine, urging partners to increase pressure on Moscow.
- Zelenskyy announced meetings between Ukrainian negotiators and the American side on 9 and 10 October.

articles.title: “They were smiling as they shot at us”: The Insider speaks with Israelis whose lives were turned upside down on October 7, 2023
articles.body:
On October 7, Israel marked the third anniversary of the Hamas terrorist attack of 2023. The Insider spoke to three people whose lives were changed forever that day: a survivor of the attack from Kibbutz Be’eri, a Hamas hostage who spent two years in captivity, and a soldier who was among the first to enter Gaza as part of an armored brigade.
- 1.Pyotr Stolba, resident of Kibbutz Be’eri: “Cars and houses were burning, the whole street was littered with bodies”
- 2.Former hostage Maksim Kharkin: “They were killing people and smiling”
- 3.Vitaly Cheberdin, Israeli soldier with the 188th Armored Brigade: “The army had never done anything like this in Gaza”
Pyotr Stolba, resident of Kibbutz Be’eri: “Cars and houses were burning, the whole street was littered with bodies”
On October 7, 2023, several thousand Hamas militants broke into Israel from the Gaza Strip. They initially headed for the Be’eri and Nahal Oz kibbutzim along the border with the Strip. For the first seven hours of the attack — before the army arrived — Be’eri was defended by just 26 people. A total of 101 residents, including 10 children aged from several months to 17 years, were killed. Another 32 residents were taken hostage by the terrorists.
Three years after “Black Saturday,” just one burned-out house remains in Kibbutz Be’eri — a reminder of the tragedy. Its roof has collapsed and its walls are riddled with bullet holes. The house stands on an empty lot surrounded by a large metal fence. Just one year ago, there were more destroyed houses here, but they have since been demolished. Local residents are divided over what to do with the last one – preserve it as a memorial to the attack or remove it so that it does not remind their own children of the horror they experienced.
Pyotr Stolba has lived in Be’eri for 34 years. He immigrated to Israel from Moscow in 1996 with his wife and settled in the kibbutz almost immediately:
“There were two families living in this house: the Kipnises and the Alons. The Alon family was later rescued alive by the Israeli army, while the Kipnis couple – husband and wife – were killed by the terrorists inside the house, which they then set on fire.
At 6:30 a.m. on October 7, Qassam rockets began falling here. Of course, we went into the safe room. I was at home with my wife, my older son, my pregnant daughter-in-law, and my 10-month-old grandson.
We were told not to leave the safe rooms because there were terrorists in the kibbutz. We thought there were just a few of them. No one could have imagined that 400 terrorists would enter Be’eri.
They smashed through the glass balcony door. They shot at the glass and it shattered. They opened the door and came inside. The dog met them and started barking, and they immediately shot it.
They tried to break into our safe room, pulling at the door handle. My son and I held the door from inside. They knocked and spoke to us in English: "Come out, we won’t hurt you." But my older son had served in the territories [in the West Bank], in combat units. He said, 'Dad, we don’t talk to Arabs. Stay quiet.'
We stayed there for 19 hours, until the army rescued us.
The electricity went out half an hour after the terrorists stormed into the kibbutz. While our phones still had battery power, everyone was passing along information. The Losev family from Zaporizhzhia lived near that transformer station. They were close friends of ours. Marina was burned alive in the house. She was identified only by her teeth. Igor was found shot dead near the fence.
Marina was burned alive in the house and identified only by her teeth, while Igor was found shot dead near the fence
The terrorists were drinking on my balcony and shooting at the road. They used heavy machine guns to shoot anyone who drove past or tried to escape. They shot at chandeliers and the TV. A tree burning next to the house heated the roof tiles until they glowed and began to fall. My wife said, 'Listen, the house is collapsing!' I said, 'All we can do is pray. There’s nothing else we can do.'
When the army arrived, we went outside – everything around us was burning. Cars and houses were on fire; bodies lay in the street. The dead were everywhere: terrorists, Israelis. Children, women, and men lay on the sidewalks and in the roads.
We were taken from there to a hotel by the Dead Sea. That’s where we learned who had been killed and how. One of my friends said, 'I don’t know where my wife is, where my daughter is.' It turned out they had been killed.
I returned to Be’eri four months after the attack to get the local printing press running again. My wife and I now live in temporary housing and are preparing to move into a new home. A new military base has been built next to us. I think that will give us some protection in case of a sudden attack.
We never doubted that we wanted to return, because this is our home. But some families do not want to come back because of the trauma. Maybe with time it will somehow fade, but it’s impossible to ever completely forget that day."
Former hostage Maksim Kharkin: “They were killing people and smiling”
On October 7, Maksim Kharkin went with friends to the Supernova music festival, which was attacked by Hamas. Maksim was held hostage for two years:
“I had never been to Supernova before. It was a huge, very well-organized event, with all the necessary permits. There was police and internal security. We went there to enjoy ourselves and listen to music.
But at 6:27, a massive rocket attack began. That’s when I realized the war had started. The road was cut off, and the terrorists were already advancing. I ran into a field. At some point, a friend called me: ‘Max, where are you?’ I said I’d managed to get about 100 meters away. He asked, 'Max, come back and help me. I don’t know what to do.'
The shelling could already be heard from all sides. But they weren’t shooting directly at us yet – there had been no direct contact.
I heard my friend’s wife screaming into the phone: 'Max, help me, save me.' So I went back.
We decided to lie down in a ditch. The shelling was coming from all sides – from both sides of the road and from the direction of the party itself. The terrorists were advancing from two sides, calmly spraying everything with gunfire: rat-a-tat-tat-tat.
At some point, they reached us – and that was it. My friend managed to fire a shot. He had his service weapon, and he took one of them down, but he was immediately shot in the back.
They first shot at my head, but the bullet whistled over it. By then, I had basically given up hope.
I saw them killing everyone who was there. They were smiling – killing people and smiling. They let their victims scream out their pain, plead and cry. Then they shot them with a smile.
There was a young guy running around with a camera. I called him the “wedding photographer.” He walked around filming everything, enjoying himself.
You see how many of them there are — thirty here, another hundred there. And they’re in no hurry. Everything is fine, everything is great, it’s a celebration.
They tied my hands, pulled a stocking over my head, and took me to the Gaza Strip with another hostage. Every second could have been my last.
I decided I was already a dead man. They brought me to Gaza with my hands and feet tied and pushed me to the floor. I fell to my knees first, then they shoved me again and I fell face-first onto the floor. When I first fell to my knees, I realized that from that moment on, every second I was alive, every breath I took, was a gift.
“When I first fell to my knees, I realized that from that moment on, every second I was alive, every breath I took, was a gift.”
We were held in ordinary homes in the Gaza Strip. Apart from Hamas fighters, the only people we had contact with were the heads of the households. Their sons, boys around 15 to 17, carried machine guns and could casually transport grenades and ammunition in UNICEF bags.
If one of us did something wrong – for example, if they saw someone talking to another hostage, even whispering or communicating with their fingers – you could get a beating for that.
The house where I was held came under fire, and the upper floor was destroyed. After that, I was moved to an underground tunnel. I spent another year and four months there. Some tunnels are designed for people to live in. They can have tile, floors, and entire rooms — basically apartments. Ours was nothing like that. It was a transport tunnel. There were just concrete beams, about 20 centimeters wide and a little over a meter high. Then came a concrete arch of the same thickness, another beam, and another beam on the floor. That was it. The entire tunnel was built that way.
How did we use the toilet? I dug a hole, and that’s where I went.
At one point, there were six of us. We came down with every illness imaginable, including COVID. We never left the tunnel. Your condition gets to the point where you stand up and immediately start swaying. You can’t walk properly; you’re constantly staggering.
There was no light. The only light was a small LED bulb, if there was one. Sometimes there wasn’t. If they called you from one room to another and you didn’t have a flashlight, it was pitch-black. You couldn’t see anything, absolutely nothing.
We were fed infrequently, and it got worse as time went on. Especially during the last five months, we could easily go 27 to 30 hours without eating. Lunch was a tablespoon of some kind of sauce and half a pita. I weighed just 50 kilograms when I came out. When I entered the tunnel, I weighed 90 kilograms.
Hamas guards had a separate room for themselves in the tunnel. There was a core group that stayed there permanently, while others rotated in and out. They had a room like ours, only larger — with a satellite TV, a kitchen and food.
We’d get the shit beaten out of us, then they’d interrogate us, then we’d get the shit beaten out of us again. 'Who are you? Where are you from? What’s your mother’s name? Your father’s? What did you do in the army? Where did you come from? Why did you come here?' We had to make up some kind of half-true story.
Hamas fighters hardly ever spoke to the hostages. From time to time, they would tell us something demoralizing or offer food or other concessions in exchange for converting to Islam. Eventually, I converted to Islam, which let me wheedle a radio out of them — supposedly to listen to prayers recorded on a memory card. They had deliberately broken off the antenna, but the base was still there, along with a manual tuning dial.
I studied a little physics at the Suvorov military school. I understood that as long as electricity was running through the cables in the tunnel, you couldn’t pick up anything. But when the power was off, a cable could work as an antenna. Everyone told me, 'You’re crazy. What waves? What radio? You’re making this up.' We put it under the cable – and suddenly we had a signal!
There was no electricity in the wires from 5:30 p.m. until 9:30 a.m. That was when we listened to all sorts of things – stations from neighboring countries: Egypt, Syria, Lebanon. We quickly picked up the Israeli military station Galei Tsahal. That’s where we got our news and learned what was really happening.
I think I managed to pick up Vesti Moskvy once, or at least hear Russian being spoken. That was hugely important because I hadn’t spoken Russian with anyone for two years.
At the moment we were released, at 7:30 a.m., they lined us up and said that nothing was over yet. If anything went wrong, they would either kill us on the spot or, at best, send us back into the tunnel. From the start, I told myself I wouldn’t believe we were free until the door of the Red Cross armored Land Cruiser closed behind me.
When it did, I exhaled for the first time. But you’re still there, and they’re still all around you."
Vitaly Cheberdin, Israeli soldier with the 188th Armored Brigade: “The army had never done anything like this in Gaza”
In late October 2023, after three weeks of bombardment, the IDF launched a ground operation in the Gaza Strip. The stated goals of the operation were to destroy Hamas’s military and governing capabilities, return the hostages, and prevent further attacks on Israel.
During the operation in Gaza, tens of thousands of people were killed, and around 85% of buildings in the Strip were damaged or destroyed. The figures were cited by Nikolay Mladenov, the UN High Representative for the "Board of Peace," who is respected by both Israelis and Palestinians.
Israeli soldier Vitaly Cheberdin entered Gaza in December 2023 with the 188th Armored Brigade. According to him, the troops had initially been preparing for possible fighting in Lebanon, so the deployment south came as a surprise:
“The army had never done anything like this in Gaza. Before that, they had only entered small areas. It’s densely populated there, which makes fighting, especially with tanks, extremely difficult.
On the first day, we had to advance about 10 kilometers in our tanks and bring in several battalions so the security services could begin operating there. When we entered Gaza, I saw the sky glowing pink from the explosions. Hamas fighters started firing back. Something came flying in our direction.
We just kept moving forward, firing as we went – they shot at us, we shot back. I saw houses, movie theaters, cars, things exploding. It was like something out of a movie.
One of my unit’s main tasks was to search for Hamas weapons depots and tunnels. We mostly went to Hamas fighters’ homes looking for weapons. If we found anything – a weapons cache or other infrastructure – we blew it up on the spot.
There were also addresses where hostages were believed to be held. That was a priority for everyone, but honestly, we didn’t expect to find anyone. Whenever there was a small operation involving hostages, we dropped everything and focused entirely on it.
We didn’t want to kill anyone, but it happened. Once, we started entering a house, reacted to movement, and shot a woman. Everything was filled with smoke; the house was already on fire. There was also a dead girl inside, though it wasn’t clear what had killed her – a tank or infantry fire. Three girls were still alive, around 14 or 15 years old, along with an adult woman and two men. We took them all outside.
We gave the women food right away. The men were initially in their underwear. Obviously, that’s all they could wear when they came out. We then brought them blankets, and after some time handed them all over to the Red Cross. We fed the civilians and shared our food with them.
A man started coming out from somewhere. He was shot in the head. I don’t know by whom. He immediately fell backward, his brains blown out. His family came out behind him; they were spared.
“A man started coming out from somewhere, was shot in the head, and his family came out behind him – they were spared”
Civilians suffered mainly because Hamas put them in harm’s way. Hamas fighters don’t look like they do on TV, either. Most walk around in flip-flops and shorts, carrying a grenade launcher or a Kalashnikov. They often hide among civilians — it's guerrilla warfare.
Once, our unit spent the night in a girls’ school. I went into the teachers’ room and started looking at photographs from school parades – pictures of them supposedly destroying something resembling Israel, trampling on it, pretending to slit its throat. They’re steeped in hatred.
I still have a girl’s album that I took from one of the apartments. She draws beautifully, she has talent, but the pictures — she drew the Islamic Jihad symbol, terrorists, Yasser Arafat.
I’ll never forget this image: you’re standing in a building on high ground, with the whole city spread out below, and it’s burning — burning intensely. And you realize you’re part of all this, that you’re the reason for it.
COVID was going around there for a while. I felt sick, but I got through it relatively easily. My gunner, though, just collapsed. He was in the tank as we were attacking and advancing, lying unconscious in the back with a temperature close to 40°C. He couldn’t take part in anything and just rode along with us. We pressured the officer, and they took him back to Israel that same evening. He ended up in the hospital.
In total, I spent four months in Gaza. The first time, I came out more or less okay. But the second time, I had a completely dead look in my eyes. I didn’t feel like doing anything.
You drive into Israel and there’s so much light. We were like frightened idiots. A friend told me that when he got home, he walked into the room, went up to his mother, and asked, 'Can I turn on the light?'
The first day I got home, I couldn’t sleep because it was so quiet. The birds are singing here, while over there you had mortars pounding."

articles.title: High explosive payloads keep a human in the loop
articles.body:
Where a person sits in the decision depends on what the system is carrying, and anything with a high explosive payload will keep a human in the loop, a panel on autonomous mass heard at the Apex Europe conference in London on Wednesday.
Freddie Bradshaw, head of business development at the Estonian company Ark Robotics, said the use case has to come before the autonomy question, because the answer changes completely between a one-way strike vehicle and a resupply run.
He said: “We’re certainly seeing that it’s very important to have human in the loop when it comes to a one-way strike effector, for instance. If you’ve got a system that has a payload of high explosive, the chances are we aren’t going to allow AI to be controlling that, and we need to have some sort of human in the loop.”
Further back from the front the balance shifts, and that is where he sees autonomy earning its place, taking the cognitive burden off a commander and handing it to the system so that one person can manage a fleet.
Antony Quinn, the Europe director of Havoc, argued that the vocabulary needs tightening before the debate can go anywhere, since human in the loop and human on the loop get used interchangeably and mean different things. Adding waypoints and watching a vessel follow them round makes the operator the bottleneck, which defeats the point of mass in the first place.
Three things have to be right in his account before any of it works, the first is the human interface, which should use simple accessible language and let an operator give intent and supervise instead of constantly intervening or monitoring camera feeds. The second is trust, earned by designing, testing and assuring the system the way trust is extended to an officer commanding a tactical unit. The third is policy and doctrine, which he does not think needs reinventing.
He said: “There is a point at which the system, whatever it is, is trusted to the person or computer you have trained, with its boundaries and actions on, and doctrine already supports this. So yes, humans are critically important in or on the loop, but a lot of it is not that unfamiliar, actually.”
Mr Bradshaw made a related point about interfaces, saying his company works to ensure its own plugs into a number of command and control systems so it can be operated through NATO compliant architectures, and that it has to be easy enough to use that scaling is possible at all.
From the user’s side, Oleksii Krymeniuk, the chief unmanned systems officer of the 2nd Corps of Ukraine’s National Guard, gave the position a name. “I’m not a huge believer in full autonomy. I’m more a believer in something that could assist our guys in the staffs and on the ground and help them make faster and more efficient decisions,” he said.
What he wants next is one operator running many drones, which he was careful to distinguish from swarming. The arithmetic is what makes it matter, since a mission needing dozens of aircraft currently needs dozens of operators, and bringing that ratio down multiplies what a unit of fixed size can achieve. Mr Bradshaw agreed that ground autonomy has not arrived yet, saying there is still a way to go in the uncrewed ground vehicle domain.
Mike Wilmot, head of UK land at Helsing, came at it from the opposite direction, arguing that there are tasks where an automated process deserves more confidence than a person does, with air defence engagement the obvious case. He drew an ethical conclusion from that.
He said: “There isn’t just a financial expense of sending an F-35 across the forward line of enemy troops. There is also a potential human expense, and if we have that safety confidence in a platform to be able to deliver its task, then there does become an ethical consideration of why send a human pilot or a collection of human pilots when you could first send autonomous platforms.”
None of the four speakers argued for removing the person altogether, and the disagreement between them was about where the line falls, not whether there should be one. Mr Quinn’s closing advice to anybody buying this technology was that the decision making does not need to change as much as people fear, and that a degree of the caution around it is unjustified.

articles.title: Ukraine’s drone pilot calls it his proudest strike: cheap FPV drone detonating over two tons of explosives packed inside Russian mine-clearer
articles.body:
"Skipper", an FPV company commander in Ukraine's 413th Raid Unmanned Systems Regiment, has described destroying a Russian UR-77 mine-clearing vehicle with drones during the 2023 counteroffensive as the strike he is proudest of, according to Army TV.
The UR-77, nicknamed "Zmiy Horynych" after a fire-breathing serpent of Slavic folklore, carries a rocket-fired line charge to blow paths through minefields, as per Militarnyi. Each charge carries more than two tons of explosives, which is why a cheap FPV hit can trigger a blast far larger than the drone itself.
"It exploded so hard that I thought it was a small nuclear blast. There are more than two tons of plastic explosive inside, and when it went off after the second hit, it was something unbelievable," Skipper says.
Skipper joined the army at the start of the full-scale invasion and moved from infantry and aerial reconnaissance to commanding an FPV unit. His regiment now operates on the Zaporizhzhia front, where FPV drones conduct combat missions.
From sailing yachts to FPV drones
In civilian life, Skipper was a sailing instructor, and he says the sport partly helps in military work, especially his knowledge of navigation and radio communication. He is convinced that a technological edge can be one of the keys to victory.
He counts the UR-77 strike among his unit's early work, from a time when few Ukrainian units were using FPV drones at all, he says. The hit came during hard fighting in the counteroffensive, when his crews were among the first to work the FPV niche.
Russia turns a mine-clearer into a wrecking tool
The UR-77 was built in the 1970s for a different war, one of fast tank thrusts that needed enemy minefields cleared quickly. Its base rides on the chassis of the 2S1 Gvozdika self-propelled howitzer, and its charge can cut a lane six meters wide, with some anti-personnel mines detonated across a band up to 15 meters wide.
Modern combat changed that role. The classic mine-clearing use remains, but Russia now more often turns these machines on Ukrainian fortifications, using the line charge to flatten defenses rather than open a path.

articles.title: Iran threatens to block ‘illegal’ routes through Strait of Hormuz
articles.body:
Iran threatens to block ‘illegal’ routes through Strait of Hormuz
Iran has threatened to block what it calls “illegal” traffic through the Strait of Hormuz, saying it retains full control of the passage despite US claims to the contrary.
The waterway is one of the world’s most important energy routes, normally carrying around a fifth of global oil and liquefied natural gas shipments. Traffic through the strait has been severely disrupted since the US-Israeli war on Iran began in late February, driving up energy prices. Brent crude was trading at around $101 a barrel on Wednesday, compared with roughly $72 before the conflict.
Mohammad Reza Naqdi, a senior Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) commander and adviser to Iran’s Supreme Leader, said on Wednesday that several transit routes through the strait along Oman’s coast would soon be closed.
Naqdi said the routes had been created by blasting and damaging rocky passages and were being used by small boats to carry oil through the waterway before transferring it to tankers. He described the shipments as “smuggling” and argued that they were too limited to show that traffic through Hormuz was returning to normal.
”The Strait of Hormuz is closed, and the armed forces of the Islamic Republic of Iran have full control over it,” Naqdi said, adding that the restrictions would remain until Tehran’s “legitimate demands” were met.
Iran has previously offered to reopen the strait if Washington eases military pressure and lifts its blockade of Iranian ports.
US Secretary of State Marco Rubio offered a sharply different assessment on Wednesday, saying the strait is “open” and that Iran had “lost complete control” of Hormuz.
”There’s almost as much oil flowing out now as there was before this conflict began,” Rubio told reporters.
President Donald Trump has also said the US military is helping oil shipments pass through the strait, claiming that daily flows have risen above 20 million barrels. He has blamed the global diesel shortage primarily on Ukrainian strikes on Russian refineries rather than the Middle East conflict and has urged Ukraine’s Vladimir Zelensky to halt the attacks.
Regional crude exports have rebounded significantly. A seven-day moving average reached 18.3 million barrels per day on September 30, according to provisional Kpler data cited by Reuters. The figure includes oil shipped through routes other than Hormuz.
Security risks in the strait remain high. The Panamanian-flagged tanker On Peace was hit by a projectile near Oman on Tuesday, injuring 12 crew members, according to the Indian authorities. No group has claimed responsibility.

articles.title: Russia Steps Up Sabotage Against Danish Defense Companies — Danish Intelligence
articles.body:
A Danish intelligence official said Russia has launched sabotage operations against Danish companies that supply defense products to Ukraine.
Josefine Kristensen, lead analyst with the Danish Security and Intelligence Service (PET), made the statement during a domestic security conference in Copenhagen, Reuters reported.
Kristensen said the shift indicates a significant escalation in the hybrid warfare being waged by Moscow.
“What we saw in the spring was a lot of planning, but very little carried out; what we saw in early summer is that they started to carry out a lot more,” she said.
According to her, Russia concluded that its previous large-scale attacks “did not have the effect of deterring the Western (military alliance) NATO from supporting Ukraine.”
The PET representative said Moscow retains political control over the operations, but operational boldness is increasing.
She said Russia is now “trying to hit targets that have a direct impact on the front line.”
“That means weapons production,” Kristensen said.
She also said Russia is increasingly using untrained accomplices, including homeless people and drug addicts, who are recruited via Telegram and other social media platforms.
According to PET, recruitment usually begins with simple tasks such as reconnaissance or taking photographs and then escalates into actual sabotage operations.
“It could be anyone just looking for quick money. If the first person isn’t successful, they’ll throw another one at the problem until they succeed,” she added.
The sabotage operations are taking place in various EU countries. In September, unknown saboteurs in the Netherlands disrupted rail services.
