articles.title: Pentagon chief awards Presidential Unit Citation to USS Abraham Lincoln carrier strike group
articles.body:
Diyar Guldogan
07 October 2026•Update: 07 October 2026
US Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth praised the crew of the USS Abraham Lincoln carrier strike group on Wednesday for a "historic" combat deployment, as the aircraft carrier headed to San Diego following an extended mission in the Middle East.
"What the USS Abraham Lincoln carrier strike group did, no other carrier strike group has ever done," Hegseth told the crew.
Hegseth cited 10,000 sorties, 23,000 combat flight hours and nearly 4,000 combat sorties during the deployment. He said the group dropped 1.5 million pounds of ordnance on enemy targets.
The secretary said President Donald Trump asked him to personally thank the sailors and other personnel involved in the mission, including their role in the Epic Fury operation aimed at preventing Iran from obtaining a nuclear weapon.
He also praised the carrier strike group's role in a subsequent blockade, describing it as “impenetrable since day one.”
Hegseth highlighted the length and demands of the deployment, saying the crew spent 265 consecutive days without a port call. He said the deployment was extended twice after personnel believed they would be returning home.
“Two times extended when you thought you were going home, and we asked you to do more,” he said. “And you know what you did? You did more, and it wasn't easy.”
Hegseth said the carrier strike group played a central role in the administration's effort to prevent Iran from obtaining a nuclear weapon.
“I couldn't be more proud of what you executed in this historic mission to ensure Iran never gets a nuclear weapon,” he said. Iran “will never get a nuclear weapon.”
Hegseth announced that the carrier strike group would receive the Presidential Unit Citation, one of the military's highest unit awards.
“It is with great pride today that I would like to award to you the Presidential Unit Citation,” he said.

articles.title: U.S. Air Force shows Morocco the F-35A it reportedly wants
articles.body:
- U.S. Air Force F-35As flew with Moroccan F-16s on the opening day of the Marrakech Airshow, which runs Oct. 7-10.
- Morocco’s first new F-16 Block 72 flew on Oct. 6, and reports say Rabat has discussed buying F-35s, though no sale has been approved.
U.S. Air Force F-35A Lightning II stealth fighters flew alongside Moroccan F-16s on the opening day of the Marrakech Airshow, putting the jet in front of a country that has been reported to be interested in buying it and that already fields a growing list of American weapons.
The airshow runs Oct. 7-10 at a Royal Moroccan Air Force base in Marrakech. Lockheed Martin, which builds both aircraft, posted that Morocco’s F-16s and the U.S. Air Force F-35As took to the skies to open the four-day event. According to the U.S. Department of War, the F-35A flyby is the centerpiece of about 45 U.S. military personnel taking part. The fighters come from the 48th Fighter Wing at RAF Lakenheath in England, the largest U.S. fighter wing in Europe, which flies both F-35As and F-15E Strike Eagles.
The U.S. contingent also includes two aircraft on static display: an HC-130J Combat King II search-and-rescue plane from the Alaska Air National Guard’s 176th Wing at Joint Base Elmendorf-Richardson, and a KC-135 Stratotanker aerial refueling aircraft from the Utah National Guard’s 151st Wing. The Utah National Guard has been paired with Morocco since 2003 under the State Partnership Program, which links U.S. National Guard units with foreign militaries for regular training and exchanges.
“It is an honor to be at Marrakech ahead of the 250th anniversary of the U.S.-Moroccan Alliance,” said U.S. Air Force Brig. Gen. Matthew J. French, Air National Guard assistant to the commander of U.S. Air Forces in Europe and Air Forces Africa. “Hosted by the United States’ oldest Ally, this forum best illustrates our goal of establishing strong and enduring Allied and partner forces for an evolving security environment. It makes us stronger in both our individual and combined capacities.”
Morocco was the first country to recognize U.S. independence, in 1777, and Washington designated it a major non-NATO ally in 2004.
Morocco’s air force is about to receive a major upgrade of its own. On Oct. 6, Lockheed Martin said the first of 25 new F-16 Block 72 fighters built for Morocco had made its maiden flight in Greenville, South Carolina. The U.S. approved that sale, worth an estimated $3.8 billion, in 2019, along with a separate package of about $985 million to upgrade Morocco’s 23 existing F-16s to a similar standard.
Rabat has also been one of the steadier buyers of American ground equipment in Africa, including M1 Abrams tanks, AH-64E Apache attack helicopters and HIMARS rocket launchers. In 2024, the U.S. State Department approved the sale of 612 Javelin anti-tank missiles to Morocco for an estimated $260 million.
Morocco’s interest in the F-35 has surfaced repeatedly. Reports since 2025 have said Rabat was in talks for up to 32 of the stealth fighters. The U.S. government has not announced any approval of an F-35 sale to Morocco, and neither government has confirmed negotiations.
“The Marrakech Air Show is a world-class exhibition of aviation innovation and a powerful testament to the enduring, nearly 250-year friendship between the United States and the Kingdom of Morocco. For decades, our nations have flown side-by-side, from our vital pilot training pipelines to our complex joint operations. The United States remains deeply committed to standing with our Moroccan partners, delivering cutting-edge aerospace capabilities and working hand-in-hand to promote regional peace, stability, and shared prosperity across the African continent,” said Duke Buchan III, the U.S. ambassador to Morocco.

articles.title: Israel's long road to a Gaza without Palestinians
articles.body:
Breadcrumb
With or without 7 October: Israel's Gaza endgame was always ethnic cleansing
In April 2023, six months before the 7 October attacks, Israel’s Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu held a meeting with Yoav Gallant, his then defence minister, and Alon Davidi, the mayor of Sderot - an Israeli city built on top of the historic Palestinian village of Huj.
Gallant and Davidi casually joked about flattening Gaza to rebuild Jewish-only settlements on its ruins. “I would also like to build in Beit Hanoun (in Gaza), but I will settle for Sderot,” said Davidi. Gallant replied, “In order to build in Beit Hanoun, you first need to flatten the area there.”
A month earlier, Israel’s Minister of Settlements Orit Strook said explicitly, “I don't know how many years it will take...returning to Gaza will take a lot of sacrifices. Gaza is part of the land of Israel, and we will return to it one day.”
Strook was reiterating what the deputy head of Israel’s Knesset, Limor Son-Har Melech, said the same day. “Our task now is to return to the settlements in Gush Katif and rebuild them,” he said, in reference to Israeli settlements in Gaza that were evacuated in 2005.
Israel’s finance minister and de facto ruler of the occupied Palestinian territory, Bezalel Smotrich, had also promised on the eve of the Netanyahu government’s formation in December 2022 that Israel would “return” to rebuild Jewish settlements in Gaza.
Three years into Israel's war, these statements now sound like prophetic declarations of intent.
Beit Hanoun was levelled to the ground during the war, just as Gallant said. Earlier this year, Limor Son-Har Melech led a group of settlers deep inside Gaza, planting trees to mark the first step towards rebuilding settlements in the enclave. He bragged: “Gaza will be Jewish, because only in this way will we ensure victory.”
Israel Katz, meanwhile, Israel’s new defence minister, has formally announced intentions to start building settlements in Gaza.
That is why Israel's military rabbi Amichai Friedman described the month of October 2023 as “the happiest month of my life”. He added, “We're finally realising who we are. All of this land is ours. The entire land, including Gaza and Lebanon. Gush Katif is tiny compared to what we will get with God’s help to achieve... We will destroy everyone.”
An ambition decades in the making
Seven months before 7 October, Israel’s former defence minister and right-wing politician Moshe Yaalon sounded the alarm that Israel’s “Jewish supremacist” ministers, whose beliefs, he said, reflected “Mein Kampf in reverse”, wanted to provoke “the final war” of “Gog and Magog.”
Yaalon warned that Smotrich and Ben-Gvir would try to provoke Palestinians, through massacres, for instance, to use any Palestinian retaliation as a pretext for the 'final battle'.
As soon as Itamar Ben-Gvir became Israel’s security minister, he rushed, as Yaalon anticipated, to abuse Palestinian prisoners to ignite that war. Some of his first decisions were to ban pita bread for detainees, reduce their shower time to two minutes per day, overcrowd their cells, and let a Palestinian hunger striker, Khader Adnan, die in solitary confinement.
The cruelty meted out to Palestinian detainees is thought to have served as one of the core justifications, and strategic drivers, for Hamas leader Yahya Sinwar to launch the 7 October attacks on Israel.
But even without Hamas’s attack, the concept of ‘transfer’, or ethnic cleansing, has long been embedded in official Israeli policymaking.
“You shall continue to live like dogs, and whoever wishes may leave… It's possible that in five years, there will be 200,000 fewer people, and that's an enormous thing,” said Israel’s then defence minister Moshe Dayan shortly after the 1967 war.
The “live like dogs or leave” dichotomy was reiterated in 2017 by Smotrich in a manifesto Israeli pundits themselves described as “genocidal.” Smotrich gave Palestinians three options: submit to living as inferior subhumans, leave the land, or resist and get killed.
Israel has used this policy in Gaza since the 1948 Nakba. Even before it captured Gaza officially in 1967, the Israeli government sought to push for mass migration from the enclave through intimidation, bribery, periodic massacres, and destruction of vital infrastructure.
After Gaza fell under Israeli occupation, Israel used more force, coercion, destruction, intimidation, and bribery to empty Gaza.
When Israel imposed a blockade on Gaza in 2006, economic warfare and starvation were systematically imposed, punctuated by periodic “high-tech killing sprees” to inflict the maximum destruction possible in order to make the enclave uninhabitable and force its people out.
Before 7 October, about 10% of Gaza’s population (205,000 people) had already emigrated from the Strip since the blockade started. Half of that significant figure were people who left in the five years that preceded Hamas’s attack.
A senior Israeli official even bragged in 2019 that Tel Aviv was “actively pushing Palestinian emigration from Gaza.” The official said Israel was reaching out to Western and Middle Eastern countries to encourage accepting Gazan migrants and even offered to cover the costs of travel.
Israel’s focus on displacing Gaza’s population stems in part from the fact that the overwhelming majority of the Strip’s population are refugees displaced from villages in what is now Israel, leading it to view the population as a persistent potential source of insurgency.
Israel’s then defence minister Moshe Dayan said in 1956, “Why should we blame [Palestinians in Gaza] for their burning hatred for us? For eight years they have been dwelling in Gaza’s refugee camps, as before their eyes we have transformed the land and the villages in which they and their forefathers had dwelled into our own property.”
7 October gave Israel its opening
The 7 October attacks provided a powerful accelerant for Israel’s longstanding displacement of Palestinians in Gaza.
Almost immediately, Netanyahu called on Gazans to leave, while his government ordered the mass evacuation of northern Gaza. The assault also revived an older Israeli conception of the conflict as an unfinished war of national survival, with Netanyahu later explicitly invoking the 1948 War of Independence, or Nakba.
In the first days of Israel’s response, Tel Aviv, with US help, rushed to pressure neighbouring Arab countries to transfer the entire population of Gaza into the Sinai desert under the pretext of “temporary relocation until Hamas is defeated.”
When those countries refused, Israel pushed most of Gaza’s population towards Rafah at the Egyptian border in the hope of pushing them to cross into Sinai on their own. When that failed, Israel invaded Rafah and devastated the city, only to propose sending Palestinians back towards the area again - this time into a so-called “humanitarian city” that Israel’s own former prime minister Ehud Olmert described as a concentration camp.
Even after Israel signed President Donald Trump’s 20-point plan for a ceasefire - which included Hamas’s disarmament, the withdrawal of Israeli troops, and reconstruction - Israel promptly reneged on its commitments and continued to push for building the Rafah ‘humanitarian city’.
The push to empty, and resettle, Gaza
Since the ceasefire began, Israel’s Defence Minister, Israel Katz, has repeatedly emphasised that Tel Aviv’s long-term goal in Gaza remains its total ethnic cleansing.
“There is no real solution for Gaza in the end without this migration… I think there is no other solution for everyone’s good,” he said in September, despite Hamas agreeing to lay down its arms. Katz added that Israel remains “organised and prepared to get [Gazans] out – by sea, by air, by every way possible.”
Israel’s Security Minister Ben-Gvir presented a concrete plan in September for the ethnic cleansing of 1.86 million Palestinians in Gaza over the next 7 years, called “disengagement 710.”
Through this scheme, Israel would expel 250,000 Gazans in the first year, 1.11 million by the third year, and the entire population by 2034. During the genocide, more than 100,000 Palestinians have already left Gaza.
That is why, even in the “new Rafah” camp, Israel made clear it would not allow any permanent construction with concrete, but rather would only give the caged population temporary and portable shipping containers to live in, making clear those camps are a mere transit towards expulsion.
The Israeli defence minister made clear that all Israel now needs to “finish the job” in Gaza is a pretext. “When it becomes clear that Hamas is not fulfilling its commitment. Then we will get a green light to advance militarily, territorially, and in other areas as well,” he said.
The same applies to the West Bank, where Katz revealed on Tuesday that the Israeli army has been instructed to plan for a scenario of war with the Palestinian Authority (PA). Despite the PA being Israel’s peace partner and security subcontractor, Katz made clear that Israel is ready to replicate its ‘Gaza model’ in the West Bank.
Any war on the PA “would be short and forceful and would include the use of ground and air forces and special means, the elimination and expulsion of senior officials, the destruction of weapons, and the large-scale evacuation of residents and destruction of terror infrastructure inside the cities and in all refugee camps,” Katz said, referencing the Gaza and Lebanon “models”.
Katz’s threat to the PA is not limited to an Israeli retaliation against violent Palestinian attacks on settlers or soldiers. A “war scenario” would also be unleashed if Palestinians organise a popular uprising.
“There will not be an Intifada lasting years, as there was in the past, but rather a short and forceful war with a clear decision and a change in the reality,” he emphasised.
A political consensus on Palestinian subjugation
The upcoming Israeli election is one of the most heated and competitive in the country’s history. But the one thing that unites the Israeli ruling coalition with most opposition parties is the subjugation of Palestinians.
In 2024, the Israeli Knesset saw an unprecedented moment of bipartisanship in rejecting Palestinian statehood and self-determination. In February of that year, 99 Israeli members of Knesset from both the opposition and ruling coalition voted in favour of a resolution rejecting international recognition of Palestinian statehood. Only nine members opposed the resolution, all of whom were from Palestinian parties.
In June, another resolution passed with only the same nine members opposing it. This time, the resolution rejected Palestinian statehood in absolute terms, even if such statehood comes through negotiations and diplomacy.
In this election cycle, Israel’s former prime minister and opposition leader Naftali Bennet is campaigning on calling the Trump plan for Gaza “unworkable” and opposing the plan’s promise of returning the Palestinian Authority to the enclave.
Israel’s former defence minister Avigdor Lieberman is similarly campaigning on dismantling the PA and resuming military operations in Gaza. Israel’s former war minister and likely the next prime minister Gadi Eisenkot attacked the roadmap for decommissioning Hamas’s weapons in return for the Israeli military’s withdrawal and called it a “capitulation” to Trump “without achieving the war’s objectives.”
The 7 October attacks did not create this Israeli mainstream consensus. At most, it provided the cover of war to make it more flagrant and explicit.
Israel’s stated long-term goal in Gaza and the West Bank is the natural culmination of a settler-colonial project that was created on the premise of grabbing the “maximum land with a minimal number of Arabs.”
Palestinians have for decades been pushed by Israel into ever-shrinking confines with two options left to them: submission or departure.
The only substantial debate about this endgame in Israel’s election is about the pace and packaging of that expulsion and subjugation.
Muhammad Shehada is a Palestinian writer and analyst from Gaza and the EU Affairs Manager at Euro-Med Human Rights Monitor
Follow him on Twitter: @muhammadshehad2
Edited by Charlie Hoyle

articles.title: U.S. Navy moves bunker-busting Tomahawk toward production
articles.body:
- The U.S. Navy plans a sole-source contract with Raytheon for low-rate initial production of the JMEWS warhead for the Tomahawk Block Vb.
- The notice moves the warhead from development into production but does not disclose contract value, quantity or delivery schedule.
The U.S. Navy plans to award Raytheon a sole-source contract for low-rate initial production of the Joint Multiple Effects Warhead System, a new warhead that lets the Tomahawk cruise missile strike bunkers and other hardened targets, according to a notice Naval Air Systems Command posted on October 7.
The contract would move the warhead program out of its engineering and manufacturing development phase and into production for the Tomahawk Block Vb variant. The notice did not give a contract value, the number of warheads to be built or a delivery schedule.
The Navy’s Tomahawk program office at Patuxent River, Maryland, said it intends to negotiate only with Raytheon in Tucson, Arizona, the RTX business that has been the sole developer, designer and manufacturer of the Tomahawk since 1994. The Navy said RTX alone holds the current configuration and manufacturing data for the missile and is the only known source able to do the work on schedule without duplicating costs.
The notice is not a request for competing bids. Other companies may submit capability statements by 4 p.m. EDT on October 22, which the Navy said it will consider. The Navy also noted that Tomahawk data is export controlled and not available to foreign sources.
The warhead, known as JMEWS, combines blast-fragmentation and penetration effects in a single two-stage design. It is meant to give the Tomahawk more options against hardened and heavily defended targets such as bunkers, underground facilities and missile sites, as well as against targets spread over a wide area. The Block IV Tomahawk it builds on carries a 1,000-pound-class unitary warhead.
Raytheon won a $90.4 million contract for the warhead’s engineering and manufacturing development phase, the final stage of development before production.
The Block Vb missile is one of two new variants in the Navy’s Block V modernization, which recertifies existing Block IV Tomahawks with upgraded navigation and communications and extends their service life. The Navy received its first Block V missile in March 2021. The other variant, the Block Va Maritime Strike Tomahawk, adds a seeker so the missile can hit moving ships at sea.
The Pentagon’s weapons testing office reported in its fiscal 2023 annual report that the Navy had conducted JMEWS arena tests and planned to complete the warhead’s live-fire test campaign in the fourth quarter of fiscal 2026, which ended in September. The office has not yet published an assessment of the warhead’s lethality.
In 2022, the Navy’s Tomahawk program manager, Capt. John Red, said the JMEWS variant was expected to reach initial operational capability in 2027.

articles.title: "Putin himself will sit down at the negotiating table": Zelenskyy urged the US to open Starlink for Ukraine
articles.body:
"Putin himself will sit down at the negotiating table": Zelenskyy urged the US to open Starlink for Ukraine
Kyiv • UNN
Zelenskyy urged the US to open Starlink for Ukraine and strengthen its air defense. He believes that the necessary capabilities already exist.
President of Ukraine Volodymyr Zelenskyy called on the United States to help Ukraine protect its skies and provide the necessary Starlink capabilities. He said this in a comment to Ukrainian media, UNN reports.
Details
Open Starlink for Ukraine. You opened it when responding to Iran, didn’t you? Everything worked there. Israel had full control of the skies over Iran. So, when you need it, does it work?
Zelenskyy also said that China is nearing the creation of an alternative to Starlink, which it is providing to Russia.
I said frankly: give us [what we need], help us protect the skies and dominate there, and then Putin will sit down at the negotiating table
At the same time, the President of Ukraine expressed his conviction that the United States already has the necessary capabilities to provide such assistance.
We remind you
President of Ukraine Volodymyr Zelenskyy reported that today and tomorrow, October 8 and 9, there will be "important negotiations" with partners, from which a "concrete result" is expected regarding the strengthening of Ukraine’s defenses.

articles.title: Russia attacked Ukraine with 142 drones, more than half of them jet-powered — how many were shot down
articles.body:
Russia attacked Ukraine with 142 drones, more than half of them jet-powered — how many were shot down
Kyiv • UNN
On the night of October 8, Russia launched 142 drones at Ukraine, including 82 jet-powered Shaheds. Air defense shot down or suppressed 126 UAVs.
Russia attacked Ukraine with 142 drones during the night of October 8. A total of 126 of them were shot down or suppressed. UNN reports this, citing data from the Air Force of the Armed Forces of Ukraine.
What Russia launched and from where
According to the Air Force of the Armed Forces of Ukraine, during the night of October 8 (from 18:00 on October 7), the enemy attacked with 142 Shahed-type attack UAVs (82 of them jet-powered), Gerbera drones, and Parody-type decoy drones launched from the following directions: Oryol, Kursk, Shatalovo — Russia; the temporarily occupied territory of Donetsk; and the temporarily occupied territory of the Autonomous Republic of Crimea — Hvardiiske.
How the air defense performed
The air attack was repelled by aviation, anti-aircraft missile forces, electronic warfare units and unmanned systems units, and mobile fire groups of the Defense Forces of Ukraine.
According to preliminary data, as of 09:30, air defense forces had shot down/suppressed 126 enemy Shahed-type UAVs, Gerbera drones, and drones of other types
Hits by enemy air-attack weapons were recorded at 7 locations, as well as the سقوط of downed aircraft (debris) at 4 locations.
The attack is ongoing, with several enemy UAVs in the airspace.

articles.title: US reportedly places additional order for 1,320 Ukrainian FPV attack drones
articles.body:
US reportedly places additional order for 1,320 Ukrainian FPV attack drones
The US military has placed an additional order for 1,320 F10 strike FPV drones from Ukrainian company F-Drones.
Source: Ukrainian military news outlet Militarnyi, citing F-Drones
Details: The drones have been ordered as part of the Drone Dominance programme.
Drone Dominance is a US$1 billion US Department of Defense programme to procure small strike drones over the next two years.
By 2027, the US plans to procure more than 200,000 drones under the programme.
The Ukrainian company ranks second among participants in the first stage of the programme in terms of the size of its additional order.
The additional F10 order must be fulfilled by the end of November.
F-Drones expects to receive its Ukrainian export permit in time to fulfil the contract on schedule.
Militarnyi notes that F-Drones has sufficient production capacity to fulfil additional orders without affecting deliveries of drones to the front line.
The F10 became the first Ukrainian drone to receive official authorisation for export to the US.
The first batch of 2,000 drones ordered by the US military under the Drone Dominance programme was shipped to the Pentagon in July.
F-Drones is represented in the US market by UDD Tech Corp.
Background:
- Ukraine and the United States signed a statement of intent that lays the groundwork for an unprecedented defence partnership and allows Ukrainian drones to be exported to the US for military testing.
- Back in May, CBS News reported that the US and Ukrainian governments had prepared a draft memorandum outlining terms for a potential new defence agreement between the countries focusing on the field of drones.
- On 8 July, during the NATO summit in Ankara, US President Donald Trump said that the US would purchase drones from Ukraine.
- In July, Reuters reported that the Pentagon acknowledged the US was lagging behind Ukraine significantly in terms of drone production.
	
Your support on Patreon helps us keep the news free and accessible.

articles.title: Russian factory housing Yandex data centre attacked and catches fire – photos, video
articles.body:
Russian factory housing Yandex data centre attacked and catches fire – photos, video
A fire has broken out at the Sasta plant in Sasovo, Russia's Ryazan Oblast, where a data centre operated by Yandex DC is located and which is important to Russia's defence industry. Telegram channels have reported an attack on the plant.
Source: Astra, Exilenova+ and other Telegram channels
Details: Astra said its Open Source Intelligence (OSINT) analyst had established from footage filmed by eyewitnesses that the fire had broken out on the premises of the Sasta machine-tool plant. According to Wikimapia, the Yandex DC data centre is also located at the plant. Last month, data centre employees themselves demonstrated its equipment and explicitly stated that it was located in Sasovo, Ryazan Oblast.
The Sasta plant specialises in the production of CNC (computer numerical control) metalworking machines. The company's equipment is used in Russia's defence, aerospace, transport and heavy industries.
Astra explains that Sasta's importance to Russia's defence industry lies not in producing finished weapons, but in providing the manufacturing base, as its machines are needed to produce high-precision metal parts and components. Sasta previously supplied specialised machinery to State Corporation for Space Activities (Roscosmos) facilities.
The company is also subject to international sanctions imposed by Canada, Switzerland, the EU, the UK, Australia, New Zealand, the US and Japan.
Meanwhile, Exilenova+ reported that "the Sasta machine-tool plant in Sasovo, Ryazan Oblast, has been hit".
"Missiles or jet-powered UAVs have probably been used to strike Sasovo in Ryazan Oblast," Exilenova+ suggested.
In addition, a major outage occurred at Yandex following the attack on its data centre in Sasovo.
"Power supply disruptions" were recorded, making a wide range of Yandex Cloud infrastructure unavailable.
The problems affected computing capacity, networks, data storage, databases, Kubernetes containerised application management platforms, cloud services, AI, and security and monitoring systems.

articles.title: Gaza 3 years on: The unfinished fight for Palestinian workers
articles.body:
Breadcrumb
Gaza 3 years on: The unfinished fight for Palestinian workers
Three years after Israel began its genocide in Gaza, the fate of Palestinian workers detained after 7 October remains unclear, though their odyssey of humiliation, torture, and, on occasion, murder is beyond doubt and is mostly documented by their Israeli tormentors on social media and aired live by the far-right Minister of National Security Itamar Ben-Gvir.
Gazans who had crossed the Green Line desperate to earn a living, mostly in blue-collar jobs, were stripped of their permits, rounded up, and held without contact with lawyers or families. Their treatment should push one to wonder what international trade unions did when fellow workers in this part of the world were imprisoned and abused.
Israel closed the crossings and revoked Gazan workers’ permits, turning people previously authorised to work into supposed illegal residents. Thousands were detained in Israel and the occupied West Bank. On 3 November 2023, more than 3,000 were released into Gaza, where bombardment continued. Release offered no guarantee of safety.
Workers described, in testimonies published by Human Rights Watch in January 2024, beatings, electric shocks, humiliation, and deprivation of food and water. The rights watchdog also independently documented mass detention without contact with the outside world.
International allies
Warnings of the ongoing abuse were already coming out earlier. On 11 October 2023, the Palestinian Democracy and Workers’ Rights Centre denounced violence against Gazan workers. On 25 October, it demanded their immediate release and appealed to the international labour movement. The workers’ predicament was already being placed before their supposed international allies.
Their case cuts through the claim that Palestine is somehow outside a union’s remit. These Gazan workers had employers, wages, and families dependent on their earnings. Stripped of work permits, thrown in torture dungeons for weeks, should have triggered a global public outcry among trade unionists and industrial organisers everywhere.
Calling the subsequent response universal silence would be inaccurate. The International Trade Union Confederation’s 2024 Global Rights Index described thousands of workers held in illegal detention, denied basic rights and legal representation. It recorded reports of abuse and degrading conditions, alongside two deaths in custody. The world’s principal union confederation had publicly acknowledged the violations.
Australia’s Union Aid Abroad–APHEDA published Palestinian union allegations of torture deaths in January 2024. In March 2025, the International Labour Network of Solidarity and Struggle endorsed reports from the Arab Workers Union in Nazareth concerning disappeared Gazan workers, torture and deaths in detention. These were clear acts of solidarity, but circulating allegations is only the beginning.
On 27 September 2024, nine global unions filed a complaint with the International Labour Organisation detailing the draconian working conditions of more than 200,000 Palestinian workers in Israel. The nine organisations condemned “widespread wage theft due to the suspension of work permits and the unilateral termination of their contracts.”
Signatories included the ITUC, IndustriALL, Education International, Public Services International, UNI, and the international federations representing transport, construction, food workers and journalists. The OECD’s Trade Union Advisory Committee also joined. Its stated legal focus was wage protection; however, not accountability for torture.
The demands of Palestinian unions
While such a solidarity move is worth applauding, it still exposes a long-running problem of “economism” that has long marred the trade union movement.
What resources went toward locating missing workers, supporting survivors, securing independent investigations and pursuing those responsible? A complaint about stolen wages surely matters enormously to impoverished families. It cannot substitute for a “political” campaign against imprisonment, torture, military occupation and genocide.
Palestinian unions had also identified what their counterparts could do. Their 16 October 2023 appeal asked workers to refuse to manufacture or transport weapons for Israel, challenge complicit companies and pressure governments to stop military trade. This was an action plan for international unions. Were the latter ready to organise around those demands and protect members prepared to act?
The wider response to Gaza shows that stronger positions were possible. The World Federation of Trade Unions was calling for an end to genocide by October 2023. IndustriALL’s executive committee explicitly condemned the continuing genocide in May 2024 and urged affiliates to support boycott, divestment, and sanctions.
Education International’s 2024 congress demanded an end to arms transfers to Israel. These were formal positions of international organisations, not merely statements by dissident branches.
Other unions organised material support. In November 2023, the International Transport Workers’ Federation created a Palestine Solidarity Fund. Public Services International established its Gaza fund in March 2024. By August 2025, European Union federations were demanding sanctions, suspension of the EU–Israel Association Agreement, and an end to economic relations with Israeli settlements.
Influential national unions in several countries also took a firm position in solidarity with the Palestinians, sometimes aligning with their governments’ stated positions and sometimes opposing them.
South Africa’s teachers’ union SADTU explicitly condemned genocide in 2023. Ireland’s ICTU demanded economic sanctions, while Britain’s TUC called for ending arms licenses and suspending the trade agreement. Canada’s CUPE described the assault as genocide and supported Palestinian workers’ rights organising.
In July 2024, seven US unions demanded an immediate halt to military aid: UAW, UE, SEIU, the postal workers’ APWU, flight attendants’ AFA, painters’ IUPAT and National Education Association. Their demand confronted the material support sustaining Israel’s assault, even if a letter alone could not stop it.
Disrupting the deadly occupation machine
Workplace action offered another, certainly more effective, route. A trade union representing workers in 11 major Indian ports refused to handle weapons shipments for Israel. France’s CGT endorsed workers at Fos and Roissy who refused to facilitate arms deliveries. Such examples show where unions’ distinctive power lies: in their capacity to interrupt production and transport.
Italian unions took action to another level by organising a general strike explicitly in solidarity with Gaza. On 22 September 2025, USB and other grassroots unions organised a nationwide stoppage against the genocide, disrupting transport, schools and ports.
Following Israel’s interception of the Global Sumud Flotilla, CGIL and USB called another general strike on 3 October. According to CGIL, the stoppage disrupted major services, and more than two million people rallied across over 100 cities.
Such organising efforts developed across borders. Italy’s USB, Greece’s ENEDEP, the Basque union LAB, Turkey’s Liman-İş and Morocco’s ODT called a joint ports action for 6 February 2026, demanding an end to arms shipments feeding the genocide and a trade embargo on Israel. Their initiative connected solidarity with opposition to militarisation and the erosion of dockworkers’ conditions.
But other union leaders shamefully obstructed solidarity. In October 2023, the AFL-CIO intervened against a ceasefire resolution adopted by Washington state’s Thurston-Lewis-Mason labour council. The federation eventually, under pressure, called for a negotiated ceasefire on 8 February 2024.
Germany’s DGB declared solidarity with Israel after the Hamas attacks. Its position cannot fairly be reduced to unconditional approval of everything Israel subsequently did: a July 2025 resolution demanded an end to attacks on civilians and supported a ceasefire. Yet the same resolution sharply defended Histadrut against criticism within international union bodies.
The Histadrut, for its part, is hardly an ordinary “trade union.” It has been the backbone of the settler colonisation of Palestine from the start, and a major instrument of segregation and discrimination against Arab workers. The international labour movement should isolate, boycott, and deplatform it.
Union members everywhere need to hold their own leaders accountable for these decisions. Those who blocked solidarity or defended Israel’s actions should face a challenge from below, with their record on Gaza brought into branch meetings, congress debates, and leadership elections. Members can demand disclosure of their unions’ ties to Histadrut and organise to sever them.
The fight is far from over. Missing workers must be accounted for, survivors supported, stolen wages recovered, and those responsible for torture and deaths held accountable. These demands belong alongside the struggle to end the occupation and dismantle the structures that leave Palestinian workers dependent on those who dispossess and exploit them.
The strikes and port actions point toward what comes next: sustained organising to stop arms shipments, challenge complicit employers, and defend workers who face retaliation for taking action. Every solidarity resolution needs an organising plan behind it. Palestinian workers deserve a labour movement prepared to use its power, and a rank and file ready to act when its leaders refuse.
Hossam el-Hamalawy is an Egyptian scholar-activist in Germany, focusing on the military, policing, and labour.
Follow Hossam on X: @3arabawy

articles.title: Saudi Arabia strikes back after deadly Houthi attacks on Riyadh and airports
articles.body:
Explosions heard in Saudi capital Riyadh after Houthis' deadly attacks on airports
Several explosions were reported on Thursday in Saudi Arabia’s capital Riyadh amid ongoing fighting between the kingdom and Yemen's Houthis. A day earlier, three people were killed and 36 wounded in attacks on Abha and Riyadh’s King Khalid international airports claimed by the Iran-backed rebel group.
Several explosions echoed across the Saudi capital Riyadh on Thursday, AFP journalists heard, during the war between the kingdom and Houthi fighters in Yemen.
The Iran-backed group has claimed repeated attacks on Saudi Arabia in recent days.
On Wednesday, Saudi authorities said that three people were killed in attacks on two of the kingdom's international airports, including in the capital Riyadh, after Yemen's Houthis claimed to have fired on both transport hubs.
Read moreHouthis claim attacks on Riyadh airport as Saudi-led forces strike Yemen
The Iran-backed fighters earlier took responsibility for a flurry of attacks that included firing a ballistic missile at Riyadh's King Khalid International Airport as the conflict deepens with Saudi Arabia, which backs Yemen's government.
"On Tuesday and Wednesday... Abha International Airport and King Khalid International Airport were subjected to attacks targeting their facilities," the kingdom's civil aviation authority said in a statement.
An Egyptian and an Algerian national were killed at Abha airport and a Sudanese national was killed at the airport in Riyadh, the agency said, with 36 people wounded in the attacks.
The Saudi-led military coalition that backs pro-government forces in Yemen said on X that it "destroyed the ballistic missile launch platform" used in the attack on Riyadh.
To display this content from YouTube, you must enable advertisement tracking and audience measurement.
One of your browser extensions seems to be blocking the video player from loading. To watch this content, you may need to disable it on this site.
In a subsequent statement, the coalition directly blamed Houthi forces and said it would retaliate.
"The brutal attacks by the Terrorist Houthi Militia on civilian and civilian objects in the Kingdom, most recently targeting (the two airports) will not go unpunished," it said on X.
The coalition said as a result it struck and destroyed 82 "legitimate military targets", including Houthi mountain-based ballistic missile facilities, command-and-control centres, communication systems and Houthi gathering sites.
The Yemeni group, which controls most of the country's northwest, is battling for territory against the Saudi-backed forces after the civil war reignited in July and it captured swaths of coastal land.
The fighting has displaced more than 200,000 people within the country, the United Nations said Wednesday.
Yemen's internationally recognised government this week declared a major counter-offensive and claims to have pushed Houthi fighters out of strategic areas on the Red Sea and the port city of Mocha.
Read moreYemen's Iran-backed Houthi rebels seize strategic Red Sea port city of Mocha
But the Iran-backed Houthis say they are holding their territory, and military sources from both sides contacted by AFP have not reported any major changes on the ground.
Claims by the warring parties have been impossible to independently verify with the situation moving fast and access for journalists difficult.
Flight diverted
"Our armed forces have just targeted King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh with a ballistic missile. The strike was accurate, by God's grace, and led to a disruption of air traffic," Houthi military spokesman Yahya Saree said Wednesday on X.
The Saudi-led coalition said the missile was intercepted.
The Houthis also said they targeted a military supply convoy near the airport in Aden, the interim capital for Yemen's government.
The government's Saba news agency reported missiles and drones targeting that airport.
The agency cited transport authorities as saying one of the missiles landed near the runway minutes before the scheduled arrival of a flight from Cairo, which was forced to divert to Jeddah in Saudi Arabia.
Houthi drones and missiles also targeted Saudi Arabia's Abha airport and King Khalid Air Base in Khamis Mushait, spokesman Saree said, claiming they had "hit their targets accurately".
It is the second time this week Houthis claimed to have attacked Riyadh's main airport.
Read moreYemen's government declares counter-offensive as Houthis cut vital route to besieged city
'Terrified'
Saudi Arabia leads an international coalition fighting the Houthis since 2015, and is now trying to roll back the group's latest advance.
The coalition said Monday it was providing air support for the Yemeni government's counter-offensive.
After a four-year ceasefire, Yemen's civil war re-erupted in July. Last month the Houthis seized the entire western coastline along the Red Sea in the country's deadliest fighting in years.
New clashes Wednesday in Yemen's west left at least 62 combatants dead, including 37 Houthis, military sources from both camps told AFP.
Saba also reported the Houthis fired a missile at Taiz, a city held by government forces, wounding five civilians.
Read moreYemen's government declares counter-offensive as Houthis cut vital route to besieged city
"We went out into the street to check on the wounded and saw young civilians who had been hit. The Houthi shell landed in the middle of the street, right in an area crowded with civilians," resident Al-Fateh al-Eisaei told AFP.
Yemen's government has announced a goal of retaking all Houthi territory – home to most of the country's population, and much of it held for more than a decade.
The humanitarian crisis caused by the war has left most of the nation's population dependent on aid.
Mohammed, a 33-year-old charity worker who fled from Mocha to Aden, told AFP on Tuesday that "people there are terrified" of the Houthis.
(FRANCE 24 with AFP)

articles.title: Unexploded warhead of Russian missile found near Pryluky
articles.body:
Unexploded warhead of Russian missile found near Pryluky
According to Ukrinform, the Main Directorate of the National Police in Chernihiv region reported this.
"Today, police received information that missile debris had been found on the outskirts of Pryluky. During an inspection, police officers discovered parts of a Russian cruise missile in an open area. Its warhead was found several hundred meters from the site where the missile had fallen," the statement said.
Following all necessary safety precautions, specialists removed the missile warhead for transportation and subsequent destruction at a specialized training ground.
As Ukrinform reported, on the morning of October 7, Russian forces attacked Pryluky in Chernihiv region with cruise missiles. Two entrances of an apartment building were destroyed. At the time, 18 deaths and 55 injuries had been reported.

articles.title: Syria denies troops will be sent to Yemen
articles.body:
Breadcrumb
Syria denies troops will be sent to Yemen, while expressing support for Saudi Arabia
The Syrian Ministry of Defence has denied that any Syrian forces will take part in fighting Yemen, following reports that Damascus was considering providing military assistance to Saudi Arabia in its war against the Iran-backed Houthi group in Yemen.
A Syrian Defence Ministry source told The New Arab on Wednesday evening that “there is currently no movement of Syrian forces toward Yemen.” 
This was the first statement from the Syrian government following speculation that Damascus might participate in military operations alongside Saudi Arabia.
The source suggested that a discussion on the matter may have taken place between US President Donald Trump and President Ahmad al-Sharaa during the latter’s visit to the United States in September for the UN General Assembly.
The Foreign Media Department at Syria’s Ministry of Information also responded to what it described as “claims that Syria is joining the war in Yemen,” saying that Damascus’s position is “clear.” 
It said that Syria’s support for Saudi Arabia in confronting threats to its security and stability but also added that Syria’s regional policy is “based on stability, peace, and cooperation, not on opening new fronts”.
It stressed that “any military cooperation with partner countries will take place only through official channels and existing bilateral frameworks.”
On Tuesday, Syrian President Ahmed Al-Sharaa visited Saudi Arabia amid intense fighting in Yemen between Saudi-backed government forces and the Houthis, fuelling speculation about a possible Syrian role in Yemen.
He met with Saudi Crown Prince and de facto leader Mohammed bin Salman and footage broadcast by Syrian media showed Saudi Defence Minister Khalid bin Salman accompanying the Syrian president to his aircraft as he departed.
Axios, citing three US officials, reported that Saudi Arabia and Syria were discussing sending Syrian troops to Yemen to participate in the war against the Houthis. The report said the Sharaa was seriously considering the proposal but had not yet made a final decision.
There were also reports that Saudi Arabia wants to reinforce Yemeni government forces, who are internally divided and are considered less well trained than the Houthis.
A source told Axios that Syria could send between 10,000 and 20,000 troops to Yemen. 
There are reports that Saudi Arabia considers Syrian troops better trained and more experienced using Turkish drones than Yemeni government forces.
A Syrian diplomat said that while Damascus strongly supports Saudi Arabia in confronting Houthi attacks, its focus is on domestic priorities, especially recovery from Syria’s brutal 13-year civil war.
“If Saudi Arabia requests any military cooperation or exchange of expertise, it will take place exclusively through official channels and within the framework of bilateral agreements governing relations between our two brotherly countries,” the diplomat said.
Reuters reported that US officials were worried about a sectarian dimension to possible Syrian intervention in Yemen, and that Syria had previously rejected a US request to help fight Hezbollah in Lebanon for this reason.

articles.title: Ukraine strikes Yandex data center housing two of the company’s supercomputers
articles.body:
Ukraine strikes Yandex data center housing two of the company’s supercomputers
A Ukrainian drone attack started a fire at a Yandex data center in the town of Sasovo, Ryazan region. No one was injured, but the data center has completely halted operations.
Yandex has warned that some of its services may be unavailable, and users are already complaining about outages at Yandex. Problems are also reported to be affecting Yandex’s main service, Yandex Cloud, as well as the Yandex Disk and Yandex Documents services that depend on it. Outages are also hitting the websites of Cian, Russian Railways, and the administrations of several regions.
Shares of Yandex, one of Russia’s leading IT companies, fell more than 3% amid the strike, according to data from the Moscow Exchange.
The strike hit the grounds of the Sasta machine-tool plant. Ryazan region authorities did not name the plant, saying only that the roof of “one of the enterprises” caught fire after the Ukrainian attack.
Sasta manufactures pipe-threading machines, and its products are shipped for export and to machine-building plants across Russia. Sasta also provides a production base for defense enterprises, the independent Telegram channel Astra explains. The plant is on the sanctions lists of several Western countries.
Yandex’s data center has occupied part of Sasta’s former premises since 2014. In September, center employees showed off its equipment and said they work specifically in Sasovo, Ryazan region.
The Sasovo center houses two of Yandex’s three supercomputers, which are used to train neural networks: “Lyapunov” and “Chervonenkis.” Chervonenkis is the company’s most powerful supercomputer, the independent science-focused outlet T-invariant writes. In 2021, it ranked 19th in the world’s Top 500 supercomputer list. It later entered the second hundred of the rankings amid difficulties updating its infrastructure because of sanctions.
Yandex has not yet reported on the condition of the supercomputers after the strike. The third system, “Galushkin,” is located in Vladimir.
It is unclear whether the plant or the data center was the intended target. Ukraine has not officially commented on the strike.
The attack on Yandex’s data center came shortly after Russia began striking similar Ukrainian infrastructure. Since September 23, data centers belonging to at least eight companies have been damaged or destroyed, and Russian forces have attacked some of them more than once. The Russian Defense Ministry claimed the data centers “provide for the processing and transmission of intelligence data in the interests of the Ukrainian Armed Forces.”
Many see this as a continuation of Russia’s campaign to pressure Ukraine and its residents and destroy the Ukrainian economy. Russian forces have also struck bridges, gas stations, railroads, shopping centers, and warehouses. In recent weeks, the Russian military has been striking Kyiv almost around the clock.

articles.title: Russian Bombing Forces Tuaregs to Retreat from Kidal, Mali
articles.body:
The Azawad Liberation Front (ALF) announced the forced withdrawal of its forces from the city of Kidal in northern Mali.
The group’s spokesperson, Mohamed Elmaouloud Ramadane, announced the withdrawal in an official statement.
The decision was made following massive airstrikes by the ruling military junta and mercenaries from Russia’s Africa Corps, which destroyed most of the civilian infrastructure.
The Tuareg command stated that leaving the settlement was a temporary measure aimed at preserving its personnel and logistics.
The city of Kidal has been a key political and military center of the Tuareg movement since the start of the 2012 rebellion for Azawad’s independence, when rebels first drove the Malian army out of the city.
In 2013, as part of Operation Serval, French troops and a Chadian contingent entered the city, driving out radical groups and handing control to moderate Tuareg forces.
In May 2014, an attempt by the Malian army to storm Kidal ended in defeat, after which the city remained under the full control of the Tuareg alliance for years.
From 2015 to 2022, the status quo in the city remained largely unchanged: the UN’s MINUSMA mission was deployed there, while de facto control was exercised by local Tuareg forces.
In November 2023, Malian government forces, backed by Wagner Group mercenaries, managed to temporarily seize the city after a prolonged offensive.
The rebels later regained control of Kidal, launching active operations against government forces and defeating a Russian convoy near Tinzaouaten, which shifted the balance of forces in the war.
In July, Mali’s junta forces, together with the Africa Corps, regained control of the city of Anefis in the north of the country.
The city is located approximately 100 km from Kidal and holds significant strategic importance for controlling Mali’s northern regions.

articles.title: UK imposes new sanctions on Russia’s oil, shadow fleet, war supply chains
articles.body:
UK imposes new sanctions on Russia’s oil, shadow fleet, war supply chains
The UK Foreign Office said this in a statement, Ukrinform reports.
The sanctions target 38 legal entities and individuals. In particular, restrictions were imposed on Russian oil companies Zarubezhneft and INK Capital. The UK Foreign Office said Britain had become the first G7 country to impose sanctions on Russia’s four largest oil companies. The latest measures mean that UK sanctions now cover more than 90% of Russia’s oil production capacity.
In addition, 12 more oil tankers were added to the sanctions list, bringing the total number of vessels from Russia’s shadow fleet under UK sanctions to more than 600. According to the Foreign Office, these vessels are used to circumvent sanctions and transport Russian oil, including through deceptive practices and the use of false flags.
The Foreign Office noted that the new sanctions target not only vessels already at sea but also those facilitating the supply chain used to transport Russian oil around the world.
Another 17 legal entities and individuals were sanctioned for supplying Russia with so-called Common High Priority goods. These include machine tools, electronics and materials needed to manufacture ballistic missiles, drones and other military equipment. According to the UK Foreign Office, Russia obtains some of these goods through third countries. The ministry said it was identifying those involved and taking appropriate action against them.
The UK also imposed sanctions on three cryptocurrency exchanges, two payment platforms and a related individual suspected of helping Russia circumvent financial restrictions. According to the Foreign Office, two of these entities processed transactions through the A7 financial network, which is backed by the Kremlin. Last year, it reported processing more than $90 billion in transfers.
“The message is simple: if you help Russia fund or equip this war, you will face the consequences… By sanctioning these companies, we’re not only stemming the flow of Russian oil money, but cutting off the routes used to circumvent our sanctions regime by making it harder for major Russian oil companies to rebadge their oil under the name of an unsanctioned entity,” the UK Foreign Office said.
As reported by Ukrinform, on October 1, the United Kingdom announced a new sweeping package of sanctions against Russia aimed at weakening the Kremlin’s war budget, countering propaganda, and holding accountable those involved in the torture of Ukrainian civilians and the deportation of children.

articles.title: Air Force Mulls Adding a Missile Warning System to F-15EX
articles.body:
The Air Force is looking for ways to add an integrated missile warning system into the F-15EX Eagle II fighter for the first time.
The Air Force Life Cycle Management Center posted a sources sought notice Sept. 29 as part of a market research effort, looking for potential vendors for a missile launch and approach warning system that could be quickly installed on the F-15EX.
The system has to be able to alert the fighter’s aircrew about missile threats without distracting them with too many false alarms, the notice states. It also has to use the F-15EX’s six preexisting sensor locations already earmarked for missile warning, as well as the jet’s data cables, power cables and cooling capabilities. And it has to be able to be quickly and easily installed or removed in the field by Air Force maintainers, without requiring any changes to the aircraft itself aside from installing line replaceable units in the six sensor locations, per the notive.
The notice did not say how much such a system could cost or how long the contract could last, but said those details will be in line with what such work typically requires.
The Boeing-made F-15EX is a more advanced version of the F-15E Strike Eagle, with upgrades including fly-by-wire controls and a new electronic warfare system. But while the jets are built with the features necessary for a missile warning system, they do not actually come with that capability, even though other variants like Saudi Arabia’s F-15SA and Qatar’s F-15QA do.
The F-15EX does have the Eagle Passive Active Warning Survivability System, an advanced electronic warfare suite that can jam enemies’ radar systems and thus defend against radar-guided missiles. But a new missile warning system would help defend against infrared-guided vehicles.
Other Air Force fighters have missile warning systems that can detect infrared-guided threats—the F-35 has the AN/AAQ-37 Distributed Aperture System, built by Northrop Grumman, and the F-22 has the AN/AAR-56 Missile Launch Detection system.
Years ago, the F-15C was supposed to be equipped under the Common Missile Warning System, a joint program between the Army, Navy, and Air Force. But the Air Force dropped out of that program in 2000, according to a report from the Institute for Defense Analyses. The Common Missile Warning System eventually became the AN/AAR-57, built by BAE Systems. The F-15SA has the CMWS from BAE.
The threat of infrared-guided missiles was underscored during Operation Epic Fury, when an F-15E Strike Eagle, the EX’s predecessor, was downed over Iran in April. President Donald Trump said Iran used a shoulder-fired missile—often called a man-portable air defense system or MANPADS—to hit the fighter, and MANPADS often use infrared sensors.
While the Air Force is not committing to buying a new system, the request shows it is giving serious consideration to adding it at a time when the service’s plans for the F-15EX are rapidly expanding. Just this past April, the Air Force announced it was expanding its planned fleet size from 129 aircraft to 269.
AFLCMC wants potential respondents to say what military aircraft their missile warning systems are already approved on for operational use, whether the system is currently in active production, and how many months after the contract award could the companies start delivering the system, among other issues.
Companies have until Nov. 12 to submit unclassified white papers on their systems’ technical capabilities to the Air Force.

articles.title: South Korea test-flies its first home-grown hypersonic weapon
articles.body:
South Korea test-flies its first home-grown hypersonic weapon
South Korean President Lee Jae Myung hails the test as a major step in strengthening the country’s conventional defence capabilities
South Korea flight-tested on Thursday its first domestically developed hypersonic weapon, designed to fly at least five times the speed of sound and evade missile defence systems, bringing Seoul closer to what it says could be game-changing weapons capabilities.
There was no immediate response from North Korea, which last week tested its own hypersonic missile that landed in the waters near Japan.
South Korean President Lee Jae Myung attended the test, saying it was a major step in strengthening the country’s conventional defence capabilities, according to a statement. It did not elaborate where the test took place.
The statement said the weapon separated from its booster rocket at the planned altitude, then descended and manoeuvred both vertically and horizontally before hitting a test target. It said once developed, the weapon would be able to strike key targets by surprise in the “Korean peninsula theatre of operations”.

articles.title: Pentagon Adds 1,320 Ukrainian F10 Drones to Drone Dominance Order
articles.body:
The US military has ordered 1,320 more F10 strike drones from Ukraine’s F-Drones, extending the first commercial supply of Ukrainian-made combat drones to the Pentagon, Militarnyi reported.
F-Drones told the outlet the drones were ordered under Drone Dominance, a US Department of Defense program worth $1 billion. The program aims to buy small strike drones over the next two years, with plans to acquire more than 200,000 units by 2027.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
According to Militarnyi, the F10 was the first Ukrainian drone to receive official permission to be exported to the US. UDD Tech Corp represents F-Drones on the American market.
By the size of its additional order, F-Drones ranks second among participants in the program’s first phase, the company said. The new order follows a first batch of 2,000 F10 drones, which the US military ordered under the same program and was shipped to the Pentagon in July.
If delivered as planned, the two orders would bring a total of 3,320 drones.
F-Drones must deliver the new batch by the end of November, as the company expects to receive a Ukrainian export permit in time to meet that deadline.
F-Drones also told Militarnyi its production capacity allows it to fill the extra order without disrupting supplies to the front. According to F-Drones CEO Stanislav Khutor, Ukrainian defenders are receiving the company’s drones on time and in full.
In July, Ukraine’s State Export Control Service had issued the country’s first official permit for the export of finished combat drones.

articles.title: UK announces new round of Russia sanctions targeting financial services, 'shadow fleet'
articles.body:
Britain's foreign office on Thursday announced new sanctions targeting individuals and entities it said were involved in the production or transport of Russian oil, facilitating military manufacturing and circumventing financial services sanctions.
The package also included 12 oil tankers that Britain says operate as part of Russia's shadow fleet and help Moscow evade sanctions on oil exports.
It also included three crypto exchanges and two payment platforms that Britain suspects Russia uses to circumvent financial sanctions.
Britain said two of those entities sanctioned had processed and facilitated transactions with the A7 illicit finance network.
Additionally, it included seventeen entities and individuals involved in the supply of goods deemed by the UK, US and EU to be vital for the Russian war effort, including Russia-based importers of machine tools, electronics and materials used to produce missiles and drones.
Russia's embassy in London did not immediately respond to Reuters' request for comment.

articles.title: Sea drone vs. air drone: Ukraine’s Sargan-3000 turns anti-aircraft gunner
articles.body:
A Ukrainian Sargan-3000 sea drone shot down a Russian Shahed flying on a mesh radio network, Ukraine's Navy reported on 7 October. Ukrainian sea drones have downed Russian aircraft before, but with missiles. This one used a machine gun.
Russia has been hitting Odesa with air attacks that come in waves with short gaps between them. Guarding the sky over water is harder than over land. Since fall 2025, Russia has also used mesh radio networks to reroute Shaheds mid-flight and dodge Ukrainian air defenses. That leaves Ukraine needing more ways to meet these drones out at sea, before they reach its ports and coast.
A Shahed steered by radio
A mesh-network drone passes its control signals along a chain of radio relays, drone to drone and on to ground antennas. That lets a Russian operator steer it in flight.
In May, Serhii "Flash" Beskrestnov, then a Defense Ministry adviser, said only about 5% of Shaheds had got through in a recent Russian strike, and predicted that Russia would answer with jet-powered versions and strikes near the border. By July, Ukraine was testing jamming against mesh-controlled jet Shaheds, he said.
The Sargan-3000 fired its Protector remote weapon station, Militarnyi reported. The station is a remotely operated 12.7-mm (50-caliber) machine gun with electro-optical sights. The outlet added that the Sargan-3000 is designed for combat missions far from Ukraine's coast.
Built for the open sea
Ukraine's Navy took the Sargan-3000 into service in April 2026, according to Militarnyi. The drone boat has a combat radius of up to 1,600 km. It moves at 40–55 knots and carries up to 450 kg of payload.
In September, a Sargan-3000 sank a Russian uncrewed boat with machine-gun fire. Militarnyi called it the first battle between uncrewed sea platforms in history. Analyst H.I. Sutton wrote that the boat carried a Protector made by Norway's Kongsberg. That is the same weapon station named in the October shootdown. Sutton added that Russian attack sea drones work closely with Shaheds, which can relay the boats' mesh radio signals.
